20800-london-lectures-of-1907:
Sharp lines divide psychism from true spiritual growth in the London Lectures of 1907. The speaker wants each hearer free to choose which path to unfold within. Clear terms, he says, must come before any wise choice of that kind.

Annie Besant, the famed theosophist, gave lectures of this sort to London crowds. Her talks treat karma, rebirth, and the growth of the soul. Theosophy then drew seekers who found old churches too narrow. These lectures show its appeal in plain form: big claims, calm tones, and a promise that hidden laws can be grasped by study.
22905-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch looks back thirty thousand years in its issue of April 7, 1920, from volume 158. A weekly journal reports, the magazine notes, that the seas around England then stood at a higher level than at present. Nothing much can be done about the matter now, Punch concedes, but it deserves a mention all the same.

That deadpan manner fills the whole number. Jokes, verses, cartoons, and mock reports treat postwar Britain with weary good humor. The Great War had ended, and the magazine's readers were learning peacetime again. A single issue preserves that mood in amber. It also shows Punch's long-lived formula, topical, tidy, and determined to find the small absurdity in every large event.
23056-the-rendezvous-1907:
Ivan Turgenev paints a birch grove in The Rendezvous, his sketch dated 1907 in this translation. Birch leaves in the grove still hold their green, though it has paled with the season. Here and there stood a solitary young birch, all red or all golden. One should have seen how brightly these flushed in the sun, its rays gliding through branches washed by sparkling rain.

Inside that shining wood, a hunter waits and watches a meeting he was never meant to see. A peasant girl and a valet from the great house keep the rendezvous of the title, and class speaks in every gesture. The piece comes from Turgenev's Sportsman's Sketches, the book that quietly indicted serfdom. Nature gets the poetry, people get the truth.
23216-sac-au-dos-1907:
Joris-Karl Huysmans wrote Sac au Dos, a story of the war with Prussia, presented here in a 1907 edition. Its narrator admits he never understood why that butchery of armies was needed. He felt no call to kill others, and none to be killed by them.

Still, he is enrolled in the Seine's Garde Mobile and follows orders. He hunts up an outfit, visits the barber, and reports by seven in the evening to barracks on the Rue Lourcine. Huysmans tells war from inside one reluctant conscript, where duty is routine and the reasons for fighting stay blank.
23219-putois-1907:
Anatole France's Putois, presented in a 1907 edition, is a family tale passed down with care. A parent hands the story on so it will not die with the older generation. The teller's grandfather, Eloi Bergeret, was a man not amused by trifles, yet he set a high value on this piece.

Bergeret called it the Anatomy of Putois, after its central figure. He even said he preferred that anatomy, in some respects, to the anatomy of Quaresmeprenant, a giant from older French tales. France wraps a small household legend in mock learning, and lets family pride do much of the storytelling.
23222-the-fe-te-at-coqueville-1907:
Émile Zola's The Fête at Coqueville, presented in a 1907 edition, tells of a small coastal village and the family that founded it. Coqueville began with the Mahés. That family settled there and grew strong at the foot of the cliff. For a long time, they prospered.

The Mahés married among themselves for centuries, so that the village holds none but Mahés. Then, under Louis XIII, a man named Floche appeared. No one knew much about where he came from. Zola sets a closed, inbred village against one outsider, and lets that contrast drive the fête-day tale.
a-vanished-arcadia-being-some-account-of: A Vanished Arcadia, some account of the Jesuits in Paraguay 1607 to 1767, by R, b, cunninghame graham, the lost missions. This book preserves that history. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
abbott-behind-scenes-mediums-1907:
David Abbott lifts the veil on seer craft in Behind the Scenes with the Mediums, his book of 1907. Abbott was a stage mage in Omaha who spent years in dark rooms as a guest. He learned each trick from the in side: slate writes, rope ties that slip, forms made of gauze, and the code talk of mates hid in the crowd of guests.

He prints the whole craft in clear, wry prose. Fans of the faith cursed his name for it. Busters cite the book more than most. It is the best guide to the tricks of its age.
adams-education-henry-adams-1907:
Henry Adams, grandson and great-grandson of American presidents, wrote his life story in the third person, as if watching a student fail. First printed in a small private edition in 1907, the book reached the public after his death. It is now counted among the great American life stories.

Adams says his schooling left him unready for a world of banks, machines, and raw power. His famous chapters set the Virgin of the old cathedrals against the dynamo of the new factories. That contrast still frames how readers think about faith, force, and modern life.
alchemy-and-the-alchemists-giving-the-se: Alchemy and the Alchemists, giving the secret of the philosopher's stone, 1907. The stone's secret. This book preserves that work. It holds its historical place. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
arabian-nights-burton-1885-vol-07:
Volume seven of the Thousand Nights and a Night, in Burton's translation of 1885, continues the great cycle. Shahrazad's tales by now fill years of nights, and the king has children by his storyteller. The frame's danger has cooled into habit, wonder, and a kind of education for the throne.

Burton keeps his method steady: literal text, full verse, and notes that range from grammar to geography. Sailors, slaves, caliphs, and demons share the stage in turn. The Arabic book had grown for centuries by accretion, and Burton honors that layered growth. Readers step in anywhere, yet the long arc rewards those who persist. Volume seven is deep water, well stocked.
arxiv-2512-00207:
Language models store facts inside their multilayer perceptron layers, arranged like key-value pairs. Owen Dugan and co-authors, including Chris Ré, study how to construct efficient fact-storing perceptrons for transformers in 2025. Earlier work proposed explicit weight constructions for such storage.

Understanding the construction improves knowledge of how models hold factual information in their parameters. Efficient storage designs could make models smaller for the same knowledge, or reveal how to edit facts deliberately. The work sits between theory and practice, treating a trained network as engineered memory rather than a black box. Explicit constructions complement statistical arguments about what trained networks probably do. They also show how much memory a given set of facts requires.
arxiv-2512-00307:
Social networks carry signed ties: friendships pull nodes together, while hostility pushes them apart. Haobin Ke and co-authors study adversarial signed graph learning with differential privacy in 2025. Balance theory lets learning methods infer edge signs from multi-hop pairs of nodes.

Training on sensitive signed graphs raises privacy concerns, because model parameters may leak private link information. The authors combine adversarial training with privacy guarantees so embeddings preserve structure and sign without exposing relationships. The work matters for platforms that analyze trust and conflict while owing their users real confidentiality. Adversarial training hardens the embeddings against attempts to extract the hidden links. Signed graphs are also the natural language of trust networks and political blocs.
arxiv-2512-00507:
Glassy materials relax toward equilibrium with a stretched exponential curve that is awkward to analyze. Shuli Chen and co-authors study the inverse spectral problem for that relaxation in 2025, using a Prony series approximation. The stretched exponential has a singularity at the origin, which makes data analysis inconvenient.

The Prony series replaces it with a sum of simple exponentials, an approach tied to the extended Burgers model of viscoelasticity. The inverse problem asks which spectrum of relaxation times produced the observed data. Recovering that spectrum helps materials scientists connect a glass's behavior to its internal structure. Prony series are sums of exponentials, each with its own relaxation time.
arxiv-2512-00607:
Simulating a Turing machine raises a basic question: how much information must be stored to certify a moment of its run? Logan Nye studies the holographic geometry of deterministic computation in 2025. Standard simulations suggest a linear relationship between a run's duration and the storage needed.

Certifying, verifying, or regenerating the configuration at a given time are the tasks Nye measures. A holographic viewpoint, borrowed from physics, asks whether the run's history can be encoded on a smaller boundary-like structure. The question links computability theory to information geometry in an unusual way. The holographic phrasing borrows from physics, where bulk information lives on a boundary. Deterministic computation is the cleanest setting for such storage questions.
arxiv-2512-00707:
Inocent Calist and Minseok Kim wrote a 2025 paper on radio channel models for future wireless networks. As networks move from 5G toward 6G, models must stay smooth and physically sound across a wide band, from FR1 up through FR3. Gaps in knowledge are worst in the mid-range band now studied for new rules.

Their approach builds a frequency-continuous model for city macro and micro cells, anchored at a mid-band frequency. Macro cells cover wide areas, while micro cells serve small hotspots. A model that bridges the bands helps engineers plan 6G service that works across all of them, not just in pieces.
arxiv-2512-00807:
Yujie Lin, Jiayao Ma, Qingguo Hu, Derek Wong, and Jinsong Su study gender fairness in vision-language models in a 2025 paper. These models learn from huge image and text collections and inherit social biases from that data. Gender bias in how people are shown is a known problem.

Many fixes take a difference-unaware stance, treating every group exactly the same. The authors argue that this can backfire. Some settings need strict neutrality, while others hold real group-specific traits that should be preserved. Their difference-aware approach, BioPro, tries to tell those cases apart. Fairer models would avoid both erasing real differences and repeating stereotypes.
arxiv-2512-01107:
Sanjog Misra introduces the idea of a foundation prior in a 2025 paper. Large language models can generate highly informative responses to prompts about people, markets, and behavior. Interest is growing in using those synthetic outputs as data in empirical research and decision-making, as if they were survey responses.

Misra argues the outputs should not be treated as real observations. Instead, they are draws from a foundation prior, the prior predictive distribution induced by the model. That framing tells researchers how much weight such synthetic data deserves. Getting this right matters as firms begin to substitute model output for costly human data.
arxiv-2512-01307:
Hongyu Liu and Zhihui Liu ask if a random process can be rebuilt from its long-run pattern. Many systems drift and spread at once. Over time they settle into a steady spread of states. That steady spread can be measured in real tests.

The pair study the reverse task. Given just the steady spread, can the drift and spread terms be found? They check when the answer is one clear process and not many. A firm yes would let staff infer hidden rules of a system from long-run data alone, a gain for science and health work.
arxiv-2512-01407:
Alexandre Sac-Morane and co-authors model how cement hardens at tiny scales. As cement paste takes in water, its inner form shifts. That form sets how strong the final paste will be. Tracking the shift helps design mixes that last.

Their phase-field model tracks growth and melt of grains in the paste. It rests on the heat rules for those changes. The model forecasts both inner form and strength traits as cure goes on. Good forecasts can cut lab trials and guide greener mixes with less waste and lower carbon cost.
arxiv-2512-01507:
Daniel Armstrong and co-authors pull strategy tips from language models for chemistry. Planning a synthesis is more than picking valid steps. Good plans join parts in a smart order. They guard key groups and form rings at the right time. Most software misses that strategy layer.

Their method, SynthStrategy, asks a model to state its latent strategy. Those tips are then turned into code that planners can use. Coded tips make the strategy clear and reusable. The work aims to lift machine plans closer to how expert chemists think through a route.
arxiv-2512-01707:
Daeun Lee and co-authors build StreamGaze for streaming video sense with gaze. Streaming tools process each frame as it comes in. They must also guess user intent for uses like AR glasses. Past streaming tests score time reasoning alone. None score use of human gaze.

Their system uses gaze signals to guide temporal thought. Gaze tells the model where the user cares. Proactive answers can then arrive before a full query. Gaze-guided streaming could make AR aids feel less like tools and more like attentive partners. Benchmark design is part of the work, since gaze use in streaming video had no shared test before this system set one out.
arxiv-2512-01807:
Guillermo Diaz-Camacho and co-authors benchmark emulators for distributed quantum computing. Big quantum tasks need linked small processors, not one giant chip. Quantum links let nodes compute jointly. Emulators let teams test that vision before hardware matures.

Their benchmark scores emulator platforms on set tasks. Feasibility studies need such scores to pick tools. Emulators also expose where protocols break at scale. Fair benchmarks guide both software teams and hardware planners toward workable distributed designs. Emulator scores span speed and fidelity together, since a fast but loose emulator misleads protocol design as surely as a slow exact one.
arxiv-2512-01907:
Boron aluminum nitride is a candidate material for the next generation of electronic and light-based devices, thanks to its ultra-wide bandgap and heat tolerance. Cody L. Milne and Arunima K. Singh use first-principles calculations in 2025 to map how its energy bands line up with those of related materials.

Band alignment decides how easily charge flows across the junctions inside a device, so designers need these numbers before building anything. The authors cover both polar and nonpolar crystal orientations and compare the alloy against aluminum nitride and gallium nitride. Their results fill a gap that had left this promising alloy hard to engineer with confidence.
arxiv-2512-02107:
Partition functions count the states of a physical theory, and for four-dimensional supersymmetric gauge theories they hide surprising mathematical structure. Palash Singh's 2025 paper proves that a class of these generalized Schur partition functions equals a very different-looking object from two-dimensional conformal theory.

On the other side of the equality stand contour integrals of vector-valued modular forms, which arise in rational conformal field theories. Bridging the four-dimensional gauge theory and the two-dimensional forms lets each side borrow the other's tools. Such equivalences are the working machinery of modern mathematical physics, where dualities turn hard counts into easy ones.
arxiv-2512-02307:
In dynamical systems, a Gibbs measure describes where a system spends its time, weighted toward expanding directions. Vítor Gomes and Bruno Santiago prove in 2025 new rigidity results for the entropy of such measures in partially hyperbolic systems, where some directions expand, some contract, and some do neither.

They show that when such a measure admits an unstable Margulis family, a kind of evenly spread structure along the expanding direction, the unstable Jacobian data must be constant. Rigidity means soft assumptions force hard structure, narrowing what these systems can do. Results like this anchor the ergodic theory of chaotic systems, where entropy is a central fingerprint.
arxiv-2512-02507:
Huadi Qu studies repeating paths in maps that preserve area, a clean model of motion on a surface. Each periodic orbit, a path that returns to its start, carries two numbers of interest. One is its action, drawn from a global function; the other is its rotation number, which tracks winding.

Qu extends recent work by Machel Hutchings on such surface maps, called diffeomorphisms. The results prove that orbits exist with certain chosen action and rotation values. Results of this kind help mathematicians map out what motions a system allows, a question with roots in classical mechanics. Such paths are the beats to which the whole map keeps its time over long runs.
arxiv-2512-02907:
Justin Gruber and three co-authors propose boosting quantum light emission with acoustic graphene plasmons. Plasmons, ripples of electrons on a surface, can greatly speed how fast an emitter radiates. That speed up, the Purcell effect, helps single photon sources shine brighter and faster.

Acoustic graphene plasmons squeeze light into very small volumes near graphene. The team proposes tunable, giant Purcell enhancement for single photon, entangled photon, and multipolar emitters. Tunable bright sources are core parts for quantum communication and sensing, where every photon counts. Tuned boosts let one source serve more than one job, a thrift that counts when each photon takes time and coin to make and catch.
arxiv-2512-03107:
Language models can sound sure while saying things with no support. Mainak Singha calls those answers hallucinations and offers a way to catch them in this 2025 work. The risk is high in finance, where wrong facts can cost money.

His framework, ECLIPSE, treats a hallucination as a gap between a model's doubt and the proof at hand. It groups many sample answers to gauge doubt, and splits a score that shows how proof is used. The author reports a large drop in hallucination rates in tests. Safer checks could help banks use these models with more care. Reported gains aside, the core value lies in a check that runs before answers reach clients or traders.
arxiv-2512-03307:
Models for table data are getting a foundation-model upgrade. Matthew Peroni, Franck Le, and Vadim Sheinin study robust tabular foundation models in this 2025 work. These models aim to beat classic methods on structured data like spreadsheets and records.

A key finding is that such models can be pretrained entirely on synthetic data. That opens room to design data generators that build in good traits, like robustness. Strong table models matter for business, health, and science, where most data sit in rows and columns, not text or images. Synthetic pretraining also lets builders stress-test models on rare table patterns safely.
arxiv-2512-03407:
Materials near jamming behave like both solid and liquid. Kumpei Shiraishi and Hideyuki Mizuno study elastic fluctuations in jammed solids in this 2025 work. They look at how the shear modulus varies from sample to sample near the jamming transition.

The average modulus scales in ways that depend on the particle potential. The fluctuations, by contrast, follow a critical exponent that does not depend on the potential. That independence hints at a universal rule. It may guide design of foams, gels, and granular materials. Universal fluctuation exponents suggest a shared mechanism hides beneath differing particle models.
arxiv-2512-03507:
Old methods from India can make computing classes more open to all. Aalok Thakkar presents that teaching approach in this 2025 work. Lessons on methods in code often lack roots and lean on Europe alone, despite calls for fair, open teaching.

Thakkar brings ancient methods from India into core computer science courses. A study with mixed methods covered many students across four class sections. He reports that teaching with history raised student interest and skill in method-based thinking. It also gave students a wider view of where computing began. Students in the study came from four class sections in all.
arxiv-2512-03707:
Robots that work beside people sometimes need to touch them, as when handing over a small object. Sundas Rafat Mulkana and co-authors tackle that safety problem in a 2025 robotics preprint. Simply avoiding all collision is not enough for handovers, because the useful action itself involves gentle, deliberate contact.

Their framework, ContactRL, folds contact safety directly into the reward used during reinforcement learning, using measured force as feedback. The robot learns motion profiles that keep forces on the person low while still finishing the task. In simulation it broke safety limits rarely while succeeding in most trials. For real use, the learned policy is guarded by an energy-based safety shield. Tests on a UR3e arm across hundreds of handovers kept normal contact forces below ten newtons.
arxiv-2512-04107:
Judging an AI tutor by accuracy alone misses whether it respects learners, context, and ethics. Shi Ding and Brian Magerko propose a broader yardstick in a 2025 preprint. Their TEACH-AI framework evaluates generative AI helpers for education through ten parts, built from a wide literature synthesis.

The framework's full name spells out its ambition: trustworthy and effective AI classroom heuristics. It is deliberately independent of any single school subject and aligned with the stakeholders who live with these tools, from designers and developers to researchers and policymakers. Alongside it comes a practical checklist toolkit with measurable indicators. The authors argue that what counts as good AI in schools must be rethought through social, theoretical, and applied lenses together. They invite the community to design evaluations rewarding co-creation, inclusivity, and long-term human impact, not just test scores.
arxiv-2601-06707:
Jie Zhou and five co-authors grade how well large language models do books and accounts in 2026. Such models are changing how folks learn, think, and search in most fields. Firms now ask if they can trust them with pro work like accounts.

That trust is a key test for the shift to digital firms, they write. They set out what pro accounting thought is, as their grade's aim. Their grade rules come from traits of the data used to train GLM models. Accounts work turns on rules, norms, and calls made on set facts. A broad test of chat skill can not catch that depth of pro work. Their rules aim to gauge what those who keep books do each day. Firms that weigh AI help gain a yardstick tied to real practice.
arxiv-2601-07007:
Swapnil Kumar Singh ID and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers oscillatory freeze from inertial holographic dark energy. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. The authors study a generalized holographic dark energy model in which. The infrared cutoff depends on the Hubble parameter and its first two time derivatives.

The inclusion of the H ¨ H term introduces a finite relaxation timescale for the horizon degrees of freedom. Which can be interpreted as an effective entropic inertia of the holographic vacuum energy. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07107:
Meng Lu and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with MedVistaGym. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. Vision language models (VLMs) achieve strong performance on general image understanding but struggle to think with medical images.

Especially when performing multi-step reasoning through iterative visual interaction. Medical VLMs often rely on static visual embeddings and single-pass inference, preventing models from re-examining, verifying, or refining visual evidence during reasoning. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07207:
Zaheer Ahmad and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with thermodynamic driving force activated phonon scattering in InN. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. Defect related disorder during InN growth is a major challenge for making high performance electronic and optoelectronic devices.

This is partly because film quality is often described using reactor specific settings instead of general physical variables. The authors show that plasma assisted MOCVD growth of InN can be described using a single thermodynamic driving force coordinate. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07407:
H. Beuther and a large team wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on a dark cloud of gas called G28.37. The cloud is an infrared dark cloud, or IRDC. It sits where two flows of gas meet and press into each other. Such clouds are cold and dense. Stars form inside them in time.

A core task in star research is to learn how such clouds form. Gas in space is thin and in motion at most spots. Yet in some spots it piles up into thick clouds. The team maps the flow of gas at the edge of G28.37. They chart its speed, its shape, and how its parts move as one. Their work tests the view that a clash of flows built the cloud. It also shows what such a flow looks like up close.
arxiv-2601-07607:
Ze Li and colleagues question a hidden assumption in holography, the duality between gravity and quantum field theory. In that duality, a field theory's total energy comes from holographic renormalization. The result depends on the bulk geometry, but also on the choice of quantization scheme. Their 2026 preprint asks what that dependence does to famous bounds.

Several widely studied inequalities rest on this energy, including the AdS Penrose inequality. Others bound how fast entanglement entropy and complexity can grow. The authors point out that these results can hinge on the scheme chosen. They then pursue a quantization-scheme-independent notion of energy. The paper warns theorists to check which conclusions survive a change of scheme.
arxiv-2601-07707:
Debargha Banerjee and Srijan Das compute extension groups in a deep area of modern number theory. Their 2026 preprint works in the category of duals of p-adic Banach space representations of GL2 over the p-adic numbers. These representations arise from the p-adic local Langlands correspondence for generic Galois representations. The authors classify the extensions completely. Extensions describe how simple pieces can be glued into larger structures.

A complete classification gives the field a firm reference point. The p-adic Langlands program links Galois representations with representations of p-adic groups, and extension data test that link. Results here can feed later work on the structure of these representation categories. The paper is aimed at specialists in arithmetic geometry and representation theory. It is a classification result, meant to be used by other scholars.
arxiv-2601-07807:
Khyathi Komalan opens a two-part project that recasts quantum field theory in a doubled categorical language. Operator-algebraic algebraic quantum field theory assigns algebras of observables to regions of spacetime. Scholars routinely move between two kinds of structure there. Inclusions of regions give inclusions of algebras. Bimodules and intertwiners implement the standard constructions used to compare observables. Their 2026 preprint sets up the double categorical approach.

Double categories can hold objects, arrows, and arrows between arrows in one framework. That richness suits a theory with both inclusions and intertwiners. Part one lays the axiomatic groundwork for the project. Later parts can then state theorems inside the new language. The paper serves mathematical physicists working on the structure of quantum field theory. It aims to unify two viewpoints that are usually handled separately.
arxiv-2601-08007:
Frank V Kowalski sets two wave equations side by side through an interference thought test. The Schrödinger equation yields interference when a beamsplitter's path has a stretch faster than a particle's phase speed. The particle is free, has nonzero rest mass, and sits in a momentum eigenstate. Such an effect cannot occur for light waves. It also cannot occur for momentum eigenstates in the non-relativistic limit of the Klein-Gordon equation. His 2026 preprint lays out the mismatch.

The beamsplitter can never outrun the Klein-Gordon wave's phase speed, so the effect is gone there. Two equations that usually agree part ways in this setup. Such gaps probe the base of wave mechanics. They clarify what phase velocity means in each theory. The paper serves physicists interested in quantum theory's basic equations. It uses a concrete setup to expose a quiet clash between the two rules.
arxiv-2601-08107: Chengyang Gu, Yuxin Pan, Hui Xiong, and Yize Chen improve offline reinforcement learning under sparse rewards. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that offline learning trains policies from fixed datasets, avoiding risky online trials. Long tasks with rare rewards still defeat many methods. Goal-based and hierarchical methods split tasks and add intermediate rewards, but they often ignore time order among subgoals. They also lean on rough reward shaping, which yields weak policies. STO-RL uses language model guidance for subgoal time order to address both gaps.
arxiv-2601-08507: S. Banerjee and four co-authors estimate sulfuric acid vapor below the Venus cloud deck. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses data from the Akatsuki radio science experiment. The team reports new constraints on how the vapor is distributed with height. Their method refines radio occultation analysis by estimating the power spectral density of the received signal. That recovers both signal intensity and Doppler shift. Sulfuric acid drives Venus cloud chemistry, so its profile below the clouds tests models of the planet's harsh atmosphere.
arxiv-2601-08607: Luca Nils Philipp, Julian Luttig, and Roland Mitric study exciton annihilation in polaritonic systems. Their 2026 arXiv paper covers strong light-matter coupling that forms hybrid quasiparticles called polaritons. Tuning molecular photophysics this way has drawn wide interest, and energy transport is a hot target. Exciton-exciton annihilation is commonly used to quantify energy transfer in excitonic systems. It has recently been applied to transport dynamics in polaritonic systems too. The authors also cover exciton-photon annihilation, clarifying how these probes read out polariton motion.
arxiv-2601-09007:
Sven Wang gives fast ways to solve inverse tasks where the rule that links cause to data is not a straight line. Such tasks ask: what hid cause made the data we see. Score based picks lead to bumpy hills with many peaks. Slow chain search can take a vast time to cross those hills, so it fails in real use.

He gives picks that plug in a first guess, or fine a pick that fits a known law. Both can be run in set time bounds on a PC. He proves they stay close to truth as data grows. A reader who solves inverse tasks gets speed with proof, a pair that is oft hard to hold at once.
arxiv-2601-09207:
Bahar Khodabakhshian and seven co-authors mark the heart wall in beating heart videos with help from point tracks. Such videos come from sound scans of the heart. Marks guide checks of how the heart pumps. The wall is hard to mark: low shade gap, noise, and form that shifts by folk. Frame by frame tools miss how the wall moves in time.

The team tracks points on the wall through time and uses those tracks as a cue. Tracks hold firm when a lone frame is dim. That cue steers the mark to the true wall path. A reader in heart scans gets a time wise mark plan that may cut drift in long clips.
arxiv-2601-09407:
Fokke Heikamp and four co-authors audit the security of path-based traceability systems in supply chains. Their 2026 arXiv paper looks at systems that track a product from factory to shelf using RFID tags and connected sensors. Such tracking supports recalls and fights counterfeiting, tampering, and theft.

A system that records every step of a product's life also creates new attack surfaces. The authors carry out a systematic security analysis of how these path records can be abused or forged. Weak points matter because firms and regulators act on the records. The paper maps where the design needs stronger protection.
arxiv-2601-09807:
Mikhail Malkov and Immanuel Jebaraj revive an old idea for heating plasmas and pushing particles to high energy. Their 2026 arXiv paper reviews magnetic pumping, one of the earliest plasma heating mechanisms proposed. Its role in astrophysics, including particle acceleration, has yet to be fully appreciated.

Pumping works because a particle's sideways momentum grows as the magnetic field grows. The link is an adiabatic invariant: the squared sideways momentum divided by the field stays nearly constant. Repeated field swings can ratchet particles upward in energy. The authors trace the idea from plasma heating to cosmic acceleration sites.
arxiv-2601-10907:
Shalini Chakraborty reflects on networking in software engineering research. Building a network is central to a researcher's growth and visibility. Yet chances and capacity to network are unevenly spread and hard to spot. Networking is often treated as a personal skill. Chakraborty argues the picture is wider than that.

A researcher's workplace, culture, and environment shape motivation and, in turn, the networks that form. Her reflection draws lessons for scholars who feel shut out of the informal web of their field. It also speaks to institutions that want fairer access to conferences and collaborations. The piece runs at the CHASE workshop on cooperative and human aspects of software engineering.
arxiv-2601-11107:
Xiaoyue Liu, Walid Klibi, and Benoit Montreuil introduce a capacity planning problem for hyperconnected supply chains. Markets swing fast, and resource sustainability presses hard. Both push supply chains toward agile, distributed, dynamic designs. The Physical Internet initiative, which routes goods like data packets, motivates the model. Capacity itself becomes modular and mobile.

The Dynamic Stochastic Modular and Mobile Capacity Planning problem plans such capacity over a network of networks. Modules can move where demand flares. Stochastic planning hedges against swings rather than betting on one forecast. The work serves logisticians who design supply networks that bend with demand instead of breaking under it.
arxiv-2601-11207:
Marco Arazzi and Antonino Nocera probe a sneaky risk in neural networks in this preprint. Some trained nets hide backdoors set by an attacker in secret. Others leak facts about the data they were trained on. Both flaws can harm use in security-critical work.

Most checks for these flaws need things that may not be at hand. They may need a clean twin model for compare runs. They may need long retraining runs or strong guesses on the attack. The title points to LoRA, a light fine-tuning method, as an oracle. That hint frames the search for a check with fewer demands. The aim is a test labs can run on nets they did not train.
arxiv-2601-11307:
Julia Schwarzbeck, Robin Neuder, Marc Spath, and Alejandro Jimenez-Saez build smart surfaces. Their 2026 preprint deals with surfaces that steer millimeter waves. The surfaces work near 60 GHz, a high band for fast links. Liquid crystal layers let each element shift the wave's phase.

The design uses a delay line layout for the elements. That layout splits the phase layer from the radiating layer. The split gives wide bandwidth for the whole surface. Phase control runs past a full 360 degrees in smooth steps. The liquid crystal film is just 4.6 micrometers thin. Arrays scale up to 750 radiating elements in this work. Such surfaces could steer beams in future indoor networks.
arxiv-2601-11407:
Cel Thys, Rodney Martinez Alonso, and Sofie Pollin make wideband radios leaner. Their 2026 preprint uses channel autoencoders with Walsh-Hadamard interleaving. Wideband links need fast analog-to-digital conversion to work. Fast conversion eats power, a key cost in radios.

Walsh-Hadamard interleaving cuts that power in a neat way. An analog Walsh-Hadamard transform spreads the signal first. Slower, cheaper converters can then handle the spread parts. The team trains neural coded modulation end to end. The neural code adapts to the hardware on its own. No redesign of the algorithm is needed for the fit. The result points to wideband links with lower energy cost.
arxiv-2601-11707:
C. Deagan and Benjamin T. Montet look at how to map dark spots and bright patches on the surface of a star. Light curves alone leave key facts unclear, since quite unlike spots can give the same change in light. The pair ask what extra facts can come from a star's small shift in place as it spins.

They show that shifts in the light centre, made by spots that turn with the star, hold facts that light curves miss. Such shifts could show if spots sit more in the north or the south half of the star. New space work with very fine place checks may soon let this method add to star maps.
arxiv-2601-11907:
Prosenjit Chatterjee and ANK Zaman build a deep learning tool to spot flying objects and grade their threat. Skies now hold more planes, drones, and UAVs than in the past. Hand checks by staff do not scale and slow real replies.

Their model rests on EfficientNetB4, a known image network. It does two jobs at once: name the object class, and rate its threat level. A dual tool could help staff triage sky threats fast. The work weighs how well this single model does both jobs.  Fast calls could help crews act before a threat grows large.
arxiv-2601-12207:
Hector Hernandez-Hernandez and Gustavo Sanchez-Herrera study quantum backreaction in a Brans-Dicke cosmology of Bianchi type I. That model has unlike expansion rates in unlike directions. The Brans-Dicke frame adds a scalar field to gravity.

They use an effective Hamiltonian that holds mean values, quantum spreads, and cross terms between degrees of freedom. Those terms let quantum effects feed back on the expansion. The work shows how that feedback shapes early universe paths. It links quantum spread to cosmic form.  Cross terms are the part that lets back reaction act.  Mean values alone would miss that two way pull in the model.
arxiv-2601-12607:
Anurag Acharya and five co authors present a cloud based workflow where many AI agents do science together. Large language models are now common across scientific fields. On their own, though, they cannot run simulations or make complex chained decisions. Agent systems bridge that gap by calling external tools and resources.

A multi agent workflow splits a big task among specialized agents. The cloud setting gives those agents shared compute and data access. Together they can plan, run code, and weigh results in a loop. Such systems are gaining ground fast in labs and industry. The work shows one design for that pattern. It points to a future where routine science steps run with less human hand holding.
arxiv-2601-13107:
Carlos Franzreb, Arnab Das, Tim Polzehl, and Sebastian Moeller find a leak in a famed speech data set. Speaker hiding tools aim to mask who spoke, while they keep what was said. Tests of such tools lean hard on LibriSpeech, a set of book reads.

The leak is in the words, not the voice. Each speaker in the set read books that are quite distinct. So the words a person uses can give away who they are. Even a perfect voice mask cannot stop that leak. The find means past scores for voice hiding may look too good. Teams must test on data where word choice does not tag the speaker.
arxiv-2601-13307:
Z. Gelles, A. Chael, and E. Quataert model how black hole jets shine in polarized light when seen from the side. A prior paper in the series treated jets seen face on. Real jets are seen at a tilt, though. Tilt changes the pic in deep ways.

The team treats thin, still, symmetric jets at the scale of the light cylinder. Due to shape and fast motion tricks of light, the left and right sides of the jet do not match in polarized shine. The size of that mis match can tell the tilt and how fast the jet plasma speeds up. For hole watch teams, the marks give new reads on spin and jet launch.
arxiv-2601-13407:
Mengman Wei, Stanislav Listopad, and Qian Peng join survival models with a therapy knowledge graph to map opioid use disorder paths. The ill oft starts with a script opioid and then moves through birth, calm, and slip back stages. Big health file cohorts linked to rich survey data now let teams model risk stage by stage.

One such cohort is the All of Us program in the United States. The team pairs a survival model, which times each stage shift, with a graph of therapy facts. The graph states which cures link to which stage and risk. Joined, the two give a path map that is both timed and rich in care facts.
arxiv-2601-13507:
Anqi Zhao, Peng Ding, and Fan Li firm up two stage least squares for clustered data. In such data, lone reads nest in groups, like repeat reads on users or panel data on firms, trades, or zones. Such nests are the norm in firm research, not a rare flaw.

Two stage least squares is a stock tool when a cause is tied to its noise. Cluster nests bend its error reads if they are brushed aside. The team gives a form that owns the nest in its sums. For firm and social staff, a causal tool that fits their true data shape beats one that asks them to fake lone reads.
arxiv-2601-13907:
Cosmin-Iulian Irimia sets out a blockchain-based system for digital documents in a thesis from 2026. Paper-based document management has long faced issues of security, authenticity, and efficiency. Digital files still face forgery, loss, and unauthorized access. Irimia proposes a decentralized infrastructure to notarize, sign, and share files.

Blockchain records can prove a file existed and was not changed. Decentralized storage avoids a single point of failure or control. The thesis lays out the design for official document use. Such systems could cut fraud in contracts, diplomas, and permits. The plan fits files that must be kept for years. Courts, schools, and firms all need proof that a file is the true one.
arxiv-2601-14007:
Junyu Zhang and co-authors test if language models truly grasp abstract human values in 2026. A model might handle a value word as a mere statistical pattern. Or it might link the word to real events and choices. Their BACH-V framework splits conceptual understanding into three capacities.

One capacity interprets abstract concepts, and a second grounds them in concrete events. The third applies abstract principles to regulate concrete decisions. The names are Abstract-Abstract, Abstract-Concrete, and Concrete-Concrete. Testing each layer shows where a model's grasp of values breaks down. The split into three tests makes flaws in a model easy to spot. Each test can be run on its own with plain tasks.
arxiv-2601-14607:
Chaohua Liang and Jun Matsushima present a seismic learning method in this 2026 paper. Their framework, SeisBind, is a physics-aware multi-modal contrastive learning design. It aims to transform complex seismic wavefields into human-readable physical representations. Seismic data record how waves move through the earth, and they are hard to interpret directly.

The title spells out the method: physics-aware tri-modal representation binding via contrastive learning. Three modes of data are bound into one shared representation. Contrastive learning pulls matching views together and pushes others apart. Readers get a way to turn raw wavefields into physical terms that geophysicists can read and use.
arxiv-2601-15007:
M. S. Laad and Prosenjit Haldar study a sharp change in how a material conducts. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with the Falicov-Kimball model, the simplest model of fermions with strong interactions. The model hosts a quantum critical point tied to a smooth metal-insulator transition.

The critical behavior they find is anomalous, meaning it breaks the usual rules. The model is also known to match a model of a binary alloy with annealed disorder. The authors probe what makes this continuous transition act so strangely in three or more spatial dimensions.
arxiv-2601-15407:
Mitchell Woolley works on conformal field theory in a 2026 arXiv paper on reduced superblocks. The paper looks at mixed four-point correlators of half-BPS operators. These are basic building blocks used to probe how such theories behave. The study covers the most symmetric cases known. They are the three-dimensional theory with eight supercharges, the four-dimensional theory with four, and the six-dimensional theory with (2,0) symmetry.

The focus sits at next-to-next-to-extremality, a regime named in the title. Evidence in the abstract stays narrow and technical. It names the theories and the objects under study, and little more. Readers should expect a specialist math-physics paper. Its value lies in the shared treatment of all three maximal cases at once.
arxiv-2601-15607:
Lenworth Thomas, Tjaden Bridges, and Sarah Bergbreiter teach small drones to sniff out sources in a 2026 arXiv paper. After disasters, finding the source of pollutants or harmful particles matters fast. Plume tracking is the standard approach to that hunt. Small quadrotors could work near people and in tight spaces. Their size is also the problem. Gas sensors that fit them are often slow and insensitive.

The team takes a different route: follow the airflow itself. Their quadrotor uses a single flow sensor to seek the source. Moving air carries the plume's signature, and flow can be sensed quickly. A single cheap sensor keeps the drone light and simple. For search teams, a nimble source-seeker could shorten the time to find leaks and hazards.
arxiv-2601-16007:
Chak-Wing Mak and a large team benchmark physical reasoning in AI models in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their benchmark is PhysicsMind. It tests mechanics in both simulation and the real world. Foundation vision-language models and world models face the tasks. Physical reasoning means predicting how objects move and interact. Prediction is the second half of the title's charge. Models that caption well may still fail at forecasting a rolling or falling object.

Mechanics is a strict testmaster: answers are right or wrong by physics. Sim and real versions of tasks expose the reality gap. A model can ace rendered scenes yet stumble on true footage. Benchmarks of this kind guide builders of embodied AI. Robots need prediction that survives contact with the real world, not just with simulations.
arxiv-2601-16107:
Adithya Sineesh and Akshita Kamsali test deep nets for reading Raman light data. Their 2026 preprint deals with a lab method that reads stuff from how it scatters light. Deep nets now oft beat old chem maths on this task. But past tests were oft run alone, on one data set. They were also checked against weak or ill fit rival nets.

The pair run a fair test across open data sets. They pit deep nets against each other on shared terms. A shared test shows which nets truly lead and which lag. It also shows where scores drop on new data. The work gives labs a firm base to pick a net.
arxiv-2601-16507:
Junjie Shi and coauthors grow prompts for code agents from need texts. Their 2026 preprint, named REprompt, deals with code built with model help. Models now fill code, act as base for agents and aid free code work. Good prompts steer those acts to what users need. Hand prompts oft miss needs hid in long need texts.

Need led growth draws prompts from the need text steps. Drawn prompts tie each code ask to a clear need part. Ties cut drift of code from what was asked for. They also ease checks that code meets each need. The work joins need craft to code agent use.
arxiv-2601-16607:
Markus Kuba studies card guesses after one bent riffle shuffle. His 2026 preprint deals with a guess game with full feed back. A deck of n cards sits in known order at the start. One riffle shuffle then bends that order in a chance way. The bend rests on a chance p that is not one half.

The guesser learns each card as it is named in the game. Full feed back lets past calls guide next calls in the chain. Kuba sums the best guess path for that bent shuffle. Bent shuffles part from the fair case in sharp ways. The work is a pure chance game study.
arxiv-2601-16707:
Shengnan Hu and Yuanyuan Li study how mass moves best from place to place. Their 2026 preprint looks at shapes with dents, not smooth round forms. The source zone is a flat shape with straight sides. A cost map guides where mass should go. From that map, a height-like field sets the flow.

The team proves a sharp bound on that field's bends. The bound holds across the whole dented shape. It also holds for a wider class of shapes. Such bounds keep flow plans from wild swings. They aid tasks in image work, trade, and load spread.
arxiv-2601-16807:
Pratyay Ghosh and Ronny Thomale map odd magnet states on a leaf-like grid of atoms. The grid, named for the maple leaf, twists spin rules in rare ways. Spins can line up in bent, non-straight forms. Some forms break time-flip or mirror rules. Some break both, and some keep both. Their 2026 preprint sorts these forms by which rules they break.

Spin waves in each form split by spin aim in odd ways. The split shows at key points in the wave map. Such states could host new tech based on spin. The sort gives labs a guide for hunts in real crystals.
arxiv-2601-17107:
Qinkai Yu and a large team hide a mark in scan AI to prove who owns it. Fine scan tools cost dear tagged data to train. That cost makes the tools rich goods worth theft. Their 2026 preprint, StealthMark, plants a proof mark in such a tool. The mark is a backdoor keyed to doubt in the tool. It stays hid from plain use and tests.

Owners can call the mark forth to prove theft. Thieves can't spot or scrub it with ease. Such marks guard the worth of care AI work. They may curb theft of trained tools in health.
arxiv-2601-17207:
Maedeh Makki and four co-authors present NewPINNs, a learning frame for equations that rule physics. Standard physics-informed networks learn by punishing gaps in the equations. They also punish missed edge conditions through loss terms. NewPINNs takes a new path. It puts a classic solver right inside the training loop.

Learning goals then come from solver consistency. The network must agree with what the trusted solver gives. That link keeps training tied to known good math. It may cut the drift that loss-only training can allow. For engineers, the draw is clear. They gain fast neural models that still respect the solvers they already trust.
arxiv-2601-17407:
Prajwal Chauhan, Salah Eddine Choutri, and Saif Eddin Jabari present a lean neural operator for physics equations. Fast surrogate models stand in for costly solvers. They serve aerodynamics, porous media design, and flow control. Many current operators are heavy, with too many parameters. Heavy models train slowly and deploy poorly. The team's design uses dilated squeeze and excitation blocks.

Those blocks widen the view while keeping size in check. The aim is speed with care kept high. A light operator can run on modest hardware in real time. That opens live design loops that heavy models block. Engineers gain a tool that fits the pace of design work.
arxiv-2601-17807:
Sherjeel Shabih and a large team of co-authors build a living database for perovskite solar cell research. Their 2026 preprint starts from a clear problem. Papers now appear far faster than people can read and log them by hand. The top database for perovskite cells has not been updated since 2021, even as work in the field has grown fast.

A knowledge gap grows when records stall in that way. The team's answer is a database that updates itself as new work appears. Such a system can track results, materials, and methods across the whole field. Researchers gain a current map of what has been tried and what works. That map can save time and point to gaps worth filling.
arxiv-2601-17907:
Numan Halit Guldemir, Oluwafemi Olukoya, and Jesús Martínez-del-Rincón build a malware classifier that can adapt as threats change. Their 2026 preprint presents FARM, a frame for sorting Windows program files into malware families. Classifiers decay over time because malware shifts. New families appear, and old ones change their traits. The authors call this drift, and they split it into drift in inputs and drift in labels.

FARM is built to detect drift and adapt with only a few labeled examples. That few-shot skill matters because labeling new malware is slow and costly. A system that keeps up with drift stays useful far longer. The work targets security teams who must sort fresh threats each day.
arxiv-2601-18207:
James Burgess and co-authors train search agents that read scientific papers to answer questions. Their 2026 preprint presents PaperSearchQA. Search agents are language models that reason and query sources before they answer. Recent training rewards only the final answer, through reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. Most such agents practice on general questions. That leaves them weak for the technical search that science, engineering, and medicine demand.

The authors build a setting where agents search over scientific papers themselves. Training there should sharpen both the search steps and the reasoning. Reliable paper search could save experts hours of digging. The work extends a hot training method into the domain that needs it most.
arxiv-2601-18307:
Alberto Dinelli, Ludovic Dumoulin, and Karsten Kruse find string-like defects in a fluid that renews itself. Their 2026 preprint studies active matter with two kinds of order at once. Many living systems show such mixed order while their material turns over nonstop. The fluid in view is nematopolar: it has nematic alignment and polar direction together, plus renewal. In it, the authors find stable topological strings. Each string joins two nematic point defects by a defect line in the polar field.

Stable strings in a renewing fluid are a surprise worth study. They may model structures in tissues and cell layers. The work joins topology with the physics of living matter.
arxiv-2601-18607:
A review takes stock of how black holes eat, and how the meal drives jets and winds. A black hole is a plain thing on its own, set by its mass and its spin. We see it by the stuff it pulls in. The rate of that pull is a third key fact that shapes all we see. The review pulls data from small holes in our galaxy and from huge ones in far cores.

At a key rate, the meal changes form. A bright, thin disc gives way to a hot, thick flow. That swap flips the light of the hole and the strength of its jets and winds. The review shows how one frame can hold both small and huge holes. A shared frame helps staff read new data from each kind with the same eyes. It also sets what the next round of sky shots should test.
arxiv-2601-19007:
Emily C. Ehrhardt and Felipe Tobar speed up a workhorse method for learning from data. Gaussian processes give not just a guess but a measure of doubt, yet training them is slow on big data. The math rests on a matrix that links each pair of points, and for a common smooth kernel, many far off entries sit near zero.

The pair cut those near zero entries away, leaving a banded matrix that is far cheaper to flip and weigh. That cut makes the likelihood, the score used in training, much faster to compute. Faster training opens Gaussian processes to larger data sets where their doubt estimates are most prized.
arxiv-2601-19107:
Vijay Janapa Reddi teaches machine learning from the hardware up, in a course tool called Tiny Torch. Students often learn the algorithms of the field without ever seeing the systems that run them. They study gradient descent without measuring memory, and attention without feeling how its cost grows with input size.

Tiny Torch has students build the systems from first principles, so each cost is measured, not just stated. They learn, for instance, why a common optimizer needs three times the memory of a simpler one. Engineers who know both the math and the machine write models that are cheaper to run.
arxiv-2601-19207:
Matthew Britton, Sasha Pak, and Alex Potanin make Rust code restructuring safer with proofs that nothing changed. Refactoring tools are daily equipment, and pulling a block of code into its own function is among the most used moves. Rust's ownership and borrowing rules make that move far harder to automate safely.

Their work extends the REM toolchain with a new way to prove the old and new code are equivalent. A proof, not just tests, backs each automated move. For a language that sells safety, a refactoring tool with proofs fits the culture and the need.
arxiv-2601-19307:
Vincent Bansaye and three co-authors turn a cell level model of blood making into smooth equations. Blood is made in stages: stem cells, immature cells, then mature cells, with growth and change at each step. Their stochastic model tracks three cell types across many immature compartments.

As the number of compartments grows without bound, they derive a hydrodynamic limit: a system of partial differential equations with boundary conditions. The result treats blood making as a continuum. Such limits let medical modelers use fast smooth math where a cell by cell simulation would drown in detail.
arxiv-2601-19707:
Yunyue Wei, Chenhui Zuo, and Yanan Sui work on controlling systems with many moving parts. Robots and biological systems can have huge state and action spaces. Exploring those spaces well is essential, yet standard exploration in reinforcement learning is undirected. Its quality falls sharply as the action space grows.

Many methods shrink the space first, but that limits what the policy can express. The authors propose exploration guided by value estimates, steered through a flow-based method. Guidance should focus trials where they teach the most. Keeping the full action space preserves the system's flexibility. The work targets high-dimensional control in robotics and biology, where random flailing learns almost nothing.
arxiv-2601-20107:
Zhuchenyang Liu, Ziyu Hu, Yao Zhang, and Yu Xiao work on visual document retrieval, where a system finds the right page from a query. New vision-language models such as ColPali match queries to fine detail on each page. The cost is a very large index, since each page is stored as many vectors.

The authors propose a pruning method that keeps the middle structure of a page and drops the rest. Earlier pruning tools cut index size a lot but failed at very high compression rates. A smaller index that still finds the right pages would make visual search cheaper to run at scale.
arxiv-2601-20307:
Xinyu Li and eleven colleagues study how to predict post-click gross merchandise volume for online ads. Ranking models for ads once aimed at rates, such as the chance of a conversion. The objectives have shifted toward direct business value: the money value of what a user buys after clicking.

The authors present a benchmark, insights, and methods for this prediction task, with attention to delayed feedback, since purchases can land long after the click. Predicting value rather than clicks helps platforms price and place ads by real return. It also aligns the model's goal with the merchant's actual revenue.
arxiv-2601-20507:
Philipp Mao, Li Shi, Marcel Busch, and Mathias Payer present TÄMU. It emulates trusted applications at the interface where they meet the outside world. Phones rely on trusted execution environments to run security-critical code and guard secrets. That code is split into components called trusted applications.

A flaw in one trusted application can compromise the whole environment. TÄMU emulates these components at the GlobalPlatform API layer, which makes them testable outside real hardware. Emulation at scale would let security teams hunt for bugs in the most guarded code on a phone before attackers do.
arxiv-2601-20907:
L. Bégué-Guillou and a large team of co-authors report on a new detector array for nuclear physics. Their 2026 paper describes PISTA, the Particle-Identification Silicon-Telescope Array. It is built for high-resolution studies of fission. The fission is induced by multi-nucleon transfer in inverse kinematics. The array works alongside VAMOS++, a magnetic spectrometer at the GANIL facility in France.

PISTA has eight trapezoidal silicon telescopes. They are arranged in a corolla, or flower-like, configuration. Each telescope pairs layers to identify particles by their energy loss. The paper reports the array's performance in this coupled setup. Sharp particle identification lets physicists sort the products of rare reactions. The work supports studies of how heavy nuclei split and form.
arxiv-2601-21507:
Ivan Amelio, Quentin Ficheux, and Nathan Goldman explore fluxonium circuits as three-level quantum systems. Fluxonium is a superconducting circuit first proposed for long-lived quantum bits. Each unit can also serve as a qutrit, holding three states instead of two.

An outside magnetic flux tunes the level spacing and the links between states. The authors show how arrays of these qutrits could run quantum simulations. Three-level units pack more into each device and can mimic richer physics per site. The work maps a path from proven hardware toward larger simulation tasks.
arxiv-2601-21807:
Yuma Nakamura and co-authors try to turn a weakness of physical computing into a strength. Physical computing uses real materials and devices to compute, saving the energy that digital chips burn. But physical systems are noisy, and their fluctuations usually hurt performance.

The team proposes ensemble reservoir computing, which averages the outputs of many copies of a physical system spread across space. Averaging can cancel random noise while keeping the useful signal. Their 2026 preprint sets out this framework for physical systems in general. If noise can be averaged away reliably, cheap and low-power physical hardware could take on sensing and prediction tasks that now need power-hungry digital processors.
arxiv-2601-22007:
Sandeep Aashish and Md Saif rescue a class of gravity theories from a mathematical pathology. Some models where Lorentz symmetry breaks spontaneously, built on antisymmetric tensor fields, develop singular Hamiltonians on their vacuum states. Those singularities create problems that cannot be resolved, making the theories unfit for cosmology.

The authors borrow a trick inspired by the Stückelberg method, which restores broken symmetries by adding helper fields. They introduce an auxiliary vector field that removes the singularity. Their 2026 preprint shows the fix works for these antisymmetric tensor models. Keeping such theories healthy matters because Lorentz violation is one of the few windows where quantum gravity effects might show up in observations.
arxiv-2601-22207:
J. W. Moffat compares a modified gravity theory with the standard cosmology, probe by probe. STVG-MOG, a scalar-tensor-vector theory of gravity, aims to explain cosmic phenomena without dark matter. Moffat shows it is observationally equivalent to the standard Lambda CDM model for all probes that depend on isotropic, linear gravitational dynamics.

That equivalence covers galaxy rotation curves, cluster lensing, the matter power spectrum, and baryon acoustic oscillations, among others. The theories part ways, he argues, in large-scale anisotropic cosmology, where the universe's direction-dependent behavior could tell them apart. His 2026 preprint thus points observers to the one arena where this long-running contest can actually be decided.
arxiv-2601-22307:
Simon Kuang and Xinfan Lin close a long gap in how to track a signal's spread through a deep network. Their 2026 preprint follows the mean and covariance of a Gaussian input through residual layers, step by step. Moment matching of this kind gives a fast stand-in for costly sampling.

They derive exact forms for key activation shapes, with the step and ReLU forms as limits of a smooth one. Exact forms end years of patchwork guesses. They can speed tests of network doubt and robustness. The work is a firm math win for deep learning theory.
arxiv-2601-22407:
Marc Raventós-Tato and a large team map, at the nanoscale, how a tough steel changes phase under load. Third-generation high-strength steels gain their power from these tiny shifts. Their 2026 preprint uses a linked microscope method to track crystal form, grain angle, and phase spread at once.

The maps reach a scale of tens of atoms' width. They show how chemistry and crystal shape move together as the steel works. That joint view has long been hard to get. It can guide the design of car steels that are both light and safe. The work is a tool win as much as a steel win.
arxiv-2601-22707:
Ritesh Bhadana predicts voltage droop on a chip early, with a convolutional stand-in for costly physics tools. IR-drop, as the droop is called, can slow a chip, wear it out, or break it. His 2026 preprint notes that sign-off tools are exact but slow, and need a near-final layout.

A CNN surrogate can flag droop while the design is still young and cheap to change. Early flags save respins, which cost firms dearly. The work fits the push for AI in chip design. It trades a little exactness for much speed. That trade, early, is wise.
arxiv-2601-23007:
Francesco Campi and four co-authors calibrate object detectors for microscopy using disagreement among experts. Detectors find cells and other structures well, but their confidence scores often do not match reality. That mismatch limits trust in biomedical use, where stakes are high.

The team trains separate models on each expert's labels, then merges their predictions to mimic consensus. Where experts disagree, the merged model learns to be less sure. Honest confidence helps biologists decide which automated counts need a human second look. Consensus-style aggregation turns expert disagreement into useful signal, instead of treating one rater's labels as unquestioned truth.
arxiv-2601-23107:
Ilir Tahiraj, Peter Wittal, and Markus Lienkamp detect when a car's LiDAR sensor drifts out of alignment. Correct calibration against the vehicle is essential for safe self-driving. Even small angular errors in a laser scanner can become safety-critical on the road.

Most methods fix errors between sensors, not the single sensor fault that starts them. Their FlowCalib uses scene flows, the motion of points between scans, to spot vehicle-relative misalignment. Catching drift early lets cars flag themselves for service before perception degrades. Scene flows give the detection signal, comparing how points move between scans against how a correctly mounted sensor should see them.
arxiv-2601-23207:
Graph neural networks learn from data arranged as networks of nodes and edges. Muhammad Fetrat Qharabagh, Artur Back de Luca, and George Giapitzakis ask whether such networks can learn to run graph algorithms exactly, in a 2026 study. The question is central to understanding what these models can truly learn.

The authors prove exact learnability results under bounded-degree and finite-precision conditions. Their approach follows two steps for showing when a network can reproduce an algorithm without error. Exact results like these help separate what graph networks can do in principle from what they merely approximate in practice. The question also bears on how much trust to place in learned graph solvers.
arxiv-2603-01407:
Saad Alqithami wrote this 2026 work on how smart agents can track what is true from many points of view. In groups of agents, each one sees a different scene and holds different beliefs. Older tools split time, place, and viewpoint into separate parts, which makes joint thought brittle and weak.

Alqithami joins all three in one math structure called the Observer-Situation Lattice. Each point in the grid pairs one observer with one scene, so beliefs sit in a single shared space. Two methods run on the grid: one spreads new facts step by step, and one finds and splits clashes. Proof checks and tests on mind-reading tasks show the frame is sound, fast, and clear for group agents.
arxiv-2603-01707:
Julien Hebraud, Floriane Arrouas, Bruno Peaudecerf, and colleagues study slow relaxation in a quantum kicked rotor. Their 2026 work uses a model where a quantum rotor gets periodic kicks, as in cold-atom lab tests. When the rotor starts from rest, the effective disorder gains a mirror symmetry.

That symmetry pairs up energy states at opposite momenta with tiny energy splits between partners. Tiny splits mean huge time scales, stacked in a hierarchy from fast to extremely slow. Scattering peaks then evolve in a non-monotonic way with lopsided contrasts. After that odd phase, both peaks relax toward a shared value at a logarithmic crawl. Such glass-like slowness from one symmetry, in a fully coherent system, links quantum order to slow dynamics.
arxiv-2603-02007:
Dongxue Liu, Jiaqin Dong, Yunxing Liu, and colleagues model how laser roughness imprints onto fusion targets. Their 2026 work serves direct-drive inertial confinement fusion, where lasers crush a fuel capsule directly. Tiny surface flaws can seed instabilities that spoil the implosion and its energy gain.

Their equivalent perturbation model maps laser imprinting into a matching target surface perturbation. Fabrication flaws and thermal smoothing in the plasma enter the same frame, widening past geometric views. A threshold ratio separates regimes: below it, target flaws dominate the outcome. Radiation-hydrodynamics simulations confirm that key timings and adiabat shifts stay small below that threshold. Omega experiments support the picture, so joint control of laser and target quality can guide stable high-gain designs.
arxiv-2603-02107:

avicenna-liber-canonis-1507:
Avicenna's Canon of Medicine appears here in a Latin printing made at Venice in 1507. Gerard of Cremona had translated the huge Arabic work into Latin in the twelfth century. Avicenna, a Persian physician and philosopher, wrote the Canon in the early 1000s, and it grew into the most used medical book in the world.

The Canon gathers Greek, Indian, and Persian healing into one ordered system of theory, drugs, and treatment. It runs to about a million words across five books, covering fevers, organs, and compound medicines. European universities taught medicine from this text for some five hundred years. The 1507 Venice edition shows the book in its Renaissance form, still the doctor's bible long after its author's death.
bakunin-oeuvres-vol1-1907:
James Guillaume edited the French collected works of Mikhail Bakunin, and the first volume appeared in 1907. Bakunin, the Russian revolutionary who died in 1876, was anarchism's founding thinker. His papers had been scattered across Europe, and Guillaume, an old comrade, spent years gathering them into print.

Volume 1 collects Bakunin's early writings, including his break with Marx and his plans for a federal, stateless order. The texts argue that freedom cannot be granted by any state and must grow from free communes linked by choice. Guillaume added notes that place each piece in Bakunin's restless life. The six volumes that followed made this edition the main source for studying anarchism at its source.
