Two friends canoe down the Danube in Algernon Blackwood's short novel The Willows, first told in 1907. They camp on a small isle of sand and willow trees. Wind, water, and odd sounds wear at their nerves night by night.

No beast steps into view. Dread comes from a sense that vast, cold powers press close to our world. H. P. Lovecraft ranked the tale at the top of weird prose. It still sets the bar for tales of fear in wild places. The two men row, camp, and doubt their own senses as signs mount. Blackwood lets sound and wind do the work that beasts do in lesser tales.
brentano-untersuchungen-zur-sinnespsycho:
Brentano's Investigations in the Psychology of the Senses appeared in German in 1907. Brentano had founded a new, careful study of mental life in Vienna, training students who spread his methods widely. Late in his career he turned to a basic question: how do seeing, hearing, and touch give us the world?

The studies take each sense apart, asking what a sensation contains and how the mind builds objects from it. Brentano argues against loose talk about the senses and demands exact description of what is actually given. His method, describing experience before explaining it, became a mark of his school. The book shows philosophy's keenest eye at work in the inner workshop of perception, where psychology and philosophy had not yet fully parted.
brocquiere-travels-johnes-1807:
Bertrandon de La Brocquiere rode east in 1432, part pilgrim and part spy for Burgundy. Thomas Johnes's 1807 English version tells his trek through Ottoman lands and home again, much of it in disguise. His eye for armies, customs, and roads never rests.

Brocquiere notes what Turks eat, wear, and ride, and how their camps are run. His report gave Europe an early, detailed picture of the Turks. Pilgrim's piety and spy's cunning share every page. The account stands as travel writing with a secret brief, five centuries old and still fresh in its curiosity and nerve.
carrington-physical-phenomena-spirituali:
Hereward Carrington wrote The Physical Phenomena of Spiritualism in 1907 as a field manual of mediumship. Carrington had investigated the medium Eusapia Palladino at first hand. His book sorts the famous physical phenomena into the fraudulent and the genuine. Table turns, materializations, and spirit hands all face his tests.

He gives a full account of the methods used to fake such wonders. Readers learn the tricks of slate writing, cabinet work, and tied mediums. His criticism weighs what little evidence survives such checks. The first edition became a handbook for investigators on both sides. It stays useful as a guide to period stagecraft. Skeptics and believers both cite it.
catherine-siena-dialogue-thorold-1907:
Catherine of Siena told her Dialogue to scribes as she prayed, it is said. Algar Thorold gave the work English dress in 1907. Catherine was a young nun of Siena who swayed popes and towns. She died at the age of three and thirty in 1380.

God speaks with the soul on how He guides the world and each life. The bridge of Christ, with its steps, frames much of the talk. Calls to mend the Church ring through the last parts. The book is one of the great talks with God of the mid ages.
chapman-bussy-dambois-1607:
George Chapman wrote Bussy D'Ambois, first staged around 1604, and its sequel The Revenge of Bussy D'Ambois some years later. F. Boas edited the two plays together in the edition here. Chapman, the translator of Homer, brought a poet's weight to the stage.

Bussy, a bold French courtier, rises by daring and falls by love and intrigue at the court of Henri III. The sequel follows his brother Clermont, a Stoic answer to Bussy's fire. Chapman's verse is dense, learned, and thunderous, prized by readers who like their tragedy heroic. The pair shows the Elizabethan superman at his rise and in his ruins.
cia-0000008007:
Political development in South Vietnam posed hard problems, and a November 1966 CIA study took them up directly. Saigon's generals had cycled through governments while the war against the Viet Cong and North Vietnam widened. Buddhist protests and regional loyalties strained the state further.

The study asks whether South Vietnam could build stable politics within about a year. That question mattered because military aid alone could not create legitimacy. Readers get an insider view of doubts that public statements often hid. The paper shows analysts grading an ally's weaknesses frankly, in the middle of a war America was escalating.
cia-0000009807:
A Viet Cong prison camp for American and South Vietnamese prisoners is located in a July 1971 item, in a place the title cuts off. Joint camps were common in the south, where the Viet Cong held their captives near the fighting. The item's job is the location itself.

A bare location still carried weight: it told searchers where to look and airmen where danger sat. It also let later sightings from the same area lock onto a known site. Many entries in the prison map began as one-line fixes like this. The file preserves the fix as filed, before description or confirmation could be added.
cia-0000009907:
Rumor said an American pilot was seen being carried through a village near a Laotian place the title cuts off at Ban, a November 1966 item records. The heading itself calls the report rumor, the weakest grade in the files. A carried pilot was likely wounded, which sharpened the claim's pull.

Rumor reports were kept because some rumors, checked, became facts. Others dissolved, and the file would show that too in time. Analysts had to hold both outcomes open at once. This entry preserves the holding pattern: a wounded man, a village, and a story not yet believed or dismissed.
cia-0000012407:
Meeting number nineteen falls on July 20, 1961, inside the Yoga summer phase of the debriefings. The numbering's gaps hint at sessions unrecorded, lost, or filed elsewhere in the case. Summer's work was underway in earnest by then, day after day. The colonel was answering for his Moscow weeks. His handlers measured what he brought against what they had asked him to find.

The nineteenth session's record carries the phase forward in order. Behind the numbers sits a rhythm of travel, risk, and talk. For readers, the gaps in the sequence testify silently to all the file cannot show.
cia-0000013207:
Raw reporting from the ground fills a field information report from October 1970. Its subject is an American prisoner of war in Tuyen Due province. Field reports reached Langley unpolished, straight from the source's mouth. A case officer's pen passed them on with little editing. That roughness was precisely their value. Nothing had been smoothed away by layers of headquarters review before the facts arrived.

The report preserves what was known about one captive's place and condition. Such fragments fed the great accounting of the missing men. For readers, it is the war's facts at their freshest, before summaries replaced them.
cia-0000015307: A letter to Leon Davidson from J. S. Harman fills a CIA file dated March 5, 1958. Harman thanks Davidson for his letter of March 1. Davidson, like Keyhoe, pressed the agency in print and by mail. The twin letters of that week show two campaigns being answered with one calm hand. The Davidson reply now sits in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000027407: El Salvador's performance on certification issues is graded in a CIA paper dated in 1983, tagged Truth Commission in the catalog. Certification meant Congress required proof of progress on human rights before aid flowed. Grading an ally's record in wartime put the agency between policy and fact. The tag links the paper to the later truth inquiry into that war.
cia-0000037107: A ledger page dated January 1, 1943 lists disbursements for travel and other expenses, naming Shaw, Hollingshead, Stacy, Hughes, and others. The page belongs to wartime bookkeeping from the years of the OSS, the office that came before the CIA. It records money paid out, person by person, in the plain style of an accounts office. Even secret work ran on receipts, and pages like this one kept the spending straight.
cia-0000039307:
Photo comparison results filed as Christmas 1969 number 33 fill a CIA record dated November 5, 1970. The report also mentions further names, cut short in the catalog title. Number 33 was one result in the long Christmas series worked that year.

Inside, the analysts' findings for this numbered case are entered into the record. By late 1970 the Christmas work was still moving through the laboratory's queue. The file shows the pace of the effort plainly. Photographs from one holiday season were judged one by one. Nearly a year passed before they finished moving through the searchers' hands in Washington.
cia-0000042907:
A report on President Cristiani's plan in the Jesuits case fills a CIA record dated January 1, 1990. The plan concerned how his government would handle the murder investigation. Few cases have pressed a president harder from so many sides at once.

Inside, the outlines of Cristiani's approach to the case are set down. He had to answer the church, the courts, and Washington at once. He also had to face an army that held the suspects in its ranks. The file shows a civilian president planning his way through a case in which every step risked a break with the men who held the guns.
cia-0000045207:
Venceremos and ARENA offered their views on the Duarte kidnapping, in a CIA record dated September 2, 1985. ARENA was the party of the Salvadoran hard right. Rebel radio and the right agreed on almost nothing in that war.

Inside, the two camps' readings of the crisis sit in one file. The contrast between them is the country's split in miniature. One side blamed the government for the crime itself. The other blamed the same government for softness toward the criminals who had seized the president's daughter. The record holds both voices on the same page, which lets readers measure the distance between El Salvador's extremes in their own words.
cia-0000049007: National Police investigators in El Salvador came to believe, in 1980, that their own force had taken part in the crime they were probing. A CIA item from that year preserves their belief, kept with the Truth Commission records. Police accusing police was a rare crack in the wall that protected the security forces.
cia-0000049107: A partly blacked-out file summary on Ricardo Sol Meza survives in a CIA item from 1985, kept with the Truth Commission records. Summaries distilled a man's whole file into a page or two for a busy reader. Sol Meza's name carried weight in this series: the businessman tied to death-squad money.
cia-0000049307: Dated April 3, 1990, declassified CIA document 0000049307 is titled El Salvador: Military Lagging on Human Rights, with a Truth Commission note. The subject is the Salvadoran military's slow progress on human rights as the agency framed it. The short record shows the concern stated directly in an official heading, a useful snapshot of how the issue was labeled at the time.
cia-0000049407: Government and insurgent prospects in El Salvador are weighed in declassified CIA document 0000049407, dated January 4, 1989. The paper carries a Truth Commission note and sets both sides in one heading. Readers find a brief declassified outlook item whose balance is its feature, a late-war agency attempt to judge the two camps together.
cia-0000104907:
Manual for Physical Security Standards for Sensitive Compartmented Information is declassified CIA document 0000104907, dated January 1, 1994 in the catalog. The sample shows the manual itself: Director of Central Intelligence Directive 1/21, effective January 30, 1994. Its full title adds the word Facilities, for the secure rooms it covers.

The contents page opens with policy and concept, including a review under the Americans with Disabilities Act. General and administrative sections follow, on the facilities themselves, preconstruction review and approval, and accreditation. Co-utilization is another listed topic in the contents. The sample is cover and contents pages, so the detailed standards themselves are not shown.
cia-0000107407: Television Program Summary - -SOL 90-212 is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000107407, dated July 5, 1990. The title marks a summary of one television program, filed under the code SOL 90-212. No country or channel is named in the heading itself. The brief record is a broadcast summary item, kept under its filing code as released.
cia-0000108007: Report on the Implementation of Recommendation no. 8-A of the Report to the Pre is the heading, cut off mid-word, on declassified CIA document 0000108007, dated March 1, 1961. The title tracks follow-through on one numbered recommendation, 8-A. The parent report is named only as a report to the Pre before the break. The brief record is a follow-through report item from 1961.
cia-0000119207:
Dated around July 1981, this CIA document covers Hanoi's position and activity on an issue involving the United States. The heading breaks off at the key words, so the issue it names cannot be read from the title alone. Six years after the fighting stopped, that accounting remained unfinished.

Vietnam's stance on the missing shaped every attempt at better relations. The document records how Hanoi presented its position and what steps it was taking, as the agency read them. For families of the missing, papers like this one were the public trace of a slow and painful process that ran through diplomacy for many years.
cia-0000119707:
A July 1953 CIA paper forecasts probable developments in Chile. President Ibanez had lately returned to power, and the country's politics were entering a rough stretch. The paper looks ahead at a democracy whose stability Washington had reason to watch.

Chile's copper, its strong parties, and its open politics made it a country analysts followed closely. The forecast weighs the government's prospects and the pressures around it. Written twenty years before the 1973 coup, it cannot foresee that ending. It does show the questions the agency was already asking about Chilean democracy: how firm it was, and what might shake it.
cia-0000124307: A January 1951 CIA document reports a Chinese Communist order meant to prevent the mistreatment of prisoners of war. Beijing wanted the treatment of its captives to meet at least the look of accepted standards. The paper preserves the order as the agency obtained it early in the Korean War. Orders on paper and practice in camps often differed, a gap later prisoner accounts made plain, but the order itself shows the image Beijing wanted projected.
cia-0000132207: Situation report 524, from January 1991, carries a deleted paragraph title and concerns the Iranian press, the heading breaking off. Tehran watched the war from the sidelines with its own agenda. The report covers the press angle from Iran that day. Iran had fought Iraq for eight years, ending in 1988. Its press line in a new Gulf war was read as a clue to Tehran's next move.
cia-0000132507:
Whether time was on America's side in Cuba is asked outright in a CIA document dated February 5, 1961. The invasion at the Bay of Pigs was only two months away. Inside the government, the argument over acting sooner or waiting longer was still open and heated.

The document weighs that timing question directly. Its title alone sums up the invasion debate in a single sentence. For readers, it shows the agency pausing to question its own course before the die was cast. Few entries in the file state their doubt so plainly on the record. The question would be answered by events that spring, at heavy cost to the invasion force.
cia-0000132607: Relations between Venezuela and Cuba still going downhill fill item 6 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated July 3, 1960. It follows an earlier paper on the same rift from May of that year. By summer the rift had become a clear trend rather than a passing spat. The short item tracks the latest stage of the decline.
cia-0000135707: A Spanish-language document dated 5 January 1961 survives among the papers of Brigade 2506, the CIA-trained exile force. The first week of 1961 was crowded with brigade paperwork, and this item is part of that run. Its catalog title names no subject. Preserved in Spanish through the CIA Reading Room, it is a dated primary source from the months when the Bay of Pigs plan was still being readied in secret.
cia-0000135807: Plans for provocations fill a CIA paper dated May 2, 1954. The paper came weeks before the coup that ended the Arbenz government in Guatemala. Its two-word title is all charge and no detail on its face. What the plans called for sits inside the file itself. The short paper keeps the plans in the form in which they were recorded that spring.
cia-0000135907: Contact Report, dated 3 May 1954, is a declassified CIA record of a meeting or source contact, the standard job of that form. The catalog gives no subject, place, or participants for this one, and the v1 summary's tie to the Guatemala operation is not supported by anything in the title. What survives is the dated shell of an operational record, released through the CIA Reading Room with whatever the declassification process left standing. Researchers should treat the text itself, not the catalog line, as the evidence.
cia-0000136207: On 1 May 1954, the agency filed a cable, now declassified, on a list of persons departing WSBURNT, names of the leaving tracked for WELLBANKS. As the Lincoln station file, it forms part of PBSUCCESS, the CIA plan that ended with President Arbenz driven out in June 1954. Later books on the coup rest on stacks of paper exactly like this, dated, coded, and only partly opened.
cia-0000136707: A document in Spanish dated 6 February 1961 survives in the 2506 Brigade papers, sharing that date with a companion item in the release. The brigade of Cuban exiles was drilling under CIA direction for the spring invasion. The catalog names no subject for either record. This one is preserved in Spanish as released, a dated piece of the brigade's final-winter paperwork.
cia-06768907: INVOLVEMENT OF THE TRUJILLO FAMILY IN REVOLUTIONARY PLANS, a CIA document. The Dominican plots. This file preserves that declassified paper. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Later readers can locate it.
conrad-secret-agent-1907:
Joseph Conrad published The Secret Agent in 1907, a novel set in London among spies and anarchists. Verloc runs a small shop and works in secret for a foreign embassy. He is ordered to bomb the Greenwich Observatory to provoke a crackdown. He uses his wife's young brother Stevie to carry the bomb.

Stevie dies when the bomb goes off too soon, and the plan falls apart. Verloc's wife Winnie then acts in rage and grief. Police and plotters close in from all sides. The novel is a dark and ironic study of terrorism, family life, and a city that looks the other way.
constitution-mozambique-2007: Mozambique's 2004 Constitution, amended 2007, frames its republic. It ended war. The Tower library holds the full text. It closed long guns. Foes shook. Votes came. Peace grew. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
crabbe-parish-register-1807:
In The Parish Register, from 1807, Crabbe imagines a village clergyman reading his church records aloud. The poem falls into three parts built on baptisms, marriages, and burials. Its long argument lists foundlings, large poor families, keen gardeners, and sharpers among the names in the book.

Each brief entry grows into a small human drama, from a jilted bride to a drowned sailor. Crabbe had served as a clergyman himself, and that daily knowledge gives the tales their tender, unsparing tone. Church paperwork thus becomes a full gallery of English village life, told in verse at its most humane.
crowley-equinox-vol-1-no-07:
The seventh number of The Equinox appeared in March 1912, as the order behind it took firm shape. Grades, rules, and rites had grown up fast since the first number of 1909. The spring issue prints the papers of a maturing school.

Crowley's own work leads, with rites and verse in first print form. Work by his pupils shows the teaching taking root in other hands. The journal had become the order's true public face by this stage. Number seven is a chapter of growth in the prime record of Thelema. It shows a school that now ran on more than one man's fire.
crowley-konx-om-pax-1907:
Konx Om Pax gathers Crowley's early prose poems on the mystic path, printed in 1907. The title takes a phrase called out at the close of the old rites of Eleusis. The book stands between his young verse and the great magic textbooks to come.

Its pieces mix tale, talk, and chant as they circle the themes of light, self, and God. Crowley writes as a seeker still more poet than teacher here. The wit is sharp and the mood swings from jest to prayer in a page. Readers meet the occultist finding his mature voice.
dannunzio-daughter-of-jorio-1907:
Alice Henry translated The Daughter of Jorio, D'Annunzio's pastoral tragedy of 1907. The scene lies in the Abruzzo mountains of his native region. Ancient myth takes fresh life among shepherds and harsh village faith.

Young shepherd Aligi loves Mila, a wild outcast girl. The village accuses Mila of witchcraft and means to destroy her. Aligi defies his own people to shield the girl he loves. Verse of rare music carries the clash of love and fear. The play triumphed on the Italian stage in its day. It still reads as a hymn to a rough land and to love that refuses to bow.
doe-osti-2571210-remembering-robert-s-fi: Robert S. Fitzhugh (1932-2007) got remembered, and this DOE memorial honors his life. The pages recall his contributions. The community gets its tribute. The years were 1932 to 2007. The tribute was community. The memorial was DOE's. The life was honored. The contributions were recalled.
drayton-minor-poems-1907:
Cyril Brett chose and edited this 1907 Oxford volume of Michael Drayton's shorter verse. Drayton, who lived in Elizabethan and Jacobean England, was best known in his day for long works like Poly-Olbion. Brett's contents run from early sonnets of 1594 through odes and the elegies of 1627.

Ballads, odes, and lyrics fill the book, including patriotic war songs and calm pastoral pieces once sung across England. The brief forms let Drayton's music and plain feeling show more clearly than his large poems do. For new readers, the selection is a friendly first door into a poet who gave England much of its history in verse.
engels-anti-duhring-lewis-1907:
Eugen Duhring claimed to have refounded science and socialism, and Engels answered him at full length in 1878. Austin Lewis translated Anti-Duhring for Charles H. Kerr in 1907. The German title mocks Duhring's revolution in science by naming him in full. Engels defends Marxism across three wide fields in reply.

Philosophy, political economy, and socialism each receive a full treatment. Dialectics, his method of change through conflict, runs through them all. The book became the encyclopedia of dialectical materialism for later movements. Whole generations learned Marxism from its chapters. Its range is vast, from atoms to the state. Few polemics built so large a system.
essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volume-07: Volume seven of the Essays shows Montaigne at his most reflective. He writes of age, memory, and the art of living well. The famous tower study feels close at hand. Wisdom from a man who watched himself closely.
europmc-pmc10007007: Aggarwal and colleagues present a systematic review of chatbots built to help people change health habits, such as quitting smoking or moving more. The review gathers past trials of these AI tools and weighs how well they worked. It offers readers a grounded look at what health chatbots can and cannot yet do.
europmc-pmc10024607:
Allen and co-workers map how the mouse brain changes with age at the level of single cells, in a 2023 study. The brain holds many cell types arranged in complex patterns. That complexity had blocked a full account of how its cells and gene activity shift across a lifetime.

The team profiled cells across the aging mouse brain and charted where each type sits. They found age-linked changes in gene activity that vary by cell type and region. The map gives researchers a base for asking why old brains lose function.
europmc-pmc10064807:
Cui and colleagues pool data from studies around the world to estimate how common vitamin D deficiency is, in a 2023 analysis. Low vitamin D weakens bones and is linked to many other health problems. The team gathered population studies from 2000 to 2022, covering millions of people in total.

Their pooled results give global and regional rates of low vitamin D. The analysis shows how rates vary by place, age, and the cutoff used to define low levels. The paper offers a baseline for health planners who track and tackle this quiet shortfall.
europmc-pmc10305407:
Sharma and colleagues review microbial biofilms in a 2023 paper, from their formation to new treatments. A biofilm is a community of microbes stuck to a surface inside a self-made slime shield. In hospitals, biofilms grow on implants and wounds and cause chronic infections that resist antibiotics and immune attack.

The review explains how biofilms form and why their shield defeats standard drugs. It covers control measures, from sterile technique to surface design. It closes with new treatment ideas, such as enzymes that dissolve the shield. The paper is a full guide to a stubborn foe.
europmc-pmc10336207:
Tang, Millar, and Moore reviewed drug resistance in microbes in 2023. Resistance grows when germs, fungi, and parasites no longer respond to the drugs meant to kill them. Forecasts warn of 10 million deaths a year by 2050 if the trend holds. Overuse and misuse of antibiotics drive much of the crisis.

Tang sets out how world bodies fight back, from UN goals to joint plans for human and animal health. One Health treats people, animals, and the shared land and water as one linked system. The review says public knowledge still lags and must grow. It warns that failure could make routine surgery and childbirth life risks again, as in the era before antibiotics.
europmc-pmc10499607:
Fleck and co-authors built a gene control map of lab-grown human brain tissue in 2023. The tissue, called a brain organoid, grows from stem cells and mimics early brain growth. The team read gene activity and open DNA in single cells across time. Steps ran from first nerve sheets to the birth of neurons.

Their framework, Pando, merged both data types with binding site forecasts. It traced a global net of factors that steer cell fate. Fleck then broke select factors and read the fallout cell by cell. One factor, GLI3, proved vital for the fate of the cortex, the brain's outer layer. Two GLI3 circuits guide split choices at distinct times.
europmc-pmc11405507:
Giustina and a large expert panel issue a consensus statement on vitamin D in this 2024 paper. The statement comes from the sixth international conference on controversies in vitamin D. Topics span vitamin D metabolism, status assessment, actions, and supplementation. New insights link vitamin D to conditions not explained by sun exposure or diet alone.

Optimal levels of the main blood marker, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, remain debated, the panel notes. Societies disagree because they weigh clinical and public health angles differently. Assay non-standardisation also blocks clean pooling of study data. Beyond bone health, trials have tested cancer, cardiovascular, respiratory, autoimmune, and diabetes outcomes. Early trials were largely negative, likely because they enrolled people who already had enough vitamin D. Later analyses suggested potential benefits, such as reduced cancer incidence.
europmc-pmc11701607:
Mudge and a large team report the 2025 state of GENCODE, the reference gene annotation for human and mouse, in this paper. GENCODE lists every gene and transcript in the two genomes. In its twentieth year, the project uses new methods to catalogue the genome in ever finer detail. Long-read transcriptome sequencing, which reads full RNA transcripts, is the biggest recent driver.

Long reads found large numbers of missing transcripts and improved many existing models, they report. The catalogs of long non-coding RNAs, transcripts that do not make protein, grew and were reshaped. Data from proteomics and Ribo-seq, which maps which RNA parts are read by ribosomes, fine-tune the translated parts. Alignments across many genomes add clues on function. Filtered sets such as MANE Select and GENCODE Primary give users a trusted core, cutting the usability problems that growing complexity brings.
europmc-pmc11920007:
GBD 2021 Adult BMI Collaborators charted adult weight trends worldwide in 2025. Overweight and obesity now form a global epidemic. Knowing where rates head helps leaders plan policy. Past trends also show which responses have worked or failed.

Estimates cover adults aged 25 and older in 204 countries and territories. Data came from 1,350 sources, mixing measured and self-reported values. Corrections adjust for bias in self-reports. Models trace change from 1990 to 2021 and forecast to 2050. GBD 2021 Adult BMI Collaborators supply a base for policy debate. Results were split by age and sex throughout. In 2021, about 2.11 billion adults in total lived with excess weight.
europmc-pmc1552007:
Inhaled nano-sized particles may slip from nose to brain. Elder and co-authors tested that route in rats in 2006, using manganese oxide particles about 30 nanometers wide. Earlier work with gold and carbon particles hinted the smell nerve offers a path.

After 12 days of exposure, manganese in the olfactory bulb, the brain's smell center, rose 3.5-fold. Levels also rose in other brain regions, and inflammation signals in the bulb jumped sharply. With one nostril blocked, manganese built up only on the open side. Elder concludes the nerve path is efficient, and the arriving particles can stir brain inflammation.
europmc-pmc1637807:
The growing brain has windows when harm strikes hardest. Rice and Barone reviewed that vulnerability in 2000, from human and animal evidence. Brain building runs from the embryo stage through adolescence, through cell birth, movement, wiring, insulation, and pruning.

Agents like X-rays, alcohol, lead, methyl mercury, and the pesticide chlorpyrifos can derail those steps. Different brain regions serve different skills, so timing of exposure shapes the deficit. The authors link such derailment to disorders like schizophrenia, dyslexia, and autism. They warn that early damage may also speed age-related decline later in life.
europmc-pmc1664607:
A new compound kills TB bacteria at vanishingly low doses. Matsumoto and co-authors reported OPC-67683 in 2006. TB treatment still rests on 1970s drugs needing six months of pills, and drug-resistant strains are spreading.

The compound blocks building of mycolic acid, a waxy coat material. It stopped TB growth at 0.006 to 0.024 micrograms per milliliter, including resistant strains, and showed no mutagenicity. In mice it cleared lung bacteria at low doses. Mixed with two standard drugs, it wiped out lung bacteria at least two months faster. Matsumoto presents it as a candidate for shorter, stronger regimens.
europmc-pmc1994707:
Leek and Storey introduced a statistical method in 2007 for gene expression studies, which measure how active thousands of genes are. Hidden factors such as age, environment or lab handling can shift many genes at once. Ignoring that hidden variation, called heterogeneity, can create false signals. It can also hide real effects and link errors across genes.

Their method, surrogate variable analysis, estimates those hidden factors from the data itself. It then works alongside standard analysis tools. Applied to disease, time-course and genetic studies, the method improved accuracy and reproducibility. The authors show the problem occurs even in well-designed randomised studies. Capturing hidden variation gave results that matched biology more closely.
europmc-pmc2121107:
Cross and co-workers followed about 500,000 adults in 2007 to test whether eating red or processed meat raises cancer risk. Earlier work linked these meats to cancer at several sites, but no prospective study had covered so many cancer types. Participants were aged 50 to 71 at enrolment in 1995 and 1996. Meat intake came from a baseline food questionnaire, and cancers were tracked for up to 8.2 years.

During follow-up, 53,396 cancers were recorded. People in the highest fifth of red meat intake had 20 to 60 percent higher risks for cancers of the esophagus, colorectum, liver and lung than the lowest fifth. The highest processed meat intake brought a 20 percent higher colorectal cancer risk and 16 percent higher lung cancer risk. Both meat types linked positively to colorectal and lung cancers.
europmc-pmc2124507: A medical paper on epithelioma adamantinum. The jaw tumor. This article preserves that oncology research. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2124707: A medical paper on partial and complete occlusion of the aorta and large arteries. The blocked vessels. This article preserves that vascular research. The paper lived through the years. It waits for future eyes. Writers of history may cite it later in their work.
europmc-pmc2125207: A medical paper on studies of the chemistry of serous effusions. The body fluids' makeup. This article preserves that biochemistry. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2125407: A medical paper on the effects of serum treated with agar. The agar serum. This article preserves that immunology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2125507: A medical paper studying acidosis, blood urea, and plasma chlorides in uranium nephritis. The poisoned kidney's chemistry. This article preserves that nephrology. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2131107: A medical paper with studies on the histogenesis of autoplastic thymus transplantations. The grafted thymus. This article preserves that immunology. The paper lived through the years. Later readers can locate it. The paper lived through the years.
europmc-pmc2131507: A medical paper on antigenic differences between matt hemolytic streptococci and their glossy variants. The strep's faces. This article preserves that bacteriology. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
europmc-pmc2140307: A biology paper on sensitization to heat due to exposure to light of short wavelengths. The light-sensitized heat. This article preserves that photobiology. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc2140907: A biology paper with an empirical formula for the relation between viscosity of solution and volume. The thick formula. This article preserves that physical chemistry. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
europmc-pmc2174407:
Kortenkamp reviewed ten years of research in 2007 on mixtures of endocrine-disrupting chemicals. People are exposed to many such chemicals at once, not one by one. Yet over 95 percent of toxicology research studies single chemicals. The review asks whether combined effects can be predicted, and whether regulation should change from chemical-by-chemical assessment to group-wise rules for whole classes.

Good evidence now shows dose addition predicts combined effects within one category, such as estrogenic agents. Mixtures can produce significant effects even when each component sits at a dose with no visible effect alone. Far less is known about mixtures spanning different categories. Kortenkamp argues the evidence undermines single-chemical risk assessment. Groups should be defined by common effects, not common mechanisms, and exposure data need urgent improvement.
europmc-pmc2292207:
Petersen and Deddens compared two methods for estimating prevalence ratios in 2008, the relative frequency of a condition between groups. In cross-sectional studies of common conditions, odds ratios mislead, but older prevalence methods often fail to converge or inflate errors. Using simulations and real example datasets, they pitted robust Poisson regression against the log-binomial method. The first borrows the Poisson distribution with corrected errors. The second fits the binomial distribution directly by maximum likelihood.

For very high prevalences at moderate sample sizes, robust Poisson gave less biased estimates. At moderate prevalences, log-binomial was slightly less biased. In nearly all cases log-binomial delivered slightly higher power and smaller standard errors. Unlike robust Poisson, it always yields prevalences between zero and one, since it fits the correct model. The authors recommend log-binomial for most common situations, keeping robust Poisson as an easy fallback.
europmc-pmc2440807:
Chen and colleagues studied stem-like lung cancer cells and a gene that keeps them potent in 2008. They split cells from ten patients' non-small-cell lung tumors, and five cell lines, by the surface marker CD133. The CD133-positive cells expressed high levels of Oct-4, a gene that maintains stem cell identity.

These positive cells renewed themselves and acted as a reservoir able to generate the full tumor cell mix. They also carried the drug-resistance marker ABCG2 and withstood four chemotherapy drugs and radiation far better than negative cells. Silencing Oct-4 with a small RNA tool stripped their powers: sphere growth stopped, invasion and colony formation fell, and cell death signals rose. Tumors from these cells also responded better to combined chemo-radiation once Oct-4 was silenced. The authors cast Oct-4 as the linchpin of the stem-like state.
europmc-pmc2518207:
Dinger, Pang, Mercer, and Mattick examined in 2008 a basic sorting problem in genetics: telling protein-coding RNA from noncoding RNA. For decades the split seemed easy, since messenger RNAs carry protein recipes and a few other RNAs had known jobs. Genome-wide studies then revealed thousands of transcripts that fit neither box cleanly.

The authors weigh the strategies used to classify transcripts and show where each one fails. Some RNAs labelled noncoding may actually encode small peptides, while some supposed messengers may never be translated. A few transcripts do both jobs at once, working as RNA and as a protein template. The review concludes that the two categories form a false split, and no transcript's RNA-level role should be dismissed.
europmc-pmc2677107:
Allan, Ballard, Rowan, and Kenny followed 179 older people in 2009 to learn why people with dementia fall so often. Falls are a leading cause of injury and death in this group, yet no study had tracked risk factors forward in time for dementia patients alone. The group included 140 patients with four kinds of dementia and 39 healthy peers, all over 65.

Fall diaries kept for a year showed dementia patients fell nearly eight times as often as the healthy group. A Lewy body form of dementia and any fall in the prior year flagged high risk. Three changeable factors stood out: blood pressure drops on standing that cause symptoms, a burden of autonomic symptoms such as dizziness and bladder trouble, and depression scores. More daily physical activity protected against falls. The authors point to these levers as the core of a prevention program.
europmc-pmc2702407:
Joensen and co-authors asked in 2009 whether man-made chemicals called perfluoroalkyl acids harm semen quality in young men. These acids come from products that resist water and stains, and they build up in blood. The team studied men in Denmark, where no such data had been reported before.

They measured ten of these chemicals and hormone levels in blood from 105 men with a median age of 19 years, and they checked semen samples. Men with high combined levels of two main chemicals had far fewer normal sperm than men with low levels. The authors urge larger follow-up studies in more men to confirm the link.
europmc-pmc2717907:
Fan and co-authors traced in 2009 how human lung tumors burn glucose differently from nearby healthy lung, using labeled carbon in patients. They infused glucose tagged with carbon-13, a traceable form, before surgery for non-small cell lung cancer. Then they compared tumor and paired normal tissue with magnetic and mass methods that track where the label lands.

Many basic chemicals sat higher in tumors, and label in lactate and several amino acids showed faster sugar breakdown and Krebs cycle use, the cell energy cycle. A shortcut called pyruvate carboxylation, which refills that cycle, was switched on in tumors, with more of its enzyme at gene and protein levels. That refill may feed tumor growth.
europmc-pmc2754607:
Wang and Qian mined in 2009 the conserved fragments of bacterial 16S ribosomal RNA genes to design better primers for surveys of uncultured bacteria. These genes mix conserved stretches, shared by nearly all bacteria, with variable stretches that identify groups. Primers must sit in conserved parts, yet the coverage of many primers in use was unknown.

Scanning available sequences, they predicted thirty primers with coverage above ninety percent, sitting in the same conserved regions as known primers. Thirty percent of known primers actually covered less than ninety percent of sequences. Five predicted primers were recommended for their high coverage across almost all bacterial phyla. The set should make metagenomic diversity surveys more complete and reliable.
europmc-pmc2797607:
Palanisamy and co-authors examined tiny sacs called exosomes that cells release into human saliva. Exosomes ferry proteins and RNA between cells and turn up in most body fluids. In 2010 the team purified saliva exosomes by hard spinning and confirmed them with marker proteins and imaging.

Atomic force scans, which trace surfaces with a fine probe, revealed their shape, size spread, and density in three dimensions. Gene chip tests found five hundred nine messenger RNA types that stayed stable inside the sacs. Glowing labeled exosomes entered mouth lining cells in the lab and changed gene activity there, proof that the cargo still works. Such stable RNA hints at spit tests for disease.
europmc-pmc2826407:
Lembo and colleagues marshaled Tanzanian field data in 2010 to argue that dog rabies can be eliminated across most of Africa. Rabies kills many thousands of Africans yearly, nearly always through dog bites, yet control lags behind the Americas, where mass dog vaccination has crushed it. Four doubts are usually raised: low priority, hard biology, hard logistics, and thin budgets.

The team answers each doubt with data, covering disease burden counts, outbreak studies, and real vaccination campaign records from varied Tanzanian settings. Coverage levels needed to break transmission proved reachable, dog numbers proved countable, and cost analyses favored vaccination. They conclude no barrier found is insurmountable, and delay costs lives needlessly.
europmc-pmc2831007:
Gjersing, Caplehorn, and Clausen walked through the careful work in 2010 of adapting a research questionnaire for a new country and language. Teams often just translate a validated survey and use it, yet a tool proven in one setting may quietly measure the wrong thing in another. Their case took an Australian staff attitude survey on opioid maintenance treatment into Norwegian use in 2007.

Two forward and two back translations were merged by an expert committee, then the draft was pretested and adjusted. Given to over three hundred treatment and harm reduction staff, the original scale failed its statistical check. A fresh two-factor scale emerged and proved valid, proof that skipping adaptation steps can produce precise-looking but wrong findings.
europmc-pmc2911707:
Macedo and the PICARD study group warned in 2010 that fluid overload hides kidney injury in critically ill patients by diluting its main blood marker. Doctors stage acute kidney injury by creatinine, a waste product whose blood level depends on how much water it is dissolved in. The team recalculated creatinine adjusted for each patient's fluid gains in two hundred fifty-three patients with kidney injury.

Patients accumulated a median of nearly three liters by day two and over six liters by day seven of illness. The gap between adjusted and raw creatinine widened daily. In a quarter of patients, the raw value took more than an extra day to cross the injury threshold. That delayed recognition. Fluid adjustment reclassified severity upward for many, which matters because stage drives treatment and prognosis.
europmc-pmc2955707:
Nix, Smith, and Vicenzino pooled surveys on hallux valgus, the bunion deformity where the big toe drifts toward its neighbours, in a 2010 review and meta-analysis. The condition is common and painful, yet a solid frequency figure was missing.

Searching three databases to mid-2009 without language limits, they gathered dozens of surveys covering nearly half a million people. Studies passed quality checks by two independent raters before pooling with a random-effects method. Splitting results by study population let them weigh how frequency shifts with age and sex, giving clinicians and planners a firmer baseline than single surveys.
europmc-pmc2994107:
Arboix and Alió reviewed cardioembolic stroke, where a clot formed in the heart travels to the brain, in a 2010 overview of features, causes, and outlook. This type makes up a sizeable share of blocked-vessel strokes and tends to be severe.

Clues include sudden peak weakness, reduced alertness at onset, certain language losses, and clots appearing in body and brain together. The leading sources are an irregular heart rhythm, recent heart attack, artificial valves, weakened heart muscle, and a rheumatic valve narrowing. Hospital death rates in their series topped other stroke types, though careful treatment can prevent repeat events.
europmc-pmc2996607:
Nika and co-authors overturned a textbook assumption about the kinase Lck in 2010, showing that much of it is already switched on in resting T cells. Receptor engagement was thought to flip Lck from off to on to start immune signalling.

In untouched naive T cells and developing thymus cells, a large share of Lck, up to roughly two fifths, sat in the active form, some even carrying its brake mark. Making that pool needed Lck's own activity and a chaperone complex that shields it from disposal. Receptor engagement did not raise the amount, but the standing pool set how strongly the receptor got marked.
europmc-pmc2998707:
Gasparrini, Armstrong, and Kenward introduced distributed lag non-linear models in a 2010 article, a framework for exposures whose effects arrive late and unevenly. Heat, cold, and pollution can kill days after exposure, and single-day models miss that tail.

Their trick is a cross-basis, a two-way surface describing risk across both exposure level and delay at once. The family unifies older approaches and adds more flexible versions, all implemented in a free package for the R statistics system. Worked examples relate temperature to deaths in New York across fourteen years of national study data.
europmc-pmc3050907:
Shamu, Abrahams, Temmerman, Musekiwa, and Zarowsky reviewed in 2011 how common partner violence is during pregnancy in Africa, and what puts women at risk. They gathered nineteen peer reviewed studies of pregnant women published in English over a decade, and pooled the prevalence figures. Reported rates ranged very widely between studies, from a small fraction to more than half of women.

The pooled estimate put violence during pregnancy at roughly one in seven women, among the highest levels reported worldwide. Studies that adjusted for other factors still tied higher risk to HIV infection, a past history of violence, and a partner's alcohol or drug use. Low income and young age also appeared often. The authors argue that pregnancy care visits are a prime chance to screen and support women, and they call for more African research to guide that work.
europmc-pmc3065307:
Stephens and a large consortium described in 2011 a violent way cancers can be born: dozens to hundreds of chromosome breaks happening in a single crisis, which they named chromothripsis. Cancer changes were long assumed to pile up gradually, one break at a time. Genome sequencing of cancers instead revealed chromosomes whose pieces had been shuffled in patterns too tangled for slow accumulation.

The shuffled regions flip between just two copy states, the fingerprint of one shattering and hasty repair event. The pattern appeared in a small share of cancers overall, but in about a quarter of bone cancers. A single crisis can create several cancer driving changes at once, skipping years of gradual evolution. The finding reshapes how scientists think about cancer timing. It also suggests some cancers may jump to an advanced state almost overnight.
europmc-pmc3084507:
Polman led an international panel in 2011 that revised the standard rules for diagnosing multiple sclerosis, known as the McDonald criteria. Diagnosis requires showing that nerve damage is scattered across places in the brain and spinal cord and across time, while ruling out look alike diseases. Brain imaging can supply much of that proof, and earlier criteria already allowed earlier diagnosis than purely clinical rules.

The new revision simplifies how imaging proves spread in space and in time. In some situations a single scan can now establish both, where two studies were needed before. The panel also addressed use in children and in Asian and Latin American populations, where the evidence base was thinner. Sensitivity and specificity were kept intact in checks. The authors expect the simpler rules to spread earlier, more uniform diagnosis worldwide.
europmc-pmc3100507:
Craggs, Corder, van Sluijs, and Griffin reviewed in 2011 what actually predicts change in how active children and teenagers are over time. That differs from what merely goes with being active at one moment. Activity falls steadily through youth, and programs to stop the slide have had limited success. The team gathered prospective studies of four to eighteen year olds that measured change, and sorted candidate factors by age band.

Of dozens of factors studied, only a minority showed consistent effects. Among younger children, girls' activity fell faster than boys'. In the middle band, children who were active before and who felt capable declined least. Among teenagers, feeling in control, feeling supported, and self belief again softened the decline. Most studies relied on self reports and varied widely in design. The authors call for stronger studies to aim programs at what truly moves the needle.
europmc-pmc3114807:
Mark Mendell and colleagues reviewed studies on damp buildings and breathing health for a 2011 paper in Environmental Health Perspectives. Many surveys had linked visible damp or mould at home and work to cough, wheeze, and asthma, but proof of cause stayed unclear. The team gathered study findings through late 2009, including pooled analyses.

Across studies, damp or mouldy indoor spaces were tied again and again to asthma starting or worsening, plus bronchitis, chest infections, and allergy symptoms. The link held in allergic and non-allergic people alike. Evidence was strongest that damp worsens asthma in children. Direct measures of microbes in dust gave only patchy results, pointing both ways. The authors advise fixing damp and mould rather than testing dust to guide health action.
europmc-pmc3128707:
James Zawada and colleagues described a cell-free protein factory that scales from tiny tests to factory vessels in a 2011 paper in Biotechnology and Bioengineering. Making medical proteins inside living cells is often slow to develop, since cell health and folding must be tuned together. Their system instead uses bacterial extracts in open vessels, with no living cells to keep alive.

Because the process scales in a straight line, conditions tuned in microlitre wells, from extract handling to gene tweaks and folding chemistry, held true in standard large reactors. A human signalling protein used in medicine came out fully active at high yield within ten hours, followed by a simplified purification. The authors present the system as a faster road to making complex medical proteins.
europmc-pmc3137407:
Melanie Gooden and colleagues pooled studies on immune cells inside tumours in a 2011 paper in the British Journal of Cancer. White blood cells often gather within cancers, presumably attacking them, and many reports linked their presence to longer survival. The review asked which cell types truly predict outcome across solid cancers.

Tumours rich in general T cells or in killer T cells were tied to a clearly lower risk of death. Regulatory T cells, which calm immune attacks, showed no clear link on their own. The balance between killer and regulatory cells gave the strongest signal, though few studies reported it. The authors warn that study size and follow-up length skewed results, and urge careful design plus routine reporting of cell ratios.
europmc-pmc3190407:
Brian Ondov, Nicholas Bergman, and Adam Phillippy created a browser-based chart tool for community DNA studies in a 2011 paper in BMC Bioinformatics. Such studies estimate how abundant each organism group is, with real uncertainty in the assignments, and existing charts either flattened the family hierarchy or hid confidence. Their tool draws the hierarchy as interactive layered rings.

Ring segments size to abundance and colour to a second variable such as confidence, and users can zoom into any branch by clicking. Built with standard web technology, each chart is a self-contained page needing no installed software or plug-ins, easy to email or post online. The code is free under an open licence, with converters for popular analysis packages.
europmc-pmc3242607:
Alexandra Smith and colleagues reported blood cancer incidence by detailed subtype from a British research network, in this 2011 paper in the British Journal of Cancer. Counting these cancers accurately is notoriously hard, because diagnosis mixes microscopy, immune markers, and genetics. Their network covers a population of about three and a half million, with every diagnosis made by one integrated laboratory and recorded to trial standards.

Over five years the network recorded more than ten thousand cases, split into twenty-four subtypes. Patients ranged from infants to near-centenarians, with a median age around seventy. For several subtypes, male rates were more than double female rates, in children as well as adults. No link with deprivation appeared. The authors argue that dependable population data are achievable, and that age and sex, not social position, are the promising leads for causes.
europmc-pmc3260807:
William Chappell and a large group of co-authors reviewed drugs that block two of the cell's main growth-signaling routes, in this 2011 paper in Oncotarget. The Ras-driven cascade and the PI3K-driven cascade are switched on in many cancers, often by mutations in the pathways themselves or in the receptors above them. Together they control cell division, death, and differentiation.

When these pathways go wrong, they can also drive resistance to chemotherapy, sustain cancer-initiating cells, and speed cellular aging. The review evaluates newer uses of inhibitors aimed at steps in each cascade, including the MEK, PI3K, Akt, and mTOR enzymes. Beyond shrinking malignant growth, the authors consider suppressing cancer stem cells, slowing senescence, and possibly preventing aspects of aging, arguing these interconnected pathways deserve their central place in drug development.
europmc-pmc3266307:
Qiyuan Li and colleagues created Jetset, a method for choosing the single best probe set to represent each gene on a microarray, in this 2011 paper in BMC Bioinformatics. Many chips measure one gene with several probe sets. Those sets can disagree or even contradict one another. That leaves researchers without a clean reading for a gene they care about.

Jetset scores every probe set on three qualities. It checks how specific the set is to its target. It checks how well it covers the gene's splice variants, and how robust it stays as transcripts degrade. The best-scoring set becomes the gene's sole representative, a simple one-to-one map. In tests against protein measurements and against genes known to rise and fall together, the chosen sets agreed more strongly than the alternatives, confirming the picks.
europmc-pmc3274507:
James Kijas and an international consortium surveyed the genomes of sheep breeds from around the world in this 2012 paper in PLoS Biology. Sheep were among the first animals domesticated, roughly eleven thousand years ago in the Fertile Crescent, and breeding has since reshaped them for wool, meat, and local conditions. The team read genomic variation across a global collection of breeds to recover that history.

The structure they found records high levels of historic mixture between populations, as animals moved and were crossbred over centuries. Layered on that mixing are sharp marks of recent artificial selection. Breeders' choices stand out in the genome around traits such as the loss of horns, coat pigmentation, reproduction, and body size. The study gives sheep geneticists a worldwide baseline for tracing how selection and movement made modern breeds.
europmc-pmc3282307:
J. A. Scott Kelso reviewed multistability and metastability as organizing principles of brain coordination in this 2012 paper in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B. Coordination dynamics is the science of how parts synchronize. It appears at every scale, from small neural circuits in animals to the large networks of the human brain. It spans both action and perception.

Multistability means a system can settle into several coordination patterns; it constrains how people intentionally change a pattern and how skills are learned. Kelso gathers the key evidence and shows how the phenomenon has been measured, modeled, and theoretically understood. He then argues that adding metastability, the tendency to hover between patterns without locking in, explains the brain's flexible coupling and the creative dynamics of goal-directed behavior.
europmc-pmc3282707:
Shannon Kidd and colleagues traced where the support cells inside tumors actually come from, in this 2012 paper in PLoS ONE. Fast-growing tumors recruit an entourage of non-cancerous cells that supply scaffolding, signals, and blood vessels, but the origins of that stroma were unclear. Using multicolored tissue transplants in mice with ovarian and breast tumors, the team measured each source's contribution cell type by cell type.

Most tumor-associated fibroblasts of the two kinds tracked came from mesenchymal stem cells resident in the bone marrow. In contrast, most of the vascular and fibrovascular stroma, the vessel-lining cells, pericytes, and contractile myofibroblasts, arrived from neighboring fat tissue. Tumors, the authors conclude, draw their building crews from multiple sources in a systematic, selective way, assigning different jobs to different suppliers.
europmc-pmc3296207:
Kim and colleagues reviewed a form of cell suicide that healthy cells undergo when they lose contact with their surroundings, in a 2012 article. Normal cells die by this process, called anoikis, once they detach from the tissue matrix or their neighbors. That built in barrier makes it hard for stray cells to seed tumors elsewhere in the body.

Cancer cells that spread have learned to resist this death signal. They survive floating through blood and lymph, and doctors can now catch such hardy cells in patient samples. The review walks through the survival tricks involved, from death signaling and shape change programs to energy use and protective membrane patches. Undoing this resistance, the authors argue, could help stop spread.
europmc-pmc3306207:
Stenvang, Petri, Lindow, Obad, and Kauppinen reviewed tools for switching off tiny gene regulators called microRNAs, in a 2012 article. These small RNAs fine tune gene activity, and when their levels go wrong they contribute to many diseases, from cancer to heart and metabolic disorders. Blocking a faulty microRNA is therefore both a research method and a possible route to new drugs.

The tools in focus are short synthetic strands, nicknamed antimiRs, designed to bind and disable a chosen microRNA. The review compares the chemical designs used, how the strands are delivered into living animals, and how researchers check that blocking worked without hitting unintended targets. It closes with progress toward drugs aimed at disease linked microRNAs.
europmc-pmc3317707:
Jozefczak, Remans, Vangronsveld, and Cuypers reviewed how a small plant molecule helps defend against metal poisoning, in a 2012 article. Since industrialization, metal emissions have overwhelmed natural cycles, and excess metals poison living cells largely by stirring up damaging oxygen based chemicals. Plants cannot flee contaminated soil, so they rely on chemical defenses, with the molecule glutathione at the center.

Glutathione grips metal ions directly, neutralizes harmful reactive chemicals, and carries signals that switch on wider defenses. Its sulfur bearing building block gives it this triple talent. The review follows each role in turn, from keeping metal levels balanced inside cells to fighting oxidative damage and passing alarm signals under metal stress. The authors frame glutathione as a key player that breeders and engineers might strengthen to protect crops on polluted land.
europmc-pmc3366107:
Wootton surveyed two decades of trials testing whether telemedicine helps manage five widespread long-term conditions: asthma, COPD, diabetes, heart failure, and hypertension. Rather than pooling outcomes statistically, the synthesis categorised each intervention by the results its own investigators reported, giving a high-level view of the whole evidence base.

The review found 141 randomised trials covering nearly thirty-eight thousand patients. Most reported positive effects and almost none reported negative ones, a pattern Wootton reads as publication bias. Trials were typically short, with a median of six months, and few examined cost-effectiveness. His verdict: the overall evidence for telemedicine in chronic disease remains weak and contradictory.
europmc-pmc3410907:
Voight led a consortium in 2012 that designed the Metabochip, a custom DNA-testing array for metabolism and heart traits. Genome-wide scans had already found hundreds of spots tied to diabetes, heart disease, body weight, and blood fats, plus thousands of near-misses. Following up so many spots one trait at a time would be slow and costly.

The chip reads nearly two hundred thousand chosen markers in one go. It lets researchers confirm borderline spots and zoom into proven ones, while comparing results across related traits on the same footing. The paper reports how well the chip captures variation, how to fill its gaps by statistical guessing, and the cost savings over single-trait kits. Similar custom arrays, they argue, are powerful follow-up tools.
europmc-pmc3433407:
Pai and colleagues argued in 2012 that bedside testing for infectious diseases in poorer countries fails or thrives on far more than the test itself. Enthusiasm for point-of-care diagnostics is rising, but a good test on the shelf does not guarantee adoption. Barriers stack up across money, regulation, policy, and the beliefs of users and providers.

Their framework treats point-of-care testing as a spectrum: technologies from simplest to sophisticated, users from lay people to specialists, settings from homes to hospitals. What counts as point-of-care, they insist, is successful use at the point of care, so programs matter more than gadgets. Matching product design to each setting's barriers, they say, is how developers find the highest-impact model.
europmc-pmc3437707:
Nordmann, Poirel, and Dortet unveiled a rapid test in 2012 for bacteria that destroy carbapenems, the last-line antibiotics. Germs making these enzymes, called carbapenemases, resist nearly all related drugs and often carry other resistance traits too. Existing checks were slow, costly, or missed whole enzyme families, delaying isolation of carriers in hospitals.

Their Carba NP test works from a bacterial colony and watches a carbapenem drug being broken down in a dish. Against gene-based methods it scored perfectly on both sensitivity and specificity in their hands. Results arrive in under two hours at low cost, with no special gear. Any laboratory, they argue, can run it to flag dangerous carriers fast enough to stop outbreaks.

europmc-pmc3530507: Domestic violence got a mental-health review. This 2012 pooled study links domestic violence to mental disorders. The authors reveal the link. Their work guides policy. Trevillion's team led the work. The paper is a landmark. It is widely cited. It shaped victim support.
europmc-pmc3573107: HIV hideouts got a measures review. This 2013 paper compares ways to measure hidden HIV. The authors weigh the measures. Their review guides cure research. Eriksson's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped HIV cure trials.
europmc-pmc3584907: E-learning got a poor-countries review. This 2013 paper reviews e-learning for medical schools in poor countries. The authors map the challenges. Their review guides educators. Frehywot's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped global health training. The review is widely taught.

europmc-pmc3634007: Activity got a motion-gravity split. This 2013 paper splits motion and gravity in activity signals. The authors reveal the split. Their work guides research. van Hees's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped wearable research.

europmc-pmc3833107: HIV got a shame-and-pills review. This 2013 review links shame to missed HIV pills. The authors weigh the evidence. Their review guides policy. Katz's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped HIV care. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3839907: Depression got a UK-Biobank study. This 2013 study maps mood disorders in 172,000 Brits. The authors reveal the rates. Their work guides psychiatry. Smith's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped mental-health research.
europmc-pmc3906607: Dementia got a 20-year checkup. This 2013 paper compares dementia rates across 20 years. The authors reveal the comparison. Their work guides geriatrics. Matthews's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped dementia policy. It is a landmark.
europmc-pmc3908707: Alcohol got a long-term-harms review. This 2013 paper reviews alcohol's long-term harms. The authors map the harms. Their review guides policy. Shield's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped alcohol policy. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc4008607: Toxicity got a cocktail-effects review. This 2014 review measures chemical cocktail effects. The author weighs the measures. Their review guides toxicology. Cedergreen's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped chemical safety. The review is widely taught. Regulators rely on it.
europmc-pmc4045207: Bacteria got an inside-plants review. This 2014 paper reviews bacteria inside plants. The authors map the inside. Their review guides microbiology. Brader's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped plant science. The review is widely taught. Students rely on it.

europmc-pmc7331607: Doctors and scientists took on synovial cell cross-talk with cartilage plays a major role in the pathogenesis (how the disease develops) of osteoarthritis in this 2020 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc7350507: This 2020 research paper covers immune phenotyping based on the neutrophil (first-responder immune cell)-to-immune cell ratio and igg level helps predict disease severity (how bad it gets). Introduction: a recently new breathing disease named COVID-19 has quickly spread across the world. Better ways to spot trouble early give doctors a head start on treatment.
europmc-pmc7616807: Doctors and scientists took on the 2021 report of the lancet countdown on health and climate change: code red for a healthy future in this 2021 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.

europmc-pmc7967607: Doctors and scientists took on the impact of COVID-19 on mental health in adolescents: a systematic review (a review of every study) in this 2021 review paper. The authors gathered every relevant study they could find and weighed the results together. Having the evidence weighed in one place saves busy doctors from sifting through dozens of papers alone.
europmc-pmc8012207: A fresh look at single-cell (one cell at a time) atlas of early human brain growth highlights heterogeneity (mixed results) of human neuroepithelial cells and early arrived with this 2021 research paper. The human cortex comprises diverse cell types that emerge from an initially uniform neuroepithelium that gives rise to radial glia. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc8078907: This 2021 research paper covers the safety and immunogenicity of one versus two doses of the COVID-19 vaccine BNT162b2 for patients with cancer: interim analysis. The efficacy (how well something works) and safety profiles of vaccines against SARS-CoV-2 in patients with cancer is unknown. If later work backs it up, the finding could open a new path for treating the illness.
europmc-pmc8185607: This 2021 research paper covers underlying medical conditions linked to severe COVID-19 illness among children. Importance information on underlying conditions and severe COVID-19 illness among children is limited. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc8189907: A fresh look at swarm learning for decentralized and confidential clinical (in patients) machine learning (computers learning patterns) arrived with this 2021 research paper. Fast and reliable spotting of patients with severe and heterogeneous illnesses is a major goal of precision medicine. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc8385107: Published in 2021, this research paper takes on dysregulated cholesterol homeostasis results in resistance to ferroptosis (an iron-driven form of cell death) increasing tumorigenicity and metastasis (cancer spread) in cancer. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc8386807: A fresh look at multicenter epidemiologic study of coronavirus disease-linked mucormycosis, India arrived with this 2021 research paper. During September-December 2020, we conducted a multicenter retrospective study across India to evaluate epidemiology (how diseases spread in populations). europmc-pmc8409907: A 2022 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at the risk factors and disease profile of post-preventive shots SARS-CoV-2 infection in UK users of the COVID. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. A sharper test or warning sign can change outcomes, since earlier care usually works better.
europmc-pmc9259607: A fresh look at signaling (cell-to-cell messaging) pathways involved in ischemic stroke: mechanisms (the inner workings) and treatment treatments arrived with this 2022 research paper. Once the chain of events is mapped, future treatments can be built to break it.
europmc-pmc9261907: A fresh look at hypoxia signaling (cell-to-cell messaging) in human health and diseases: implications (what the findings mean) and prospects for therapeutics (treatments) arrived with this 2022 research paper. Oxygen is essential for most biological (from living things) reactions in mammalian cells. Once the chain of events is mapped, future treatments can be built to break it.
europmc-pmc9262707: A 2022 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at oxford nanopore r10-4 long-read sequencing (reading DNA letter by letter) enables the generation of near-finished germ genomes from pure cultures and metagenomes. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc9337707: Doctors and scientists took on fine-mapping from summary data with the "sum of single effects" model in this 2022 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc9674007: This 2017 research paper covers maternal H3K27me3 controls DNA methylation (chemical tagging of DNA)-independent imprinting. Mammalian sperm and oocytes have other epigenetic (gene-switching) landscapes and are organized in other fashions. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc9885707: A 2023 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at car-cell therapy in the era of solid tumor treatment: current problems and new treatment advances (new steps forward). The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Results like these feed the work that turns lab findings into future treatments.
fbi-vault-special-counsel-mueller-invest: Part seven of the FBI Vault's records on the Special Counsel Mueller investigation. The probe examined Russian interference in the 2016 election. This section holds more of the released material. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
ferrero-greatness-decline-rome-vol-1-190:
Guglielmo Ferrero's The Greatness and Decline of Rome, Volume 1, appears in Henry J. Zimmern's translation of 1907. Subtitled The Empire-Builders, the volume covers Rome from the Gracchi to Caesar. Ferrero, an Italian historian, reads Caesar's age as modern politics in ancient dress. Parties, finance, and empire drive his story.

He treats the conquests of Gaul and the civil wars with brisk narrative skill. The book was the great popular Roman history of the early 1900s. Scholars faulted some bold guesses, yet readers loved its pace. Ferrero wrote for the educated public across Europe and America. Volume 1 of five opens his lively, disputed epic.
flammarion-mysterious-psychic-forces-190:
Camille Flammarion brought a star man's fame to the dark room in Mysterious Psychic Forces, his book of 1907. Flammarion was the most loved voice on the stars in France. Late in life he turned his keen eye to seers. He sat with Eusapia Palladino, the famed name from Italy, and weighed her feats through long, strict tests in his own rooms.

He grants strange force, yet keeps his doubts in plain view. His rank made the book a mark on the main land. It shows a great mind torn twixt awe and care. Its fame still stands.
ford-privy-seal-1907:
Privy Seal, published in 1907, is the middle volume of Ford's Katharine Howard trilogy, his historical sequence on the fifth wife of Henry VIII. The first volume brought Katharine to court; this one charts the machinery around the throne.

Thomas Cromwell, the king's great minister, falls as factions shift, and Katharine rises toward the crown through a court of spies and suitors. Ford tells Tudor politics as atmosphere and impression rather than pageant. The trilogy was his bid for serious standing as a novelist. Read together, the three books build one of the finest historical sequences in English.
forster-longest-journey-1907:
E. M. Forster published The Longest Journey in 1907, his second novel. Forster later said it was the book of his that he felt closest to. It draws on his Cambridge years and his unease with respectable English life.

Rickie Elliot, a lame and sensitive Cambridge graduate, writes stories and searches for honest connection. He marries into a dull, controlling family and betrays his own gifts. Then a rough half-brother appears, and Rickie must decide what loyalty really means. The story turns tragic as Rickie tries to rescue the brother he first denied. It is Forster's most personal and painful novel.
francke-history-western-tibet-1907:
August Hermann Francke was a Moravian missionary and scholar who lived for years in Ladakh, on India's border with Tibet. His History of Western Tibet, published in 1907, is the pioneering history of that high Himalayan land. Francke read its chronicles, inscriptions, and folk songs at first hand.

He traces the kings of Ladakh from the old Tibetan empire through Buddhist rule to the Dogra conquest of the 1840s. Rock carvings and royal songs fill gaps where written records run thin. The book remains a base source for the history of Ladakh and of Tibetan Buddhism on India's frontier.
freeman-light-of-soul-1907:
Harper published By the Light of the Soul in January 1907, with pictures by Harold Brett. Freeman dedicated the novel to Harriet and Carolyn Alden. Chapter one places young Maria Edgham in a church vestry during the weekly prayer meeting.

A young man reads aloud that God chastens those he loves, and a soft sob answers behind Maria. Mrs. Jasper Cone, who lost her baby the week before, is weeping there. Maria feels spite at the sound, which opens her long inner struggle. The drama stays inward, as conscience, desire, and the claims of others pull a dutiful woman toward a fuller life.
frus-1861-d107:
Gideon Welles, the Secretary of the Navy, received a letter from William H. Seward on 19 October 1861. The letter is document 107 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Most papers in the volume cross the ocean, but this one crosses the cabinet room. The Navy ran the blockade that Britain watched so closely. Seward and Welles had to keep their stories straight, since each naval act could become a diplomatic crisis by the next mail. Welles, a former newsman, kept a famed diary that still ranks beside this record. A famed diary beside a full record gives the Navy's war a double witness.
frus-1861-d207:
On 11 July 1861, Mr. Wood wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as Document 207 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. It belongs to the first summer of the Civil War, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d307:
A letter from Mr. Varas reached Secretary of State William H. Seward on 7 August 1861. It stands as Document 307 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. It belongs to the first summer of the Civil War, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.
