Inbound mail like this one showed Washington how the war looked from outside its own posts. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d107:
Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London was the reader in mind when William H. Seward wrote on 18 July 1862. It stands as Document 107 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. The letter comes from the summer of 1862, the war's second year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d207:
Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed Lord Lyons on 6 February 1862 in a note printed as Document 207 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Lyons was the British minister in Washington, the man Seward saw most among foreign envoys.

February brought the Union a bright win with the fall of Fort Henry in Tennessee, news that colored foreign readings of the war. Britain and France both measured their steps by such results. A brief Seward note in this month belongs to the constant traffic between the two offices. Through it Washington argued that the Union would win and should be left to do it.
frus-1862-d307:
The third Seward dispatch of 23 August 1862 stands as Document 307 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Like its mates, it went from Secretary of State William H. Seward to William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris.

Read alone, a third same-day letter looks like a fragment. Read with Documents 305 and 306, it completes the Department's Paris brief for that mail. The habit of judging these papers in clusters, not singly. Is the first skill the Foreign Relations volumes teach, and the August cluster teaches it well. Dayton, a former senator from New Jersey, held the Paris post from 1861 until his death in 1864.
frus-1862-d407:
Dated 5 August 1862, this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward went to Horace J. Perry at the legation in Madrid. It stands as Document 407 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's official diplomatic record.

Three days after his last order to the same desk, Seward was writing again, a sign of how fast the Spanish questions moved that summer. Confederate agents sought ships, coal, and sympathy in Spanish ports. Union agents worked to shut those doors. The dispatch belongs to that contest, and it shows the steady, almost daily hand Washington kept on its smallest European posts during the Civil War.
frus-1862-d507:
James Shepherd Pike sent this report from The Hague to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 25 June 1862. It is Document 507 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's official record.

Pike wrote on the day the Seven Days battles began in Virginia, though weeks would pass before he knew it. His letter dealt with the Netherlands as he found it that week. He found a careful ministry and a busy press. He also found merchants counting the cost of the war. Reports of this kind look routine, but they were the only eyes Washington had in The Hague. Read in sequence, Pike's dispatches show Dutch opinion holding roughly steady for the Union through the shocks of that summer.
frus-1862-d607:
Thomas Corwin reported from Mexico to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 28 August 1862. The dispatch is Document 607 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's official record.

Corwin wrote from a capital whose government was fighting a French invasion with scant money and men. His late-summer report described the republic's endurance and the French advance as they appeared from Mexico City. Washington, then losing battles of its own, could offer Mexico sympathy and a clear record of protest. Corwin's letters supplied the facts that record required. The dispatch keeps the Mexican file's grave, steady tone through the war's darkest month for both republics.
frus-1862-d707:
James R. Partridge wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 26 August 1862. Partridge was an American envoy in Central America, a Maryland lawyer sent out by the Lincoln government. The letter is document 707 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Envoys in the small republics reported on local politics, trade, and the transit routes that linked the Atlantic and Pacific. Partridge's letter belongs to that watch. Washington's stake there was out of scale with the posts' size, since a future canal made every mile of the isthmus count. This dispatch is one page of the record that stake produced.
frus-1863p1-d107:
On 2 March 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this letter to Charles Francis Adams, the eleventh of twelve dated that day. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 107 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The next-to-last sheet of a batch often mops up: a late fact, a small claim, a word of tone. Seward's eleventh letter of 2 March sits in that place in the row. The batch it belongs to is the marvel. It re-laid a whole brief in a day, for the post that could most help or harm the Union. This letter is one of its last strokes.
frus-1863p1-d207:
From Washington on 23 May 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 207 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

Instructions like this one show how the Lincoln government ran a war abroad while fighting one at home. The paper trail is the diplomacy itself, order by order. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d307:
Washington's orders to London on 9 October 1863 came in this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 307 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Seward's orders set the line Adams had to press on the British government. They told him what to demand, what to soften, and when to wait. By then the British government had moved to hold the Confederate rams, and the sharpest crisis of the year was cooling. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d407:
In Washington on 3 March 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 407 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

The two men met and wrote constantly, and both knew a quarrel between their countries could hand the South its independence. That shared fear kept the tone correct even when the words were sharp. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d507:
Secretary of State William H. Seward took up his pen on 12 May 1863 and wrote to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d607:
Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington wrote this official letter to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 10 August 1863. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad.

The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d107: On November 9, 1943, Churchill wrote to Roosevelt, as both men counted down to their journeys. His message is Document 107 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The prime minister would travel by warship and aircraft through the Mediterranean, as the president would by sea. The record gives the date and the two names and no subject. The message is printed in the Foreign Relations series among the departure papers.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d207:
Robert Kelley, the American chargé in Ankara, sent a long most-secret telegram to Washington late on 10 November 1943. It follows his report of 8 November and gives the British ambassador's own summary, shared that afternoon on his return from Cairo, of the Eden and Numan talks.

Numan had flatly refused Allied air bases, citing German power to bomb Turkish cities and a public not ready for war. On joining the war, he said Turkey would want to help in earnest, not stand aside making faces at the Germans. Above all he feared Soviet entry into the Balkans, and wanted pledges that Moscow sought no land or bases there. He agreed to take the questions back to Turkey's leaders.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d307:
An American draft of the Cairo communiqué, dated 25 November 1943, carries handwritten amendments by Harry Hopkins. The draft itself was dictated by Hopkins the day before and put before Roosevelt; this version adds three closing paragraphs naming those who attended the conference.

Its text says the three leaders and their military missions have agreed on future operations against Japan from China and Southeast Asia, and promises unrelenting pressure by sea, land, and air. Japan's Pacific islands will be taken from her forever, the land stolen from China, such as Manchuria and Formosa, returned, and Korea made free and independent after Japan falls. The three nations pledge to fight on together until Japan surrenders unconditionally. Hopkins' margin notes add phrases about conquests taken by violence and greed.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d407: Harry Hopkins passed President Roosevelt a short handwritten note at Tehran on 1 December 1943, during the political meeting of the three leaders. The whole note takes three lines. It opens with the time, ten past eight in the evening. Hopkins then asks whether Roosevelt wishes, at dinner, to introduce the method of the Allied occupation of Germany after her collapse. Nothing in the entry records the President's answer.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d507:
Prime Minister Churchill handed this composite memorandum to Harry Hopkins on December 7, 1943, the day after the Second Cairo Conference closed. A composite paper gathered several points into one document for the President's side. The State Department printed it in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Churchill was a tireless writer of minutes and memoranda, and handing one to Hopkins was his way of placing British views directly before Roosevelt. The paper belongs to the argument that continued even as the delegations packed to leave Cairo. For readers, it shows the Prime Minister still pressing his case on paper after the formal sessions had ended.
frus-1944-quebec-d107:
State Department staff prepared a briefing paper dated September 5, 1944. Briefing papers state a question, the facts, and a recommended position. The department printed this one in the Quebec 1944 volume. It was ready one week before the conference.

Good briefing papers let a leader master a topic fast. Department experts distilled files into a few clear pages. The Quebec agenda gave them plenty to distill that September. Germany's treatment, allied aid, and Pacific strategy all needed decisions. For readers, the paper shows expertise being packaged for power. It is the staff system working exactly as designed.
frus-1944-quebec-d207:
The Joint Chiefs met on September 16, 1944, to turn the Roosevelt-Churchill zones agreement into a formal paper. Leahy presented his memorandum outlining the British and American areas, with access to northwestern seaports and passage through the British area. Marshall and King wanted one port specified under complete American control, able to handle some 10,000 tons of supplies daily.

King proposed Bremen, and Marshall drafted the paragraph vesting control of Bremen and its staging areas in the American zone commander. The amended memorandum was approved for the Combined Chiefs, later circulated as C.C.S. 320/26. The meeting also heard Stilwell's grim report from China and approved Marshall's draft message from the president to Chiang Kai-shek.
frus-1945-50-intel-d107:
Acting Secretary of War Howard Petersen wrote to Quinn, the new director of the Strategic Services Unit, on 3 April 1946. The SSU was on its third chief in a year. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Petersen's letter belongs to the unit's last season, when its absorption into the Central Intelligence Group was being arranged in detail. A department's acting secretary writing to a shrinking unit's chief shows the end being managed from the top, not left to drift. Readers can follow the SSU thread to its close in these spring papers. Each one moves men, money, or duties from the old remnant to the new group, until the remnant's name fades from the file.
frus-1945-50-intel-d207:
The Deputy Director of Central Intelligence (Wright) addressed a memorandum to the President’s Special Counsel (Clifford) on 28 January 1947. It is document 207 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. The first peace-time setup paired the National Intelligence Authority at the top with the Central Intelligence Group below it.

A short memo could set a meeting, kill a plan, or start one. This one played its part in that daily traffic. Whole policies can be traced through chains of such notes, each one moving the matter a step. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d307: The title "Memorandum for the File" heads a text dated 16 November 1948. It stands as document 307 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. The first Dulles Report season had begun: an outside team judged the CIA while the agency and its partners answered back. The form is brief by design: one event, one date, and the names that make the entry checkable.
frus-1945-50-intel-d407:
Director of Central Intelligence Roscoe Hillenkoetter wrote once more to Sidney Souers of the National Security Council on 27 December 1949. The memo is document 407 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Souers, the Council's executive secretary, had led the CIA before Hillenkoetter and knew its weak points well. Notes between the two men linked the agency to the White House staff. This late December memo closes a year of steady paper between the CIA and the Council. The year end date gives the memo a stock taking tone, closing one year of the young system.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d107:
Germany's surrender terms were drafted long before the war ended. The European Advisory Commission worked in London under terms set at the Moscow Conference. It sent the three allied governments this report, with a draft instrument titled “Unconditional Surrender of Germany.” The report is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

The commission calls its draft mainly a military instrument in three parts. The preamble has Germany admit the complete defeat of her armed forces on land, at sea, and in the air. Short military articles then order all German forces to stop fighting. Later parts let the allied representatives take the first steps of control. The text became one of the basic papers of the occupation.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d207:
De Gaulle asked Roosevelt to hurry arms for eight French divisions, and Ambassador Caffery cabled the letter's text from Paris on 2 January 1945. The cable is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. The French leader writes as an ally straining to field more men.

Germany will not be beaten completely, de Gaulle argues, without new forces thrown in. France, despite three million men lost or absent, can raise her strength powerfully and fast, and burns to do so. Her arms factories are restarting, but machine tools are battered and raw materials short. America armed eight divisions in North Africa, an effort not lost, and has lately agreed to equip eight more. He thanks the President, and begs speed: the French army can use all of it in battle within three months.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d307:
In place of a missing meeting record, the editors of this FRUS volume supply a short note on what can still be known. No account of the session's substance survives in the files, they explain. What remains comes from Secretary Stettinius's own later book and from a cable he sent that day.

From those scraps, the note reports a decision. The American and British chiefs of staff backed approval of the zones of occupation in Germany. Stettinius then wired Ambassador Winant in London so the plan could move ahead. The note is a small lesson in how editors rebuild a record from fragments.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d407: Stettinius wrote this brief message by hand at Yalta on February 9, 1945, and Hiss carried it to Gladwyn Jebb during the foreign ministers' meeting. Its point was care about blame. The delegations must be sure that no duty rested on them in relation to states such as Iceland, Turkey, or Egypt joining the world body. Hiss's notation dates the errand to 12:30 that afternoon. He also recorded that he inserted the word Egypt himself. The slip survives in the Hiss collection.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d507:
Shipping waits for Washington in this memorandum from James Byrnes to the President, dated March 8, 1945. At Yalta, Byrnes recalls, Churchill had wished to discuss shipping and the British import program. Hopkins and Byrnes advised Lord Leathers that the problem was too complicated to settle so far from the basic data. It would have to be resolved in Washington.

Leathers accepted that view, Byrnes reports. He said several times that he would come to the United States at an early date to discuss the shipping situation. The excerpt, from the Roosevelt Papers, shows a Yalta side issue being deliberately postponed — and the postponement holding.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d107:
The U.S. Chiefs of Staff set out their view on staff size for Terminal in a memorandum dated June 28, 1945. The paper, C.C.S. 880/3, is document 107 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It answers a British memorandum of June 25 on how the two military staffs should be manned at the Berlin meeting.

Large military staffs should not be taken, the American chiefs hold, and detailed talks needing a big staff, on the scale of earlier conferences, should not be held there. They plan to bring only very small staffs, and they expect the agenda to be handled quickly. Subjects needing deep study belong in the normal Combined Chiefs of Staff machinery. If the British see the agenda differently, the Americans ask to be told.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d207:
Edward Page recorded Molotov probing the Italy item in a memorandum extract dated July 11, 1945. The extract is document 207 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Ambassador Harriman had called on Molotov to ask whether he had questions on the American agenda sent over on July 7.

Molotov asked whether it was proposed to study the peace treaty for Italy. Harriman replied that his letter spoke only of policy toward Italy, and he did not know whether the President would propose studying the treaty at Berlin, or whether such study was timely. He asked whether the Soviet government had studied the matter. Molotov did not answer that question. He said, however, that he was anxious to know whether anything was being prepared on a draft treaty. The fencing shows both sides testing each other's intentions before the leaders met.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d307:
Barnes warned from Sofia on July 9, 1945, that American silence was costing ground in Bulgaria. His subject was Russia's threat of force against Turkey over the Straits. Washington had made no public response while the United Nations charter was being signed. Local Communists, he wrote, drew their own lesson from that.

To them, silence proved American weakness beside Soviet strength. The claim strengthened Communist hands and weakened the Bulgarians still fighting for a free course at home and abroad. Barnes argued that quiet diplomacy, with only private words in Moscow, could never better matters in the region. His cable pressed for a firmer public stand.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d407:
A fight over one sentence fills Winant's extracts from London of July 7, 1945. On July 6 the European Advisory Commission agreed the preamble to the French zone agreement, and approved the report that would accompany it, except for its final sentence. That sentence recommended the four governments order their commanders in Germany to fix, jointly, the Berlin area France would occupy.

The American, British, and French delegations approved the sentence. The Soviet representative, Gousev, pressed for its omission. He insisted that since the Crimea decision formed the French zone from the American and British zones, the French area in Berlin must also come from those two zones alone. The sentence stayed in dispute.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d507:
Warsaw travel and Polish troops in Britain fill Winant's cable from London of July 9, 1945. Hankey has postponed his departure for Warsaw until July 12, the Foreign Office official said, and may not leave until July 15. Britain is negotiating in Moscow for a direct air service to Warsaw, but he may have to fly by British plane to Berlin, then by Russian plane on to Warsaw.

On Polish troops, the War Office has issued a circular to all British commanders of Polish detachments. They are to assure the Poles under their command that no Pole will be returned to Poland against his will. Britain also hopes to abolish the Polish Ministry of Defence in the immediate future.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d607:
An extract from a briefing paper on Japan's surrender, dated June 29, 1945, sets goals on the Cairo Declaration. It is document 607 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The paper is the same briefing text that appears in extract in two other documents of the volume.

The minimum goal is twofold. The Soviet government should adhere to the Cairo Declaration. The three powers should also agree to consult each other and China before acting on its land terms. That would back the return of Manchuria and Formosa to China and a free Korea. It would also stop any one power from setting up a friendly regime on its own. The maximum goal goes further. The powers, with China's help, would jointly back the growth of a strong, democratic, independent Korea.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d707:
Turkey's foreign minister Saka called on Ambassador Winant in London on July 13, 1945, to state his country's case. Winant's secret summary is document 707 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Saka came with the Turkish ambassador at his side.

Saka said Turkey had been willing to admit that its friendship treaty with Russia needed revision. Ankara had asked Moscow what it proposed as the basis for a new treaty. No answer came until Molotov returned from San Francisco. Then, to Turkish surprise, he set preconditions for even considering a revised treaty. Russia would expect the cession of Kars and Ardahan in the east. It would expect Soviet bases on the Straits as well. An understanding on revising the Montreux Convention was the third demand. Despite supposed Yalta assurances, Saka said, Turkey now had grave fears of Soviet intent.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1007:
Soviet delegates presented this proposal on the German navy and merchant marine to the foreign ministers on July 19, 1945. It claims a one-third share for the Soviet Union across the board. The share covers the whole German navy, even ships still building or under repair when Germany surrendered.

A third of naval reserve weapons, ammunition, and supplies would also pass to the USSR, matched by ship class. So would a third of the German merchant marine. Transfers would start on August 1 and end by November 1, 1945. An expert commission, named by the three Allied naval commands, would handle the handover of ships in ports at home and abroad.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1107:
Charles Yost, executive secretary of the Central Secretariat serving the American team, wrote this memorandum on 9 August 1945. That date fell a week after the Potsdam Conference ended. The secretariat was the summit's paperwork hub, the office that handled schedules, papers, and the flow of records.

A wrap-up note like this one belongs to the work of closing out a summit. Files had to be sorted, copies made, and the record put in order for the trip home. The text shows the plain, needed labor that turns weeks of talk into a usable archive. Big events run on small tasks, and this is one of them.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1207:
Prime Minister Tito and Foreign Minister Subasic of Yugoslavia wrote jointly to President Truman on 25 July 1945. Tito, the partisan chief turned ruler, led a government the West did not fully trust. Subasic spoke for the royalist strand joined into that government.

A joint appeal from the pair sought American goodwill for the new Yugoslav state. Belgrade wanted standing, aid, and a hearing while the summit weighed Balkan questions. The letter shows Yugoslavia courting Washington while keeping Moscow close. It is a bid from a small state caught between giants, made in the most formal way open to it.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1307:
Harrison wrote to Stimson on 21 July 1945, keeping the Interim Committee channel warm. The committee's acting chairman reported to the war secretary as the summit's first week closed. Their subject was the atomic file: the test's meaning, the choices ahead, and the words to use about both.

By then the full test report had reached Potsdam and the president had been briefed. The choices about the bomb's use were narrowing. Harrison's notes helped Stimson carry them. This message is one more link in a quiet chain. That chain ran from a New Mexico desert to a German palace, by way of two men's pens.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1407:
A second Caffery cable to Secretary Byrnes is dated 6 August 1945. Caffery's Paris embassy was reporting on several French questions at once that week. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Secretaries of state read only a slice of the paper their departments produce. So cables sent to Byrnes by name mark the files Caffery most wanted decided. Two in one day to the secretary is a strong signal from an ambassador. Read with the cables to the acting secretary from the same dates, this one shows sorting by rank. Routine matters went down one channel. The pressing ones went up the other.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-107:
A second delegation memorandum dated July 25, 1945 joins the American staff papers in the Potsdam record. The volume holds several such memos from the same day, a sign of the workload. Each carried a piece of business between offices or up to senior men. This one was printed in the second Potsdam volume of the official Foreign Relations series.

Staff memoranda rarely make dramatic reading, and that is their strength. They record what officials thought they knew on a given day. Historians use them to date ideas and trace who pushed them. The memo adds one firm point to the map of the conference's middle days.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d807:
Kirk reported from Rome on July 23, 1945, in document 807. The ambassador in Italy wrote to the Acting Secretary as Potsdam passed its midpoint. Italy's peace terms were among the questions shadowing the talks. His report joined the Italy thread in the second Potsdam volume.

A midpoint report from Rome shows a capital recalculating. Early summit news had reached Italy; hopes rose or fell with it. Kirk filtered that mood for Washington. Readers see an envoy managing both facts and feelings. The document adds the view from a beaten country's capital at the hour its fate was being weighed elsewhere.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d907:
American drafters wrote this working paper on restitution at Babelsberg on July 22, 1945. A file note names Collado as its author. The paper lists the kinds of looted property that could be claimed back, wherever they were found.

The list covers heavy farm and factory equipment, machine tools, and unique machinery. It also covers rolling stock and other transport gear. A fourth class holds art, religious and cultural objects, libraries, and lab gear. Lost items in that class could be replaced with similar enemy property. Claims would be handled by the owner's own state.
fuller-star-in-the-west-1907:
An army officer took Crowley in earnest as a poet when few would, in 1907. The Star in the West, by John Fuller, is a critical essay on Crowley's works. Fuller would later win fame as a theorist of war and the tank.

He reads the young Crowley's verse and prose as the work of a major, strange gift. The essay sorts the books, weighs their worth, and defends their fire against a cold press. It is the first serious study of Crowley as a man of letters. The book catches him before the legend swallowed the writer.
gao-gaoreports-b-296307: Delta Dental of California doubled its July 2005 protest — two case numbers, one dental-services fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-297207: Marine Industries NW took its December 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-297807: Al Long Ford took its April 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The dealership said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Car dealers get the same full hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-299407: International Filter Manufacturing took its April 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict. The firm said the agency's award was unfair; the call tests the protest in full. Filter makers get the same clean hearing as any other bidder.
gao-gaoreports-b-316107: This 2008 GAO ruling is about availability of Funds for Purchase of Replacement Voting Equipment at Election Assistance Commission. GAO's legal decisions tell agencies what federal funding law allows. Agencies follow these rulings when spending federal funds. The full text sits with this description in the library.
gao-gaoreports-b-400107: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Exec Plaza, LLC. The August 1, 2008 ruling examines how the agency evaluated the bids. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts. The full text sits with this description in the library.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-407: Assembling Uncle Sam's books was still shaky in 2005, and GAO's audit says the process for the consolidated statements needed work. The auditors delivered the blunt grade. The nation's ledger deserved cleaner math. The statements had to hold up. The nation's ledger deserved cleaner math.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1007: The Treasury's backup plans needed shoring in 2006, and GAO's report says alternative funding options would strengthen resilience to market shocks. The findings prescribe the cushion. The report warns that the nation's wallet needed a spare. The backup had to be ready.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-607: Federal statistics needed better safeguarding in 2006, and GAO's report says expanded use of key dissemination practices would protect their integrity. The findings prescribe the practices. The report warns that the nation's numbers should be trustworthy. The integrity had to be guarded.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-807: Child care access needed better information sharing in 2006, and GAO's report says more review by HHS could enhance access for families. The findings demand the knowledge. The report warns that the littlest learners needed the system to work. The access had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1007: Bases about to swell with reassigned troops needed roofs, pipes, and power on a deadline — and GAO's 2007 report doubted the Army's build plans could keep up. The findings flag a support race against the clock: barracks and utilities due before the boots arrived. Miss, and readiness pays.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-307: Studying how doctors practiced could save Medicare millions in 2007 — GAO's report says a sharper focus on practice patterns would boost program efficiency. The findings make the data case for feedback. The report bets that measuring medicine carefully will improve medicine.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-407: The Capitol's caretaker needed to stay the course in 2007, and GAO's report says committed, sustained leadership had to continue the progress. The findings credit the gains. The report warns that the marble halls needed steady hands, not rotating ones. The dome deserved steady stewardship.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-707: The cheese market smelled funny in 2007 — GAO's report says oversight of the spot cheese trade had grown, but manipulation worries stuck around anyway. The findings probe the dairy dealings for rigged prices. The report's lesson: even cheddar has its sharp traders, and watchers must stay sharp too.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-807: Joint warfighting needed joint supply lines in 2007 — GAO's report says the Pentagon's distribution fixes could use a boost. The findings target the seams between the services' supply chains. The report's lesson: allies in battle should not be strangers in logistics.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-907: Troops' job rights were getting sloppy handling in 2007 — GAO's report says the Labor Department needed better quality checks on reemployment claims. The findings target the machinery behind the promise that service would not cost a career. The report demands proof the system worked for the returning.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-407: The Government Accountability Office dug into military Training: Compliance with Environmental Laws Affects Some Training Activities, but DOD Has Not Made a Sound Business Case for Additional Environmental in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-607: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on critical Infrastructure Protection: Further Efforts Needed to Integrate Planning for and Response to Disruptions on Converged Voice and Data Networks. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gervase-tilbury-otia-imperialia-leibniz-:
Gervase of Tilbury wrote the Otia Imperialia, meaning imperial leisure, for his royal reader in the early thirteenth century. This text follows the edition prepared by Leibniz in 1707. Gervase mixed history, geography, and marvel into three parts, or decisions, meant to amuse and inform an emperor.

His book of marvels is the famous part. It tells of wonders from many lands, including a well-known tale of a werewolf. Gervase reports local legends beside sober chronicle without drawing a line between them. The result is the thirteenth century's own store of wonders. Kings were meant to enjoy it, and modern readers of folklore still do.
gurdon-the-khasis-1907:
Philip Richard Thornhagh Gurdon served as a colonial officer in Assam, and his 1907 study presents the Khasi people of the hills there. The Khasis stood out to early writers because descent and property passed through women, not men.

Gurdon describes Khasi villages, clans, and customs, along with their system of inheritance through the youngest daughter. He gives long attention to ancestor worship, divination by eggs and other signs, and the sacred forests where no tree could be cut. Myths and folk tales fill out the picture. The book remains a basic early source on a society ordered around the mother line.
hague-conventions-1899-1907:
Delegates from around the world met at The Hague in 1899 and again in 1907 to write rules for war. The two peace conferences produced a set of conventions that stand as the first broad attempt to bind warfare by law. Governments hoped that agreed rules could limit cruelty even when nations still went to war.

The texts ban weapons such as poison gas and expanding bullets, and set rules for prisoners, neutral states, and the sick and wounded. They also created a court for settling disputes between nations by arbitration. The rules did not stop the world wars, but much of their language still shapes the law of armed conflict today.
history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-volum: Volume seven: the court of Sans Souci, the round table of wits, and Frederick the philosopher-king. Music, conversation, and the business of state fill these pages. Carlyle shows the king in his most civilized aspect. The enlightened despot at home.
hodgson-glen-carrig-1907:
Shipwreck throws a crew into a weird sea in William Hope Hodgson's first novel, from 1907. They find a vast swamp of weed in the far south seas. Strange beasts and lost ships wait in the gloom. The men must fight their way out by boat.

Told as a plain log, the tale keeps a tight grip. Fear comes from slime, rot, and things that lurk at the edge of sight. Hodgson knew the sea from his own years at sail. That grit gives the wild tale real weight. Weed men, crab beasts, and hulks of dead ships crowd the swamp. Each fight costs blood, which keeps the wild tale tense and grim.
hrdlicka-skeletal-remains-early-man-nort:
Ales Hrdlicka, the Smithsonian anthropologist, issued his survey of claimed early human bones in 1907. It appeared as Bulletin 33 of the Bureau of American Ethnology. Claim after claim of very ancient people in North America had reached the newspapers.

Hrdlicka examined each skeleton and site with strict skepticism. In case after case he found recent burials or weak evidence. His verdicts set the terms of debate about the first Americans for decades. Later discoveries moved the dates back, but his demand for proof endured. The bulletin became a standard reference for anyone claiming ancient American remains afterward.
james-pragmatism-1907:
William James published Pragmatism in 1907, the book that named a movement in philosophy. James gave the work first as lectures in Boston and New York. Pragmatism tests ideas by their practical results in experience. Truth, he argues, is what proves itself good in the way of belief over time.

He applies the test to God, free will, and the design of the world. The style is warm, vivid, and full of homely examples. Critics charged that he made truth mere usefulness, and James replied for years. The book shaped American thought far beyond philosophy. It remains the classic statement of the pragmatic method.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-07:
Volume 7, from 1897, spreads across Quebec, Huron country, and Cape Breton. Thwaites shows the mission pushing out in three directions at one time. Each front had its own risks, peoples, and hopes for new converts in the field.

Most weight falls on the new Huron mission in these pages. Its start opens the long road that ends in loss and death. Reports from the coast and the river round out the full picture. The pace of the whole chronicle quickens in this one volume. Readers feel the bold age of French America get fully under way.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lyon-abraham-de:
Abraham de Lyon, one of the first Jewish settlers in colonial Georgia, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Family tradition says he was born in Spain, but early records call him a vine-grower from Portugal. He arrived in 1733, the year Oglethorpe founded the colony. He settled in Savannah and soon became a freeholder.

The article centers on his work with grapes. Georgia's trustees hoped to make the colony a wine country, and De Lyon raised Porto and Malaga vines to great perfection. He offered to import vines and vine-growers from Portugal with a loan of two hundred pounds. The trustees accepted, though Oglethorpe passed only part of the money to him. A trustee's agent described his vineyard in detail in 1737. The entry preserves a rare portrait of a Jewish farmer shaping a new colony's plans.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-major-julius-10:
Julius Major, a Hungarian composer, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born on December 13, 1859, at Kaschau on the Hernad river, he began studies meant to make him an engineer. He left that path for the national music academy in Pesth. There Volkmann and Erkel taught him.

The article follows his work as a teacher and organizer. He taught music at several institutions and, by 1904, at the Jewish teachers' seminary in Budapest. At the Pesth gymnasium he built a pupils' orchestra. In 1894 he founded the Hungarian Women's Chorus. Two years later he opened a school of music that drew considerable popularity. Major was also a fine pianist known for chamber music. His works include two trios, violin sonatas, a piano concerto, and a Hungarian Sonata. The entry shows a composer who built musical life as much as he wrote it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-margolis-max-le:
Max Leopold Margolis, an American philologist, receives an entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Meretz, Russia, on October 15, 1866, he was the son of Isaac Margolis. He studied at Berlin's Leibnitz gymnasium and at Columbia University. His doctorate came from Columbia in 1891.

The article tracks a swift academic climb. Columbia gave him a fellowship in Semitic languages the year he graduated. From 1892 he taught Hebrew and Bible at Hebrew Union College in Cincinnati, rising to assistant professor. In 1897 he moved to the University of California as assistant professor of Semitic languages. Associate professor followed in 1898. Since 1902 he had acted as head of the department. His works include a study of a Columbia manuscript of Megillah and notes on Semitic grammar. The entry catches a young scholar remaking the study of Hebrew in America.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-may-mitchell-10: Mitchell May, a Brooklyn lawyer who sat in the United States Congress, is given a very brief entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906, contributed by Cyrus Adler. He was born in Brooklyn, New York, on July 10, 1871, and was educated at the Brooklyn Polytechnic Institute and at Columbia Law School. He served as a member of the Fifty-sixth Congress, from 1899 to 1901. Beyond that, the entry notes only that he held several positions in Jewish communal organizations.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-melol-moses-hay:
Moses Hay Melol, a compositor and translator at Leghorn, is entered briefly in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Richard Gottheil and Meyer Kayserling. Son of Jacob Raphael Melol and brother of David Hayyim Melol, he worked in the Hebrew printing world of Leghorn between 1777 and 1793, the years of his known publications.

In 1777 he translated or edited the "Sefer Azharot ha-Kodesh" and the Book of Ruth, both printed at Leghorn. Fifteen years later he put into Ladino the "Seder Hattarat Nedarim," the ritual for dissolving vows, as practised in the yeshivah Gemilut Hasadim, a text his Spanish-speaking readers could use directly. A kinsman, Mordecai Melol, edited an "Alegria de Purim" the same year. The notice is three sentences long, resting on Ersch and Gruber's encyclopedia and Kayserling's bibliography of Spanish-Portuguese Jewish literature.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mesha-10707:
Mesha was king of Moab. Emil G. Hirsch and Caspar Levias retell his story from Second Kings in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A sheepmaster who paid Ahab the wool of a hundred thousand lambs and as many rams, he rebelled against Ahab's son. Israel, Judah, and Edom invaded by the long road south of the Dead Sea. The Moabite Stone confirms why. Mesha had fortified the north. Elisha's trenches filled miraculously with water, the Moabites mistook the sunlit flood for their enemies' blood and charged into ruin. The allies wasted the land and besieged Kir-haraseth.

Then comes the famous horror. His breakout with seven hundred men failed. Mesha took his eldest son, the heir, onto the wall. He offered him as a burnt offering to Chemosh, in full view of the besiegers. "Great wrath" fell on Israel. The invaders went home. They left Mesha in undisturbed possession.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-midrash-halakah:
Midrash Halakah is the method by which the rabbis anchored Jewish law in the words of the Bible, proving old rules from verses and deriving new ones. Joseph Jacobs and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach explain it in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The name itself is modern, coined by Nachman Krochmal; the Talmud called the work investigation of the Torah.

The article divides the method into three ages. The oldest midrash defined laws by close, almost dictionary-like reading of the words. The younger Halakah reasoned by fixed rules and combinations of verses, drifting further from the plain sense. Later teachers often cited a verse as mere support for a law already held. Collections like the Mekilta, Sifra, and Sifre preserve the method book by book.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-modiano-joseph-:
Joseph Samuel Modiano was a rabbinical author of Salonica at the end of the eighteenth century. Gotthard Deutsch and M. Franco notice him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His family came from Modena in Italy. Its Salonica descendants were prominent in finance and industry. He corresponded with Ḥayyim Abulafia, the rabbi of Smyrna.

Two books carry his name. Uryan Telitai, printed at Salonica in 1795, collects novellae on Talmudic treatises by the great medieval commentators. Among them are Naḥmani, Ibn Migash, and Yom-Ṭob ben Abraham. Later Salonica rabbis and Modiano himself are included too. His responsa, Rosh Mashbir, appeared only after his death. They came out in two volumes, in 1821 and 1840. The entry is short, as befits a scholar known through his books.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mordecai-ben-ni:
Mordecai ben Nissan ha-Zaḳen was a Karaite scholar of Krasnoi-Ostrog in Poland. He is known by a book written to answer a Dutch professor. Isidore Singer and Isaac Broydé explain him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He studied under Joseph ben Samuel of Kalisz and David ben Shalom ha-Zaḳen. While still young he mastered Rabbinite as well as Karaite literature.

In 1698 Jacob Trigland, professor of theology at Leyden, sent four questions about the Karaites to David ben Shalom. He asked whether the sect was the old Sadducees or Anan's creation. He asked who Aquila was and who wrote the Moreh Aharon. He asked whether the Karaite Bible differs from the Rabbinite one. Mordecai's answers became his Dod Mordekai. It was printed at Vienna in 1830. It is a Karaite self-portrait for a Christian scholar.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-ben-josep:
Moses ben Joseph ben Merwan ha-Levi was a French Talmudist of the middle twelfth century. Solomon Schechter and A. Peiginsky wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He was the nephew and pupil of Isaac ben Merwan ha-Levi, and he directed the yeshiva at Narbonne. Colleagues addressed him with honor as the great scholar, Nasi Rabbi Moses.

His ritual decisions and Talmud comments are quoted often, and younger scholars wrote to him with hard questions. His pupils included Abraham ben David of Posquières and Zerahiah Gerondi, both later famous. If he is the Moses who signed a Narbonne divorce paper in 1134, he was also among the first cabalists of southern France. The entry leaves that point open.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mulder-samuel-i:
Samuel Israel Mulder was a Dutch educationist born at Amsterdam on June 20, 1792. Isidore Singer and E. Slijper wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He grew up in the Tongeleth circle, young men who studied the Hebrew language together. In 1826 he became regent of the Amsterdam theological seminary and reformed it.

Mulder's fame rests on his Dutch Bible translation of 1824, the first made from the Hebrew, and often reprinted. With Lehmans he published a Dutch-Hebrew dictionary in two volumes. His Bible for Israelite youth ran to seventeen volumes, finished in 1854. Giessen gave him a doctorate, and in 1860 he received the Order of the Netherlands Lion.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nantes-11307:
Nantes is a French city whose Jews some historians trace to the tenth century. Isidore Singer and S. Kahn wrote the Jewish Encyclopedia article on the community. A Hebrew and Latin receipt of 1234 proves Jews were there by then. In 1235 crusaders killed several of them before sailing for the Holy Land.

In 1239 Duke Jean of Brittany ordered every Jew expelled, their debts annulled and pledges returned. He even freed past killers of Jews from all punishment. Spanish converts later found shelter in Nantes until Louis expelled them in 1615. Bordeaux merchants won fair rights in 1744 but were thrown out in 1773. By 1904 only some thirty-five families remained.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-newman-alfred-a:
Alfred Alvarez Newman revived the blacksmith's art in England. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in London in 1851. He died there in 1887, still young. He founded the Old English smithy in Archer street.

In four years Newman lifted art ironwork by taste and energy. His Haymarket smithy was arranged like a picture. It became a fashionable resort in the London season. He read papers to the Society of Architects on his craft. His second love was Anglo-Jewish history and archeology. He gathered a unique set of Jewish prints and tracts. His efforts helped save Bevis Marks synagogue from demolition. The ancient house of worship stands partly by his work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-novgorod-11607:
Novgorod is among Russia's oldest cities. Herman Rosenthal and S. Janovsky wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It stands on the River Volkhoff. Its life runs back to the ninth century. Its bishop Luka bore the surname, the Jew.

Some scholars take that name as Jewish origin's proof. Hanseatic trade brought the town foreign wealth early. Jewish merchants visited it by the 1400s. In the famine of 1445 some sold themselves. Eastern merchants and Jews bought the starving townsfolk then. Open contact bred a coolness toward Christianity there. The Judaizing Heresy arose in Novgorod in 1471. Skhariyah of Kiev came in a prince's suite. Lithuanian Jews helped him spread the teaching widely. The city itself holds few Jews today.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ona-ah-overreac:
Ona'ah is a Hebrew term for a wrong in trade. The board and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It names a sale at too high a price. It also names a buy at too low a price. In both cases fraud is held to be at work.

Jewish law set the limit at a gap of one sixth. A good worth six coins must not sell for seven. It must not be bought for five coins either. If the gap held, the wronged side could void the deal. The claim had to be made with speed. The buyer first had to show his buy to a trader. Roman law knew a like rule, but a wider one. There the gap had to pass two to one.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ottingen-elijah:
Elijah ben Abraham Öttingen was a rabbi at Wengrow, in Poland. Gotthard Deutsch and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in the first half of the sixteen hundreds. His full name adds the words ben Mordecai ha-Levi. That marks him as a Levite by birth line.

His first work was Berit ha-Lewi, out at Lublin in 1645. It sets out the prayer of Moses in Deuteronomy. It reads that prayer in 365 ways, a way for each day. It weaves the 613 laws of Moses through the whole. Its tales come from the Midrash and the Talmud. A second, larger work of his is named by Fürst. No more is known of that work at this time. His notes on one tract may be the work of older men.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pennsylvania-12:
Pennsylvania was one of the thirteen first states of the Union. Cyrus Adler and A. S. W. Rosenbach wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The state took its name from William Penn. King Charles the Second granted him the land in 1681. The article then follows each city and town.

The first recorded Jews came before Penn himself. In 1655 three Jews asked to trade on the Delaware River. Stuyvesant refused them, but his directors overruled him. Jews then traded with Indians and Swedes along the river. Philadelphia's first known Jewish resident appears in 1703.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-philistines-121:
The Philistines were a sea people on the coast south-west of Jerusalem. Emil G. Hirsch and Ira Maurice Price wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Their land was a wide and fertile plain. It ran from Ekron down to the brook of Egypt.

The Bible says the Philistines came from Caphtor. Most scholars now place Caphtor on the island of Crete. They picture roving pirates from the northern sea. The newcomers landed on the plain south of Joppa. In time they took the tongue and gods of the land. Their cities still held giants in David's day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-plessner-elias-: Elias Plessner was a German rabbi, son of Solomon Plessner. Isidore Singer and I. Bröck wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Berlin in 1841 and died at Ostrowo in 1898. He took his doctorate at Tübingen in 1870. He served Hanover, then Rogasen, then Ostrowo as rabbi. He published his father's sermons and writings in 1884. His own books treat women, gravestones, and great rabbis.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-posner-karl-lud:
Karl Ludwig von Posner was a Hungarian maker of printed goods, born in 1822. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. In 1852 he founded the largest printing house in Hungary. It joined printing, stone printing, and book binding in one firm. He died at Budapest in 1887.

The state sent Posner as its agent to shows abroad. He went to London, Vienna, and Triest in that role. In 1884 the minister of education charged him with a new task. He was to bring map copying into Hungary. The country owes him much in print and paper arts, the entry says. King Francis Joseph made him a noble in 1873.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-przemysl-12407:
Przemysl is a city of Galicia, once the capital of Red Russia. Gotthard Deutsch and M. Schorr wrote its article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A Russian writer names the city in the year 981. No word of Jews there comes until 1437, though. Even then they show up only now and then.

The first count of the city dates from 1542. It found eighteen Jewish families in Przemysl then. Seven of them owned houses of their own. They paid a set tax each year for being Jews. Other towns of Red Russia held still fewer Jews then. The article follows the slow growth of the community.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabina-iii-of-u: Rabina III of Umza gets only a three-line notice in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906, written by Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach. The entry calls him a Sabora of the first generation. It gives his death as Adar in the year 508. It then says plainly that nothing further about him is known. The note rests on Sherira Gaon's letter, as printed in Neubauer's collection, and on Grätz's history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-razsvyet-12607:
Razsvyet was a Russo-Jewish weekly founded at Odessa in May 1860. Herman Rosenthal and J. G. Lipman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Osip Rabinovich founded it. It was the first Russian language journal for Jewish interests.

The article tells how hard permission was to win. Officials first demanded the paper appear in Yiddish instead. They also placed it under a distant censor. Help from N. I. Pirogov finally won full approval. The paper's motto was Let there be light. Its aim was to spread learning among Russian Jews. It also hoped Russians would know their Jewish neighbors better. The entry marks a first step in Russian Jewish journalism.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reubeni-david-1:
David Reubeni was an Arab adventurer born about 1490. Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He said he came from Khaibar in central Arabia. He died in Llerena, Spain, after 1535.

The article follows his journey from 1522 onward. He left Khaibar and traveled through Nubia and Palestine. At Venice in 1524 he claimed an eastern Jewish mission. He entered Rome on a white horse that year. Pope Clement VII gave him an audience. He told of a Jewish kingdom ruled by his brother Joseph. That kingdom stood near the fabled Sambation River. Portugal's king at first promised him ships and cannon. The entry reads like a tale of courts and claims.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rohling-august-:
August Rohling was a Catholic theologian and anti-Semitic author born in 1839. Isidore Singer and Gotthard Deutsch wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Neuenkirchen in Hanover, Prussia. He studied at Münster and at Paris.

The article says he taught at Münster, Milwaukee, and Prague. He retired in 1901 as a Prague cathedral canon. His field was Hebrew archaeology, without great scholarly fame. His anti-Jewish book Der Talmudjude appeared in 1871. It was often reprinted and widely quoted. The writers call it a faulty abstract of Eisenmenger. Josef Bloch accused him of ignorance and forgery. Rohling sued for libel, then withdrew at the last moment. The entry documents a polemicist whose book outgrew its merits.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-saint-symphorie:
Saint-Symphorien d'Ozon is a town in the ancient French province of Dauphiné. Richard Gottheil and S. Kahn wrote its entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. In the fourteenth century it held a large and wealthy Jewish community.

In 1355 the dauphin Charles granted that community important privileges, for a special tax. The city's leading banking house belonged to the Cohen brothers. Their clients included clerics, priests, nobles, and prominent townsmen there and at Vienne. Yet Jews still paid special highway tolls, by foot or on horseback. In 1396 three Jewish youths were fined 200 gold francs on a mocked charge.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-isaa:
Samuel ben Isaac ha-Sardi was a Spanish rabbi of the early thirteenth century. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He studied in Provence under Nathan ben Meïr of Trinquetaille, then returned home.

Samuel was a contemporary of Nahmanides, whom he consulted on Talmud questions. Solomon of Montpellier, Maimonides' fierce foe, praised his learning in a letter. That letter begged support against philosophy, in Solomon's campaign of the time. In 1225 Samuel wrote his Sefer ha-Terumot on Talmud civil law. It is divided into gates and chapters, like a code.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schorr-naphtali:
Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Naphtali Mendel Schorr. He was a Galician Hebrew writer. Schorr died at Lemberg on December 14, 1883. In 1861 he founded the Hebrew weekly Ha-'Et. Only twenty-two numbers of that paper appeared. He worked as an editor and translator as well as an author.

In 1855 Schorr edited Bedersi's Beḥinat ha-'Olam at Lemberg. He also edited the Baḳḳashat ha-Memim. To that work he added a German translation. His own Hebrew commentary, Patshegen ha-Ketab, went with it. His Har ha-Mor gathers tales from medieval Jewish history in three parts. It appeared from 1855 to 1875. His Mas'at Nefesh turns the Brahmanische Weisheit into Hebrew. He signed his journal pieces with a mark built from his names' last letters.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-seligsohn-samue:
Joseph Jacobs and Gotthard Deutsch wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Samuel Seligsohn. He was a Hebrew poet. Seligsohn was born at Samoczin, in Posen, in 1815. He died there on October 3, 1866. The entry is brief. It records the one book he published and the works he left behind in manuscript.

His Ha-Abib, an epic poem, appeared at Berlin in 1845. The title means the spring. A second epic treats the destruction of Jerusalem. That poem never reached print. Various essays of his also stayed in manuscript. The entry rests on two notices in the Jewish press. One comes from the Orient of 1845. The other comes from the Allgemeine Zeitung des Judenthums of 1866, the year of his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shapiro-constan:
Constantin Shapiro was a Russian photographer and Hebrew poet born at Grodno in 1841. Herman Rosenthal and S. Hurwitz wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. Raised in yeshivot, he secretly studied Hebrew language and literature. His fanatical circle persecuted him for seeking secular knowledge.

Shapiro left home for St. Petersburg and entered its art academy. He soon left to learn photography instead. As a photographer he published portraits of Russian writers and Gogol scenes. His first Hebrew poem, printed in 1885, made a strong impression at once. It placed him among the foremost Hebrew poets. His later verse kept its strength, lightness, and simple diction until his death in 1900.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shohet-13607:
Shohet is the trained slaughterer licensed to kill cattle and poultry by Jewish rite. Cyrus Adler and Schulim Ochser wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the office. The Bible names no specially appointed slaughterer at all. Its verbs for slaughter still hint at governing rules.

Tractate Hullin says any fit adult male may slaughter. A Tosefta passage allows women and even Samaritans the role. A baraita limits the work to a certified expert instead. That expert must handle the knife with proven skill. Rules stayed stable until the sixteenth century, the entry says. Joseph Caro then barred women from the office in his code. He feared they might faint while doing the work. The entry charts who may slaughter, and how that answer changed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-b-menasy:
Simeon ben Menasya was a tanna of the fourth generation, a peer of Judah ha-Nasi. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. With Jose ben Meshullam he formed a society called the Holy Community. Its members split each day into three equal parts.

One third went to Torah study for the members. One third went to prayer, and one third to work. Simeon is not mentioned in the Mishnah itself. One sentence in Hagigah under his name is a later addition. Other legal sentences of his survive in the Tosefta and Talmud. His homilies are more numerous than his legal rulings. God counts the pious as daily martyrs, he taught. That reading turns a psalm verse into comfort for sufferers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-slouschz-nahum-:
Nahum Slouschz was a Russian Hebrew writer born at Odessa in November 1872. Herman Rosenthal and Frederick T Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He learned rabbinics from his father at home. At nineteen the Chovevei Zion sent him to Palestine. He was to found a colony there if he could.

That mission failed, and Slouschz returned home again. He became an ardent follower of Herzl and Zionism. He founded Zionist branches across southern Russia. He studied at Geneva and then at Paris. In 1903 he took his doctorate at the University of Paris. His thesis traced the rebirth of Hebrew literature. He then lectured on Neo-Hebraic literature in Paris.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solovyev-vladim:
Vladimir Sergeyevich Solovyev was a Russian publicist and friend of the Jews. Herman Rosenthal wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in 1853 and died in 1900. In his article Russia and Europe he opposed anti-Jewish views. He fought the Slavyanophil party's stance against the Jews there.

He joined the Society for the Promotion of Culture Among Jews. He also took an active part in historical society work. Even on his deathbed he is said to have prayed for Jews. His chief works dealt with Western philosophy in crisis. Others dealt with Russia and the universal Church. One major work was titled The Justification of the Good.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-steinbach-emil-:
Emil Steinbach was an Austrian statesman born at Vienna in 1846. Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born there on June 11 of that year. After law studies at Vienna he practiced as a lawyer. He soon joined the Ministry of Commerce in government service.

From 1891 to 1893 he was minister of finance under Taaffe. In 1894 he became president of the Supreme Court of Austria. He still held that high post in 1905. He had embraced Christianity during his career in public life. His books dealt with property in letters and insurance law. Later works treated the state and modern private monopolies in 1903.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sulzbacher-loui:
Louis Sulzbacher was an American jurist born in Germany in 1842. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born in the Rhenish Palatinate on May 10. He was educated in Germany as a young man. Later he emigrated to the United States.

In 1900 Sulzbacher became a judge of Puerto Rico's Supreme Court. He resigned that post in 1904. The same year he took a federal judgeship. It covered the Western District of Indian Territory. The short entry traces a migrant lawyer's rise to two benches. It shows Jews serving in America's new island and western courts. Readers get the bare outline of a judicial career. His appointments mark trust placed in an immigrant judge.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-talkar-daniel-r:
Daniel Rahamim Talkar was a Beni-Israel soldier in British India. Joseph Jacobs and J. Hyams wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He enlisted in the 4th Rifles in 1842. He rose step by step through native officer ranks. His service spanned three hard campaigns.

Talkar became adjutant in 1857 and subahdar in 1861. In 1848 he marched from Karachi to Mooltan. Wounded, he still stormed the breach with his regiment. The city and fort fell in January 1849. He won a medal and clasp for that campaign. Persia brought another campaign in 1856 and 1857. He fought at Bushire and at Khooshab there. In 1878 he gained the rank of subahdar-major. The entry preserves an Indian Jewish soldier's full service record.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-temple-plan-of-:
A step-by-step plan of the Second Temple comes from Talmudic sources here. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Mount Moriah, they report, measured five hundred cubits square. It was walled on all sides and lowest in the east.

Each gate gets a name, a size, and a use. The southern Huldah gates served entry and exit. The eastern Shushan gate bore a model of Susa, Persia's capital. Mourners and the unclean used the northern Tadi gate. A low fence called the soreg ringed the inner courts. Steps, chambers, and courts follow in close detail. Readers get the Temple as the rabbis pictured it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tribes-the-twel:
The twelve tribes of Israel, their number and origin, are debated here. Emil G. Hirsch wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Older theory took the patriarch stories at face value. On that view, tribes grew from Jacob's sons by natural increase. Most modern scholars reject that simple account.

Two problems drive the rejection, Hirsch argues. No nation elsewhere grew from one family alone. The census numbers in the Bible are far too large. The tribal lists also disagree with each other. Twenty different orders appear across the records. Only one order ever repeats in full. Some lists group tribes by their mothers. Others group them by land and position. Descent looks more like theory than fact.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weasel-14807:
The weasel is listed among unclean animals in Leviticus. Emil G. Hirsch and I. M. Casanowicz wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Some scholars render the Hebrew word as mole instead. The weasel family has several species in Palestine and Syria. The Talmud names the common weasel often.

It lives on dung heaps and in wall cracks. It burrows in the ground and kills larger animals. It threatens farm hens with its sharp, pointed teeth. Above all it endangers the cat. A proverb mocks false friends as weasel and cat wed. People also used weasels to clear houses of mice. The entry gathers these scattered old notices.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yizhak-ben-samu:
Yizhak ben Samuel ben Marta was a Babylonian scholar of the 300s and 400s. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was a pupil of Rabbi Nahman in his youth. He put queries to that man on gifts and rites.

In the name of Rab he passed on words of law. Those words treat the writ that frees a wife. They treat the way Rab blessed the close of the Sabbath. Great men of the age sought his word as well. Zeera called him by the high name Rabbenu once. Rami bar Hama put a hard query to him in turn. At Nisibis he heard Simlai rail at free oil use. He brought a full tale of that speech back with him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zedakah-box-152:
Zedakah box is a chest in which free gifts for the poor are put. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The first such chest stands in the tale of Jehoiada. That priest made a chest with a hole in its lid.

He set that chest by the altar at the south gate. All gifts for the mends of the shrine went in it. In the Second Temple there were thirteen such chests in use. Each bore the shape of a horn, wide at the base. Coins were dropped in at the thin top of each one. The cash in them served gifts at the shrine and the poor. In late times the chest was called the kuppah in short. Each week it fed the poor of the town on Friday.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zutra-mar-ii-15:
Mar Zutra the Second was an exilarch who raised a revolt and ruled a short-lived Jewish state. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born about 496, he died about 520 and ruled from 512 to 520. His father Huna had held the exilarch's office under the Persian king Firuz.

Legend surrounds his birth, which came after his grandfather's dream of a last cedar tree. At fifteen he was installed as rightful exilarch over a rival who had bribed the king. Zutra then led four hundred Jewish warriors against Persia and taxed non-Jews in his state at Mahoza. Defeated at last, he and his grandfather were captured and put to death.
journal-of-discourses-vol-07:
America slides toward civil war in the sermons of Volume Seven, from 1860. Young reads the coming bloodshed as judgment on a guilty nation. The Saints, driven out years before, should stand apart and watch.

Discourses warn the flock not to join the quarrel brewing back east. Prophecies of ruin for the republic mix with calls to build Zion. Grain stores, home crafts, and unity get pressed as sacred duties. The prophet views Babylon's fall from a mountain refuge, unmoved. His calm scorn for the Union's fate startles modern readers still today. The Saints are told to plant, store, and let Babylon fall alone.
joyce-chamber-music-1907:
James Joyce was twenty-five when this first book appeared in 1907. It holds thirty-six short love lyrics, written in his youth in Dublin, set out like songs for a singer and a small group of players.

The poems speak of love's hopes, partings, and gentle sorrows in clear, musical lines. Joyce later grew dismissive of them, but their craft is real: each lyric is tuned like the chamber music of the title. Readers who know only the later, harder Joyce meet a different writer here. The book is the apprentice work behind the prose that remade the novel.
kalevala-vol-1-kirby-1907:
Elias Lonnrot built the Kalevala from the sung tales of the Finns. W. F. Kirby gave the epic English dress in 1907 as The Land of the Heroes. Book one holds Runos One to Twenty-Five of the whole. The Kalevala is the great epic of Finland.

Old Vainamoinen sings the world into shape at the start of the tale. The forging of the Sampo, a mill of wealth, drives much of the plot. Heroes woo, raid, and feast from the wild north to the farm lands. Kirby kept the trochaic beat of the Finn songs in his dress.
kalevala-vol-2-kirby-1907:
Elias Lönnrot gathered old Finnish songs from singers in Karelia and built them into the Kalevala, the national epic of Finland. W. F. Kirby put the poem into English, and his second volume appeared in 1907. It carries the story from runo twenty-six to the fiftieth and last.

Lemminkäinen returns to the frozen north uninvited and pays for his pride. The tragic hero Kullervo walks his dark road to ruin. Then the heroes raid the north for the Sampo, a magic mill that brings wealth, and lose it at sea. The final songs tell of a virgin mother and a child king, a clear echo of the coming of Christ.
kenelm-chillingly-volume-07:
Volume seven of Kenelm Chillingly opens Book Seven at dusk, with Tom Bowles arriving at a friend's cottage. The chapter first sounds its keynote: talk about Tom himself. A supper is planned for that night at Will Somers's house. A wedding-day memory and Tom's habits of success fill the opening talk.

Tom's secret is let out during the evening, and the talk turns to love. Can love sink a man, or can it lift him? The question carries the book's long argument about Kenelm's future. Around the supper table, Lytton gathers his country characters for plain-spoken debate. This volume brings the wandering story home to the people Kenelm left behind.
lea-inquisition-spain-vol-3-1907:
Henry Charles Lea's third volume on the Spanish Inquisition, from 1907, maps the spheres where the Holy Office reached into daily life. Blasphemy at the card table, bigamy, sorcery, and false mystics all fell under its eye. The alumbrados, Spain's illuminated visionaries, get a full treatment from Lea.

Protestants in Spain, few and hunted, pass through his pages, as do the censors who licensed every printed book. Lea shows a tribunal that policed speech, prayer, and print as much as belief. His evidence is the case files themselves, and his judgments are measured and bleak. The volume explains how the Inquisition shaped Spanish minds for three centuries.
lea-inquisition-spain-vol-4-1907:
The fourth volume of Henry Charles Lea's History of the Inquisition of Spain, from 1907, brings the long story to its end. The tribunal declines through the eighteenth century and dies, at last, in the nineteenth. Lea follows it also into Spain's colonies across the Atlantic and the Pacific.

Censorship, the Index of banned books, and the final suppressions fill these chapters. Lea counts the cost: the trials, the burnings, the silence laid on a nation's thought. His four volumes, built from the archives, remain the fullest history of the Spanish Inquisition in any language. The set is a monument of American scholarship and of quiet, relentless prose.
london-love-of-life-1907:
Jack London published Love of Life and Other Stories in 1907, gathering tales written after his Yukon years had made him world famous. The title story is among the most famous short stories ever written about survival. London was by then the highest-paid writer in America.

In Love of Life, a starving prospector, robbed of his gold and crippled, crawls across the tundra toward a distant ship. He fights hunger, a sick wolf, and his own despair with nothing but will. The Story of Keesh tells of a clever Eskimo boy who outwits his tribe's hunters. Other tales return to the Klondike and the prize ring. London's subjects are appetite, endurance, and the thin crust of civilization.
london-road-1907:
Jack London published The Road in 1907, a memoir of his teenage years as a hobo in the 1890s. At sixteen he had left factory work, ridden freight trains across America, and begged his way from door to door. The book tells those years straight, with photographs of his companions.

London describes stealing rides, dodging railroad guards, and surviving thirty days in a brutal penitentiary for vagrancy. He explains the tramp's codes, slang, and storytelling art: a good road kid could talk a housewife out of a meal with a well-shaped lie. The Road made the hobo a literary figure in America. It also shows where London's sympathy for outcasts was earned.
machen-hill-of-dreams-1907:
A young writer from Wales burns with visions he cannot sell or escape in The Hill of Dreams. Machen's novel of 1907 follows Lucian Taylor from a Roman-haunted town to a garret in London. The book is his own life in a glass, barely veiled.

Lucian's dreams of the old Roman city under his home grow richer as his real life starves. Art, poverty, and a pagan past pull him down a bright, doomed road. The novel is the cult classic of the decadent revival of its age. It is Machen's most personal and most prized work.
margery-gred-a-tale-of-old-nuremberg-vol:
Volume seven of Margery opens near the stables, with Uncle Christian growling. He swears the 'old owl' shall have something to remember him by. Matthew bridles Margery's bay nag while the gentlemen's horses are saddled. Margery has stolen out, meaning to ride after Ann.

The old folks railed at the plan in their fears for her. Wicked deeds have lately been done on the high roads and in this wood. The town constable requires seven mounted men as outriders. Still the misguided maid rides into danger for her friend. Ebers fills the volume with pursuit, peril, and loyalty. Gred's courage shines against her elders' fears.
mark-twain-a-biography-volume-iii-part-1:
