Volume three, part one of Paine's biography covers 1900 to 1907. It opens with 'The Return of the Conqueror.' Twain came home from his world tour with his debts paid. Newspapers and public made a stir seldom given a private citizen.

He had left staggering under obligation and won his fight single-handed. Howells said he had behaved like Walter Scott, and millions rejoiced. Sorrow walked beside the triumph, for loss had struck his house. These chapters show the white-suited sage of the new century. Honors, interviews, and public causes fill his seventies. Paine writes as friend, secretary, and witness of it all.
marx-capital-vol-2-1907:
Karl Marx wrote Capital as the great work of his life. Ernest Untermann gave Book Two English dress in 1907, and Friedrich Engels had shaped the text for print. Book Two deals with the flow of capital through trade. Book One, on the make of goods, stands just past.

Money turns to goods, goods to more goods, and goods back to money in Marx's scheme. He tracks how fast the wheel turns and where the flow can jam. Rent, trade, and the banks all take their place in the loop. The book is the hard core of his scheme of how wealth moves.
memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-volume-07: Etext 3557 names volume seven of Bourrienne's Napoleon memoirs. Gutenberg dates its release to December 2002, with a first posting in 2001. A year label, 1804, appears in the file head with the title. Below that head sits nothing but the project's license and gift text. Since no sentence of the memoir itself is preserved in the sample, this entry can report the author, volume, and file facts only.
metchnikoff-prolongation-life-mitchell-1:
In The Prolongation of Life, in Mitchell's 1907 translation, Metchnikoff gathers his hopeful essays on growing old well. He returns to the gut, where he believed poisons from bad microbes slowly wear the body down. Sour milk and yogurt stand at the center of his advice.

He points to long-lived peasants who ate fermented milk daily and urges readers to copy the habit. He also weighs how science might one day soften the fear of death itself. The book spread the yogurt habit across Europe and fed public interest in senescence, the study of aging.
my-novel-volume-07:
Edward Bulwer-Lytton's seventh book opens with a question on courage. Uncle Roland asks if courage is just not feeling fear. That, he says, would be mere body, like being a table. Mr. Caxton is glad to hear the point.

Caxton owns that he feels fear in all dangers, body and soul. His wife recalls how he faced a bull last week. Blanche kisses his brow at the memory. Caxton insists he was frightened, yet stood his ground. Honor, Roland argues, is what makes true courage. The family debate gives the novel's heroes a standard to meet.
nider-preceptorium-1507:
Johannes Nider guides troubled souls in his Preceptorium, in Latin in this 1507 printing. The fifteenth-century theologian treats confession, conscience, and temptation in full. Demons and their wiles trouble the sinners his priestly readers must counsel, absolve, and guard in a world that felt heaven and hell very near.

Nider also wrote the famous Formicarius on witches and spirits. This handbook shows the late medieval Church at its pastoral work. Rules, cases, and warnings fill its careful Latin chapters for confessors. It gives a frank look at what worried Christians on the eve of the Reformation, a generation before Luther shook the world.
ocean-of-story-kathasaritsagara-tawney-1:
Volume seven of Penzer's Ocean of Story, begun in 1924, continues Tawney's translation of Somadeva's Kathasaritsagara. The ocean's later books gather tales of ascetics whose curses bend kingdoms, and of love that survives death, disguise, and long separation. Naravahanadatta's fated rise threads quietly beneath the abundance.

Penzer's notes in these volumes draw heavily on the vampire tales and the Panchatantra for parallels. Tawney's rendering, first made in the early 1880s, gains new readers through Penzer's apparatus. The Sanskrit poet's art lies in pacing: no tale overstays, and each promises a better one behind it. Volume seven sustains that promise deep into the cycle. Few story collections anywhere match this one's stamina.
openalex-w1987358907:
Lissette Sanchez-Aranguren and co-authors wrote this review on preeclampsia. Their paper is dated 2014 in the catalog record. Preeclampsia brings high blood pressure and protein in urine. It appears at the twentieth week of pregnancy. It affects roughly five to ten percent of pregnancies.

The condition can prove fatal for mother and child. It weighs especially heavily in developing countries, they note. Faulty vessel lining, called endothelial dysfunction, is central. Oxidative stress helps drive that vessel damage, they argue. The review gathers evidence on that stress pathway. Better grasp of it may yield earlier tests and care.
openalex-w2015613907:
Oriana Ovalle-Rivera, Peter Laderach, Christian Bunn and colleagues projected climate shifts for Arabica coffee. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2015. Warming and changing rain can cut coffee yield and quality. They can also raise pest and disease pressure. Earlier work covered single regions only.

Theirs was the first global study of Arabica suitability. They modelled world growing areas with many climate models. They projected conditions for the 2050s. Suitability fell at low altitudes in Mesoamerica. Parts of South America at higher elevations could gain. Ethiopia and Kenya were projected to gain suitability. India and Vietnam were projected to lose it. Overall, production may shift among major coffee regions.
openalex-w2041499507:
Yves Carlier, Faustino Torrico, Sergio Sosa-Estani and colleagues gave recommendations on Chagas disease passed from mother to baby. Their paper appeared in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2011. Chagas disease can pass during pregnancy. Infected newborns need early diagnosis and treatment. A 2010 world health resolution urged action on this route.

The recommendations cover newborns of infected mothers. They also cover siblings and pregnant women. Early testing can catch infections before symptoms harm the child. Howard Y. Chang, Julie B. Sneddon, Ash A. Alizadeh, and a large team linked wound healing to cancer in PLOS Biology in 2004. When skin is cut, fibroblast cells switch on a set of genes to close the wound. Tumors switch on much the same set, which is why cancers are sometimes called wounds that do not heal.

The authors used that gene pattern to sort real tumors. Cancers that showed the wound pattern tended to grow and spread more, and patients fared worse. That makes the pattern a useful warning sign. It also gives doctors a possible tool for judging risk. A gene test based on healing signals could help guide how strongly a cancer should be treated.
plos-pbio-0020207:
Andrew Fortna, Young Kim, Erik MacLaren, and a large team compared gene copies in humans and great apes for PLOS Biology in 2004. Genes can be gained or lost as species split. The team measured copy numbers across the ape family tree to find changes unique to each line.

Human-specific gains and losses stand out as candidate traits that set us apart. Some involve genes tied to the brain and to smell, two areas where humans differ from other apes. A clean list of lineage-specific changes gives evolution research sharp targets. Each entry can be tested for what it does, rather than guessed at from the full genome.
plos-pbio-0030007:
Adam Woolfe, Martin Goodson, Debbie K. Goode, and a large team hunted conserved DNA in PLOS Biology in 2005. Some DNA stretches do not code for proteins yet are nearly identical across vertebrates. Such strong conservation hints they do a vital job, likely guiding development.

The team found these stretches cluster near genes that control how embryos grow. Placed near a gene in a developing fish, many of them acted as switches that turned the gene on in specific tissues. That confirmed the guess: conserved non-coding DNA holds instructions for body building. The catalog became a resource for finding the switches behind birth defects and for reading the genome's dark matter.
plos-pone-0000007:
Casper Breuker, James Patterson, and Christian Klingenberg studied why fruit fly wings come out so reliably the same shape. Development is noisy, yet a Drosophila wing lands close to its target form again and again. That steadiness is called developmental buffering. Their 2006 paper argues the buffering has a single basis.

Working from wing measurements, the team tested whether one shared mechanism damps the many small disturbances that could warp a growing wing. A single basis would simplify a tangle of older theories, each invoking its own buffer. The claim matters beyond flies: reliable development despite noise is a basic problem for every animal, humans included.
plos-pone-0000107:
Marta Martínez-Diez, Gema Santamaría, Álvaro D. Ortega, and their team studied mitochondria across the cell cycle in PLOS ONE in 2006. Mitochondria, the cell's power plants, must be built and split between daughter cells as the cell divides. The team tracked how new mitochondria form and move through that cycle.

They also probed the role of 3′UTRs, the tail regions of gene messages that control where and when proteins are made. Those tails appear to help place mitochondria-making proteins where they are needed. The study links two levels of control: the timetable of division and the fine print on gene messages. Both matter for cells that must double their power supply on schedule.
plos-pone-0000207:
Wayne M. Getz, Scott Fortmann-Roe, Paul C. Cross, and colleagues published this ecology methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It presents LoCoH, a set of nonparametric kernel methods for building home ranges and utilization distributions from animal location data. A home range map estimates where an animal actually spends its time.

Older range methods often drew smooth blobs that included land the animal never used. LoCoH builds ranges from local hulls of points, respecting rivers, fences, and other hard edges. Wildlife researchers adopted such tools widely for tracking data, from collared lions to tagged birds.
plos-pone-0000307:
Tonio Ball, Benjamin Rahm, Simon B. Eickhoff, and colleagues published this brain imaging paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. The amygdala, the brain's alarm center, has subregions with different jobs. The authors combine functional MRI with probabilistic anatomical maps to measure the response properties of human amygdala subregions in living people.

Treating the amygdala as one blob blurs its real organization. Splitting it by anatomy while scanning activity gives a cleaner picture of which part does what. The method helps research on fear, emotion, and anxiety disorders aim at the right subregion.
plos-pone-0000407:
Masaki Fujita, Hisako Takeshita, and Hitoshi Sawa studied how cells know when to stop dividing and specialize, using the worm C. elegans, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Their focus was cyclin E and its partner CDK2, proteins best known for driving cells into division. The team examined cells that had divided unequally and then settled into a resting, quiescent state.

The authors report that cyclin E and CDK2 help hold those resting cells back from finishing their differentiation. That is an unexpected brake role for proteins famous as accelerators. Worm embryos are a classic system for watching single cells choose their fates. The finding adds a twist to how division machinery and specialization are coordinated.
plos-pone-0000507:
Trinh Thanh Thuy and colleagues documented tuberculosis among people with HIV in a Vietnamese province, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. TB is the leading killer of people with HIV worldwide, and An Giang Province in 2001–2004 gave the team a defined place and period. They reported the epidemiology of HIV-associated TB there and the outcomes of TB treatment.

Treatment outcomes show whether programs work in practice, not just in trials. In the early 2000s, Vietnam was scaling up both HIV and TB services, and their overlap was poorly documented. Local numbers like these guide where joint TB-HIV care will save the most lives.
plos-pone-0000607:
Christopher L. Reyes and colleagues froze a cell delivery machine at steps of its work cycle, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The machine is the signal recognition particle receptor. It guides new proteins to the cell's surface for export. The team used X-ray methods to solve the receptor's shapes, catching forms it takes mid-job.

The mid-job shapes are the frames between the still pictures in textbooks. They show how the machine truly moves as it works. Protein targeting is basic to all cells, and its parts are targets for drugs that jam bacterial export. Frames like these turn a rough sketch of a pathway into a true plan.
plos-pone-0000707:
Philip Bejon, Edna Ogada, Tabitha Mwangi and colleagues reported extended follow-up of two candidate malaria vaccines tested in Kenyan children. The approach, called FFM ME-TRAP, gives two weakened poxvirus vectors in sequence. Both deliver ME-TRAP, an antigen from the malaria parasite's stage before it enters red blood cells. The original trial followed children for nine months.

Over that first period, there was no evidence the vaccines provided protection. Extended follow-up asks whether any effect appears or fades later. Reporting a negative result in full is valuable science: it closes one road clearly and steers vaccine programmes toward better candidates.
plos-pone-0000807:
Yuval Tabach, Ran Brosh, Yossi Buganim and colleagues analyzed where working transcription factor binding sites sit in human genes. Transcription factors regulate expression by binding specific DNA sequences. A binding event counts as functional when it affects gene expression. Function also shows in evolution. Real binding sequences are conserved over time. Binding motifs appear more often than chance would predict.

Their wide-scale analysis appeared in PLOS ONE in 2007. It reveals a strong bias of functional binding toward the transcription start site. That site is the point where copying of a gene begins. That geography matters for genome annotation. Predicted sites far from start sites deserve more skepticism than ones clustered where regulation actually happens.
plos-pone-0000907:
Michael McDevitt, Debjit Chattopadhyay, Jaspreet Jaggi and colleagues tracked carbon nanotubes in mice with PET imaging, for PLOS ONE in 2007. Tiny engineered materials may one day carry drugs or imaging agents through the body. Whether they suit medicine depends first on how they meet living tissue.

The team attached yttrium-86, a radioactive label, to single walled carbon nanotubes. PET scans then showed where the tubes went in the mice. Watching a material's path is the basic safety step for any nano device. Their work gives later studies a way to follow these tubes without cutting tissue.
plos-pone-0001007:
Luis Diaz, Catherine Foss, Katherine Thornton and colleagues imaged bacterial infections in muscle and bone with a PET tracer, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Standard scans can find an infection but often cannot say what it is. That lack of specificity is worst for musculoskeletal infections, where inflammation from other causes looks similar.

Bacteria carry a thymidine kinase enzyme that takes up certain tracers. The team used a labeled form, FIAU, with PET and CT scanning to exploit that trait. A scan that lights up bacteria themselves, not just swelling, could guide antibiotics and surgery far better. The paper reports an early test of that approach.
plos-pone-0001107:
Yanmei Huang, Ginka Genova, Mary Roberts and colleagues showed how an RNA binding protein times a daily emergence rhythm, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The core parts of the circadian clock are increasingly known. The output pathways, how the clock drives timed body events, remain elusive.

LARK is a fruit fly RNA binding protein working downstream of the clock. The team show it selectively regulates the circadian eclosion rhythm, the timed emergence of adult flies, by controlling levels of the E74 protein. One output wire, traced end to end, shows how a general clock produces a specific appointment. Development keeps such appointments strictly.
plos-pone-0001207:
Proteins in a cell form a web of interactions, and certain highly connected proteins, called hubs, organize that web into modules. Guangxu Jin and colleagues analyzed the yeast protein-protein interaction network in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Earlier work had split hubs into party hubs, which act with the same partners at once, and date hubs, which change partners over time.

The authors report that hubs decorated with network motifs, small recurring wiring patterns, organize modularity dynamically. In plain terms, the network's modules are not fixed blocks but shift as conditions change. Their analysis refines how biologists picture the cell's organization.
plos-pone-0001407:
Long-Jun Wu and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a scaffold protein in the brain called neurabin. The protein is rich in the spines where nerve cells meet. It helps shape those spines and build the links. Less was known about its role in learning and memory. The team filled that gap with mouse tests.

Mice lacking full neurabin action showed weak long term strengthening of brain links. They also showed poor fear based memory tied to place. The pair of results ties one spine protein to both cell change and behavior. It helps show how small spine parts support the act of forming a memory.
plos-pone-0001507:
Barbara Di Ventura and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study that rebuilds a cancer guard system in yeast. The guard, p53, halts the cell cycle or kills the cell when DNA is hurt. A web of chemical changes tunes its acts, but that web was hard to untangle in human cells. The team rebuilt its key partner's work in yeast.

In yeast they could switch each change on or off at will. That gave a clean read on what each change does to p53. Yeast lacks the rest of the web, so signals stay clear. The system should speed tests of p53 drugs and faults found in tumors.
plos-pone-0001607:
Mathieu Picardeau and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study that reads the genome of a harmless water germ. Its kin include germs that cause leptospirosis, a grave ill caught from tainted water. This strain lives free in water and harms no one. It is the first such mild kin to have its full code read.

Its code holds 3,590 protein coding genes spread on three DNA rings. Set beside its harmful kin, the code shows what was gained or lost as some lines turned to disease. That contrast is the fastest route to the genes that make a germ dangerous. It also grounds future work on this germ family.
plos-pone-0001707:
Xing-Yun Song and co-authors tested a growth factor supply route for spinal cord repair in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. BDNF, short for brain-derived neurotrophic factor, helps nerve fibers regrow. But the blood-brain barrier and a truncated receptor on astrocytes block BDNF applied in the body or the brain, limiting its use as a drug.

The team's approach supplies BDNF from the periphery instead, and they report it promotes regeneration of ascending sensory neurons after spinal cord injury. The full text gives the injury model, the delivery method, and the regrowth measures. A workable supply route for BDNF would matter for the many nerve diseases where the factor helps in principle but cannot reach its target.
plos-pone-0001807:
Andreas Dahlgren, Per Lundmark, Tomas Axelsson, and their co-authors tested a hormone receptor gene for links to height in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Human body height is a complex genetic trait with high heritability. The team ran an association study of 17 candidate genes for height. They used the Uppsala Longitudinal Study of Adult Men, which follows 1,153 elderly men born in central Sweden.

They report an association of the estrogen receptor 1 gene, ESR1, with body height in adult males from two Swedish population cohorts. The full text gives the variant data and the size of the effect. Estrogen governs growth plate closure in both sexes, so its receptor is a biologically sensible height gene.
plos-pone-0001907:
Patrik Nosil and Cristina Sandoval studied stick insects to test how new species form, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Populations split into new species in stages, from slight variety within a group to full split with no mating between them. How far apart two groups look, and whether they still breed, tends to grow as the split deepens.

The pair asked how many traits of the niche, the way of life of each group, drive that split. If more niche traits differ, the split may run faster. Stick insects that feed on unlike host plants give a clean test. The work sharpens ideas about how ecology drives the birth of species.
plos-pone-0002007:
Sean Rands and Heather Whitney asked whether the warmth of a flower can pay its pollinators, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Some plants offer more than nectar: they offer heat, which cold-bodied insects value. Bumble bees can govern their own body heat to a degree, yet when given a choice they feed at warmer flowers.

The pair weighed whether that taste for warmth makes sense under optimal foraging, the rule that feeders pick the best gain for effort. If heat cuts the energy bees spend on warming up, a warm flower is a real reward. The work joins plant and insect energetics in one account.
plos-pone-0002107:
Sigal Nakav and co-authors tested calming the immune system ahead of time with a cell signal, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Adenosine levels rise during inflammation and tune the response through four receptors. One view held that adenosine stokes inflammation through its A1 receptor, and calms it through the A2A receptor.

Against that split, the team report anti-inflammatory preconditioning by agonists, drugs that switch the A1 receptor on before an insult lands. Preparing tissue ahead of harm is a known trick in heart care. Extending it through adenosine's first receptor could yield new care for inflammatory disease.
plos-pone-0002207:
Karl Vandepoele and co-authors studied a chromosome swap in a young Belgian patient with neuroblastoma, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Neuroblastoma is a cancer of early childhood. The patient's chromosomes carried a balanced translocation, a swap between chromosomes 1 and 17 present from birth, which may have helped trigger the tumor.

The swap falls in a region, 1p36, that is often deleted in many tumor types and likely holds tumor suppressor genes. The authors show the swap disrupts two genes, NBPF1 and ACCN1. Cases like this one act as signposts, pointing cancer research to the genes that normally hold tumors back.
plos-pone-0002307:
Marcos Moleón, Pablo Almaraz, and José Sánchez-Zapata described a chain effect in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. A new disease can trigger heavy predation on an unrelated species. Hyperpredation happens when predator numbers rise, or the main prey collapses, so pressure on a secondary prey suddenly jumps. The mechanism is scarcely documented, and most prior cases involved predators introduced by people.

Here, an emerging infectious disease cut down the main prey, leaving predators to turn on the secondary one. The case shows how a pathogen can harm a species it never infects, purely by reshaping who eats whom. Conservation plans that ignore such indirect chains can miss the real cause of a decline.
plos-pone-0002407:
Kami led the team behind a 2008 research article in PLOS ONE. Named on the byline are Daisuke Kami, Ichiro Shiojima, Hatsune Makino, among others. Its subject is gremlin Enhances the Determined Path to Cardiomyogenesis. The critical event in heart formation is commitment of mesodermal cells to a cardiomyogenic fate.

The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002507:
Wang and other authors present their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Named on the byline are Tong Wang, Nan Gong, Jianuo Liu, among others. Its subject is proteomic Modeling for HIV-1 Infected Microglia-Astrocyte Crosstalk. HIV-1-infected and immune competent brain mononuclear phagocytes (MP; macrophages and microglia) secrete cellular and viral toxins that affect neuronal damage during advanced disease.

In contrast, astrocytes can affect disease by modulating the nervous system's microenvironment. The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full.
plos-pone-0002607:
Hooper joined co-authors to publish a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. Named on the byline are Sean D. Hooper, Jeroen Raes, Konrad U. Foerstner, among others. Its subject is a Molecular Study of Microbe Transfer between Distant Environments. Environments and their organic content are generally not static and isolated, but in a constant state of exchange and interaction with each other.

The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside.
plos-pone-0002707:
Yonghong Li and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was neither replication nor simulation supports a role for the axon guidance pathway in the genetics of parkinson's disease. The catalog record names Yonghong Li first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Susceptibility to sporadic Parkinson's disease (PD) is thought to be influenced by both genetic and environmental factors and their interaction with each other. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002807:
A 2008 study by Per Christiansen and colleagues in PLOS ONE takes up evolution of skull and mandible shape in cats (Carnivora: felidae). Authorship is credited in the record to Per Christiansen and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. The felid family consists of two major subgroups, the sabretoothed and the feline cats, to which all extant species belong. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002907:
Karine Tremblay, Mathieu Lemire, Camille Potvin and colleagues set out a computer method in 2008 to pick candidate genes for asthma. Asthma is a complex trait shaped by both genes and environment, and many strategies have been tried to find its genetic factors. Their approach is called Genes to Diseases, or G2D.

Published in PLOS ONE, the method ranks genes so that costly lab studies start with the best bets. It was built to select candidates for genetic association studies in asthma. Researchers facing long gene lists for other complex diseases may find the same ranking logic useful.
plos-pone-0003007:
Mieke Schutte, Fons Elstrodt, Linda Bralten and co-authors used exon arrays to hunt new cancer genes in 2008. Finding genes that causally drive cancer is a major goal of the field. An estimated 10 to 20 percent of cancer-linked mutations cause skipping of one or more exons in a gene's transcript.

Exon expression arrays read each exon separately, so skipping events stand out across the genome at once. Published in PLOS ONE, the strategy screens globally for that mutation class. Hits can reveal cancer genes missed by methods that only read whole-gene levels. Its full text, with tables and references, is openly available to any reader online.
plos-pone-0003107:
Andrej Benjak, Astrid Forneck and Josep Casacuberta surveyed jumping genes in the grapevine genome in 2008. Grapevine is widely cultivated, with many varieties selected since its domestication in the Neolithic period. Sexual crossing drove much of its evolution, but vegetative propagation, cloning by cuttings, increased the impact of somatic changes.

Cut-and-paste transposons are DNA pieces that move by excision and reinsertion. A genome-wide analysis catalogs them in grapevine for the first time. Published in PLOS ONE, transposons shape variety differences that wine growers prize, so the catalog has practical breeding value. The article appeared in PLOS ONE, an open access journal anyone can read free online.
plos-pone-0003207:
Thomas Tully and Régis Ferrière study flexible reproduction in a springtail in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. In a variable yet predictable world, organisms may use environmental cues to make adaptive adjustments to their phenotype. Such flexibility is expected to evolve in life history traits, which are closely tied to Darwinian fitness. Yet adaptive life history flexibility needs testing for its genetic variation and costs.

Working with a Collembola, a tiny soil arthropod, the authors examine genetic variation, genetic costs and long-term evolution of reproductive flexibility. Readers see plasticity treated as a trait with a price, not a free benefit. That framing sharpens evolutionary predictions.
plos-pone-0003307:
Maria G. Domínguez-Bello, Maria E. Pérez, Maria C. Bortolini and colleagues track stomach bacteria across populations in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The team studied diversity of bacteria and host in the Helicobacter pylori-human model. The human indigenous bacterium H. pylori diverged along with humans into African, European, Asian and Amerindian groups. Of these, Amerindians have the least genetic diversity.

The title reports that Amerindian H. pylori strains go extinct as European strains expand their host range. Readers see colonization history written in a stomach microbe. Such replacement may change disease patterns, since H. pylori strains differ in harm.
plos-pone-0003407:
Deborah A. Lewinsohn and colleagues studied child immune responses to tuberculosis in Uganda in 2008. Young children living with a TB patient face high risk of infection. Their immune systems are still maturing, so alarms may sound weaker. The team measured a key alarm signal, interferon-gamma, in whole blood samples.

The blood came from young household contacts of people with TB. Samples were tested against antigens from the TB germ. Responses in young children differed from those in adults, as the team expected. Knowing that gap helps design TB tests that work for small children.
plos-pone-0003507:
Beatriz Aranda-Orgillés and co-authors tracked a protein's ride inside cells in this 2008 paper. MID1 is a ubiquitin ligase, a tagger of proteins for handling. Faults in MID1 cause Opitz BBB/G syndrome, with midline malformations. The protein rides along microtubules, the cell's rail tracks.

An enzyme called protein phosphatase 2A regulated that active transport. When the regulator changed, MID1 movement changed with it. How MID1 travels may decide whether the body midline forms well. The study links cell transport to a birth defect syndrome. Midline defects are among the most common birth problems doctors see.
plos-pone-0003607:
Vincent Lazzari, Cyril Charles, and Paul Tafforeau studied rodent teeth across evolution in this 2008 paper. Tooth shape changes are studied by both paleontology and developmental biology. Molar crown shapes show frequent homoplasy, the same traits arising again and again. Rodent dentitions offered a detailed test case.

Their analyses found mosaic convergence in those dentitions. Unlike lineages arrived at similar teeth trait by trait, not all at once. Evolution assembled like solutions from different starting parts. Such mosaics warn against reading tooth traits as single events. Rodents are the largest group of mammals, so their teeth record a huge story.
plos-pone-0003707:
Alina Molchadsky, Igor Shats, Naomi Goldfinger, and colleagues published this cell study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The protein p53 is famous as a tumor suppressor that guards against cancer. It also helps steer cell differentiation, though reports disagreed on whether it aids or blocks that process.

The team studied p53 in mesenchymal differentiation, the programs that build tissues like bone, fat, and muscle. They found p53 plays a role whose effect depends on the fate the cell is heading toward. The result widens p53's brief from cancer guard to a guide in development.
plos-pone-0003807:
Cornelia Beck, Thilo Ognibeni, and Heiko Neumann published this vision modeling paper in PLOS ONE in 2008. Humans can spot objects using motion alone, seeing outlines where parts of a scene move differently. These kinetic boundaries arise at motion discontinuities and when one surface hides another over time.

The authors built a biologically inspired model that segments objects from such cues. It uses motion breaks and temporal occlusions the way the visual system seems to. The approach mirrors how human vision carves a moving scene into separate objects. The model runs without any color or texture cues at all.
plos-pone-0003907:
Cyril Dalmasso, Wassila Carpentier, Laurence Meyer, and co-authors scanned the genome for HIV control factors in 2008. Earlier work showed that HLA and chemokine receptor variants shape HIV progress. They also affect how much virus shows early in blood. The team wanted new genetic factors beyond those known genes.

Their PLOS ONE study covered 605 people who had recently caught HIV-1. It compared virus levels in blood plasma with virus DNA inside cells. Distinct gene regions governed each measure, the authors report. That split suggests the body controls free virus and stored virus in separate ways.
plos-pone-0004007:
Alain Bordon, Nabil Bosco, Camille Du Roure, and co-authors forced a B cell factor on early in development in 2008. OBF1 is a helper factor found only in B lymphocytes. It partners with Oct proteins at B cell gene promoters. Its known roles sat mostly in late B cell stages.

Their PLOS ONE article switched OBF1 on from the earliest stages. That forced presence impaired B cell development right at the start. Timing of a factor can matter as much as its presence. The work redraws where OBF1 fits in immune cell growth. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004107:
Magdalena Benetkiewicz, Ahmed Idbaih, Pierre-Yves Cousin, and co-authors checked a candidate gene in brain tumors in 2009. Oligodendrogliomas often lose parts of chromosomes 1 and 19 together. That loss comes from an unbalanced translocation joining the two. NOTCH2 was suggested as a gene behind these tumors.

Their PLOS ONE article reports NOTCH2 is neither rearranged nor mutated there. The negative result holds in the translocation-positive tumors studied. Ruling out a candidate redirects the search for the real driver genes. Such deletions may act through other genes on those arms. The study ran in PLOS ONE, an open journal read by labs around the world.
plos-pone-0004207:
Dongying Wu and colleagues published this genome study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Thermomicrobium roseum is a bacterium that thrives in heat, breathes oxygen, and gains energy by oxidising carbon monoxide. The team sequenced its complete genome as part of an Assembling the Tree of Life project meant to widen the diversity of sequenced bacteria.

They describe the red-pigmented, rod-shaped microbe, strain DSM 5159, and lay out its full DNA sequence. The genome shows the toolkit of a heat-loving CO eater. Such sequences help scientists place odd microbes on the tree of life and mine their heat-proof enzymes.
plos-pone-0004307:
Lei Zheng and colleagues published this vision study in PLOS ONE in 2009, the first of a pair. Eyes have limited processing capacity, so retinal networks must adapt constantly to present the changing visual world well. How adaptation in retinal networks shapes the encoding of changing information was still poorly known.

Working with the Drosophila eye and naturalistic stimuli, patterns resembling real-world light, the team characterised the dynamics of network adaptation. They show that adaptation improves the temporal representation of such stimuli. A companion paper then dissects the mechanisms behind the effect.
plos-pone-0004407:
Two cell proteins rise and fall in a repeating rhythm. Keng Boon Wee, Uttam Surana, and Baltazar Aguda model that rhythm in this 2009 PLOS ONE article. Levels of p53 and MDM2 oscillate after ionizing radiation, but the meaning of the pulses was unclear.

The p53-MDM2 feedback loop is embedded in a wider network with Akt. The authors study oscillations of the p53-Akt network and their effect on cell survival and death. Rhythm may encode how much damage a cell has taken. That code could decide whether a cell lives or dies. Oscillation timing may carry information, a view that static snapshots of p53 miss.
plos-pone-0004507:
Schizophrenia may grow out of a missing left-side edge for language, argue Alessandro Angrilli, Chiara Spironelli, Thomas Elbert, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The idea comes from researcher T. J. Crow. He suggested that the gene changes that gave humans left-hemisphere dominance for language also carry the risk of schizophrenia as a hazard.

Most people process the sound structure of language, its phonological component, mainly in the left hemisphere. The team studied people who lack that typical left-side advantage. If the brain's language system is set up differently, the symptoms of schizophrenia may follow, on this view. The study gives a testable shape to a bold theory linking language evolution to mental illness.
plos-pone-0004607:
Testing hypotheses one after another inflates false findings, a statistical problem examined by Thomas Pfeiffer, David Rand, and Anna Dreber in PLOS ONE in 2009. A controversial essay by John Ioannidis had argued that in some research fields, most published findings are false. Theoretical reasoning shows why: small effect sizes, error-prone tests, and low prior odds that a claim is true.

The authors study decision-making in research tasks with sequential testing, where results guide the next test. Each peek at the data changes the true error rate, often without the researcher noticing. The paper gives scientists and funders a clearer view of how study designs manufacture false positives, and how better decision rules could keep published science more honest.
plos-pone-0004707:
Marie Maradeo and Robert Skibbens showed that a second clamp loading complex helps hold sister DNA copies together, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Four related complexes load clamps onto DNA during copying. Only one was thought to aid cohesion, the grip that keeps sister copies paired until cells divide.

That view rested on the fact that loss of the known complex can kill cells. The team tested a related complex built around a protein called Elg1. They found it also plays a part in cohesion. The finding widens the cast that keeps genomes stable at division. Follow up work can check whether the same pattern appears in other settings.
plos-pone-0004807:
Robynn Schillace and colleagues showed that A-kinase anchoring in dendritic cells is required for antigen presentation, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Dendritic cells are the most potent antigen presenting cells of the immune system. Prostaglandin E2, cyclic AMP, and protein kinase A have all been shown to regulate dendritic cell maturation, and Activity in prior immunology studies of vaccine and infection responses.

Anchoring proteins position the kinase near its targets. The team found disrupting that anchoring impairs presentation. Precise positioning, not just kinase presence, controls function. The finding refines how immune signaling is organized. Future studies can use these results to refine both methods and theory.
plos-pone-0004907:
Mohamed Hamza and colleagues identified PPAR gamma RXR binding sites and direct targets during adipogenesis de novo, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Pathophysiology of obesity and type 2 diabetes associates with abnormal endocrine signaling in adipose tissue. The nuclear hormone factor PPAR gamma is a key affector. Genome wide binding maps during fat cell differentiation reveal direct target genes driving adipocyte identity and metabolic function.

Direct targets separate drivers from bystanders. Binding maps anchor regulatory networks concretely. Diabetes drugs already target this factor. Better maps suggest selective modulators. Such evidence helps the field move from broad claims toward tested detail.
plos-pone-0005007:
Migraine aura brings shimmering blind spots before the headache. A slow brain wave called cortical spreading depression is thought to underlie it. The wave's speed matches aura symptoms well. Its shape in animal cortex does not. Markus Dahlem and Nouchine Hadjikhani modeled the mismatch in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Their model uses particle-like waves in weakly susceptible cortex. These waves retract as they travel. That behavior fits the aura's real size and shape better. The work brings theory closer to what patients see. It may also help explain why aura symptoms start, spread and stop. Better models guide better questions about migraine itself.
plos-pone-0005107:
Malaria control in Africa focuses mostly on rural areas. Cities were long considered easier ground. Yvonne Geissbühler and colleagues ran a large urban program in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. The program was community-based and large-scale. It applied microbial larvicide to mosquito breeding sites.

Malaria infection prevalence fell in the city. Killing larvae complements nets and house spraying. Those tools target adult mosquitoes. Larval control attacks the source. The program proves the strategy works in a real African city. It was run by the community, not just researchers. That makes it a model for scaling. Urban malaria can be fought where mosquitoes breed.
plos-pone-0005207:
Bacterial vaginosis is the most common vaginal infection in the world and can lead to serious health problems. Much of the harm is blamed on vaginolysin, a toxin made by the bacterium Gardnerella vaginalis. Randis and colleagues built antibodies against that toxin in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The antibodies can both detect the toxin and block its cell-killing action. A tool that finds and stops the same target is doubly useful, for tests and perhaps for treatment. The work also confirms the toxin's central role in this very common infection.
plos-pone-0005307:
Vertebrate brains have two halves that sense, compute, and must still produce one unified response. How the two sides settle disagreements is largely unknown. Adam and Güntürkün studied that settlement in pigeons in PLOS ONE in 2009, under the name metacontrol.

In some situations, one hemisphere takes charge and the other yields. The pigeon work shows when that takeover happens and what it achieves. Understanding hemispheric control helps explain how a split brain acts as one animal, a puzzle shared across vertebrates including humans. Birds have clean split brains for tests of this kind, since each eye feeds one side. Which is why pigeons are a strong model for how two sides make one mind.
plos-pone-0005407:
Heart cells grown from human embryonic stem cells could one day repair damaged hearts, but they must couple excitation to contraction like real heart cells. Zhu and colleagues studied that coupling locally in PLOS ONE in 2009, comparing stem cell-derived heart cells with fetal heart cells.

Using patch-clamp recording and confocal microscopy, they tested how calcium entry triggers contraction in small regions. Local control of excitation-contraction coupling is a sign of maturing heart cells. The comparison with fetal cells shows how close the lab-grown cells are to the real thing.
plos-pone-0005507:
Silvester de Nooijer, Barbara Holland, and David Penny argued that predation began very early in life's history, in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Complex cells with a nucleus arose somewhere over a billion years ago. In the modern world, single cells that eat other cells by engulfing them are almost all of that complex type.

The authors reason that eating other cells was there near the start, not added later in a peaceful early world. That view changes the story of early life: hunger and defence may have driven the rise of complex cells from the beginning.
plos-pone-0005607:
Elisabet Tubau and Joan López-Moliner studied how past actions shape present ones in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Daily life is made of chains of actions, not single moves. The time a person takes to answer can reveal whether the step before still echoes.

Volunteers answered series of signals where the next step was sometimes known in advance. Knowing what comes next did not wipe out the pull of what came before. That persistence matters for designing tasks, from driving to air control, where one action follows another fast. Chains of rapid answers occur in sport and music too, where the same pull of the past can be measured.
plos-pone-0005707:
Abigail Marsh and colleagues tested in 2009 whether status poses make people look bigger than they are. Across species, dominant animals puff up to seem large. Humans also strike poses and use cues that raise their apparent status.

The team asked whether those cues change how big a person seems to others. Their tests show size judgments shift with nonverbal status cues. The link between rank and size runs deep in the mind, it seems. The finding helps explain snap judgments in meetings, contests, and daily life, where seeming large can win space and respect.
plos-pone-0005807:
Daniel Merl and co-authors built a statistical framework in 2009 for managing disease outbreaks while they unfold. Interventions against an epidemic, from vaccines to closures, each carry different costs. Waiting for full information wastes the chance to act early.

Their framework updates the best plan as new data arrive, aiming to limit spread at the least total cost. It balances acting now against learning more first. Health agencies could use such tools during flu seasons or new outbreaks. The paper is a design for decision-making under uncertainty, tuned to the realities of epidemics.
plos-pone-0005907:
Santiago Vernia and co-authors reported in 2009 that cells missing a key phosphatase suffer both stressed protein factories and failing disposal units. Lafora disease is a fatal inherited epilepsy caused by faults in the laforin gene or its partner. Laforin removes phosphate tags, and its loss wrecks neurons.

Models lacking laforin showed raised endoplasmic reticulum stress and reduced proteasome function. Two housekeeping systems failing at once could drive the neuron death. That double fault suggests treatments must ease stress and restore disposal together. The study reframes a rare disease as a systems breakdown.
plos-pone-0006007:
For a memory to last, the brain must build new protein at the right spot. Leandro Slipczuk, Pedro Bekinschtein, Cynthia Katche and colleagues traced one such building order in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper follows BDNF, a growth factor for neurons, and its effect on mTOR, a kinase that controls when cells make protein.

BDNF switches mTOR on, and that in turn governs production of GluR1, a part of a key receptor for fast brain signals. GluR1 is required for memory formation, the title notes. The chain from growth factor to receptor gives memory science a concrete path to test, and each link is a place where learning could be helped or harmed.
plos-pone-0006107:
The RecQ helicases are the genome's unwinders, and their loss brings cancer risk and early aging. Yanjuan Xu, Zhiyong Lei, Hai Huang and colleagues studied the fruit fly member of that family in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper shows dRecQ4 at work in Drosophila, in a family where three of five human members are tied to disorders of cancer and premature aging.

dRecQ4 is required for DNA synthesis and essential for cell proliferation, the title states. A fly that cannot copy DNA or divide without it gives researchers a fast model of the human disorders. The work links a single helicase to the twin foundations of growth: copying the genome and multiplying cells.
plos-pone-0006207:
A virus infection of the heart can leave lasting inflammation that the immune system itself keeps alive. Maya Poffenberger and colleagues studied coxsackievirus infection in mice lacking IL-6, an immune signal, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The early immune response is thought to decide whether the illness fades or turns chronic.

Without IL-6, the early response ran hotter, and the long-term heart inflammation grew worse. A missing calming signal thus backfired rather than helping. The result warns that blocking immune signals can have the opposite effect to the one hoped for. It sharpens thinking about treating virus-linked heart disease.
plos-pone-0006307:
The same immune brake gene tied to autoimmune disease may worsen tuberculosis. Thorsten Thye and colleagues studied a CTLA4 gene variant in an African population in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. CTLA4 restrains T lymphocytes, and one variant in it is associated with several immune self-attack diseases and weaker T-cell work.

The gene form tied to self-attack disease added to severe pulmonary tuberculosis in the study population. Weaker T-cell control may let lung infection run further. The result connects infectious disease severity to immune regulation genes. It helps explain why the same infection hits people so differently. Genes that tune the immune brakes may thus shape the fate of this lung disease.
plos-pone-0006407:
A cell division motor protein answers to the hormone estrogen in unexpected ways. Margalit Zusev and Dafna Benayahu studied MS-KIF18A, a kinesin protein, and its cross talk with estrogen receptor alpha in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. They investigated in living systems and in lab assays, at gene and protein levels.

Estrogen regulates the motor's expression, and the two interact directly. Hormones steering division machinery links endocrine signals to cell proliferation. That link matters in hormone-sensitive cancers. It also adds a target to the network around the estrogen receptor. The link may matter where hormone drugs are used to treat breast or bone disease.
plos-pone-0006507:
Sven Kroener and co-authors studied dopamine in the front part of the brain in PLOS ONE in 2009. Dopamine is a chemical messenger. It is known to help this brain area hold facts in mind for short tasks. How it does that job is still argued. The team asked how dopamine changes the work of nerve cells in this area.

They looked at how dopamine boosts the signal and cuts the noise in these cells. In plain terms, it may help wanted signals stand out from background chatter. That sharper tuning could be why dopamine helps focus and clear thought. The work feeds ideas about both normal thought and illness of the mind.
plos-pone-0006607:
Marni Falk, Julie Rosenjack, Erzsebet Polyak, and colleagues studied mitochondrial complex I in a worm model in PLOS ONE in 2009. Complex I dysfunction is a common, heterogeneous cause of human mitochondrial disease with poorly understood pathogenesis. The extensive conservation of complex I composition makes the worm Caenorhabditis elegans a useful model.

Their title reports that subcomplex I lambda specifically controls integrated mitochondrial functions in the worm. One piece of a huge machine governs overall performance. Pinpointing that piece focuses research on how the complex fails. Worm genetics allow fast testing that human studies cannot.
plos-pone-0006707:
Frank Baumann and co-authors tested which parts of the prion protein matter in living animals in PLOS ONE in 2009. Prions are misfolded, clumped copies of a normal cell protein. The normal protein is called PrPC, and mice without it stay healthy. Yet versions missing the central domain cause lethal illness. A related protein can cause similar damage.

Working in vivo, the team identified which domains of the protein are functionally relevant. Their approach separated harmless forms from dangerous ones. Knowing the key region focuses the search for how prions kill neurons. It also clarifies what the normal protein's central part normally does. The results guide both prion biology and possible treatment ideas.
plos-pone-0006807:
Rafael Dias Loyola and colleagues built global conservation priorities for carnivores in PLOS ONE in 2009. Standard schemes highlight species-rich areas facing extinction risk. Such schemes can ignore what species are like biologically. They can also ignore the cost of protecting land. Funds for conservation are limited worldwide.

The authors integrated economic costs and biological traits into priority setting. Carnivores range from tiny weasels to tigers, with very different needs. Trait-aware, cost-aware plans protect more real diversity per dollar. Their approach argues priorities should reflect ecology and economics together. The framework can extend beyond carnivores to other groups.
plos-pone-0006907:
Douglas M. Ruderfer and his team foretold drug replies in yeast from gene data in PLOS ONE in 2009. Drugs tuned to one man's genes are the aim of genomic medicine. Gene use at rest had shown it can foretell drug replies. Gene type adds a fresh layer of fact. Yeast gives a fast test bed for such bids.

Gene use and gene type, read as one, foretold drug replies more sharply. The proof in a plain beast can guide the same work in man. Sharp foretelling means less trial and error at the clinic. It also pairs old drugs with the men most apt to gain from them.
plos-pone-0007007:
Rachel Hammond, Sandra Blaess, and Asa Abeliovich studied wiring signals in the midbrain in PLOS ONE in 2009. Dopamine axons grow from the substantia nigra and ventral tegmental area toward their targets. Those targets include the striatum and other forebrain regions. The cues that guide the growing axons were only partly known.

The team showed that Sonic hedgehog works as a chemoattractant here. Midbrain dopamine axons turn toward this signal as they grow. A guidance role adds to hedgehog's known jobs in development. Faulty wiring of dopamine circuits is tied to several brain disorders, so each cue matters.
plos-pone-0007107:
Jeban Ganesalingam, Daniel Stahl, Lokesh Wijesekera, and colleagues sorted ALS patients by pattern in PLOS ONE in 2009. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis attacks the nerve cells that drive muscles. It appears in several distinct forms, and patients decline at very different speeds. Whether those forms reflect different disease processes was unknown. The team applied a clustering method to patient data.

The analysis found groups that differ in outlook. Grouping by data, rather than by first symptom, sharpened survival guesses. Groups with clearer outlooks help doctors counsel patients with more honesty. They also help trials enroll patients whose disease pace is alike.
plos-pone-0007207:
Martin Horlitz, Annabelle Lucas, and Markus Sprenger-Haussels improved a blood DNA test in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Free circulating DNA floats in human blood plasma in small fragments. Doctors and researchers measure it for cancer, pregnancy, and transplant monitoring, among other uses.

Duplex real-time PCR assays were already widely used to measure that DNA. Fragmented DNA can bias results, because only some pieces carry both target sites. The authors present an optimized, calibrated method for accurate measurement. Their work helps labs compare plasma DNA results across studies with more confidence.
plos-pone-0007307:
Gui-Rong Li, Hai-Ying Sun, Jing-Bo Chen, and colleagues characterized ion channels in human heart support cells in 2009. Cardiac fibroblasts are not the contracting heart muscle cells. Evidence suggested fibroblasts can couple electrically to muscle cells, yet fibroblast electrical properties were poorly established compared with muscle cells.

The authors grow human cardiac fibroblasts in culture. They record and characterize multiple ion channels, the pores that carry electrical signals across membranes. Their PLOS ONE catalog gives heart researchers a baseline for fibroblast behavior. That baseline matters because fibroblasts multiply in scarred hearts after injury.
plos-pone-0007407:
Stefan Niemann, Claudio U. Köser, Sebastien Gagneux, and colleagues compared tuberculosis genomes with matching fingerprints in 2009. The tuberculosis bacterium complex has low sequence diversity. It is a classic example of a genetically monomorphic pathogen, and that limited variation makes routine genotyping hard for tracking outbreaks and drug resistance in patients.

The authors study genomic diversity among drug sensitive and multidrug resistant isolates. Those isolates share identical DNA fingerprints by standard tests. Genome sequencing can still reveal hidden differences. Their PLOS ONE comparison shows how much variation standard fingerprinting misses, with implications for tracking resistant tuberculosis spread.
plos-pone-0007507:
M. Dominik Fischer and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on imaging the living mouse retina. Optical coherence tomography uses light to build cross-section images of tissue, without any cutting. It is already a mainstay of eye clinics. The team adapted a commercial third-generation scanner to the tiny mouse eye. Their goal was sections that rival traditional microscope slides.

In mouse models of retinal degeneration, the scanner delivered histology-like views in living animals. That means the same eye can be followed as disease unfolds over time. Fewer animals are needed, and each one's course is clearer. The method bridges clinic and laboratory: the same imaging serves patients and mouse studies. For inherited blindness research, that continuity is valuable. It speeds the testing of treatments meant to save sight.
plos-pone-0007607:
Beatrice Cardinali and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the small RNAs that schedule muscle development. MicroRNAs are short, non-coding RNAs that dial genes down after their messages are made. They have emerged as key regulators across biology. Two of them, miR-221 and miR-222, drew the team's attention in skeletal muscle cells. The authors tracked how the pair affects the cells' differentiation and maturation.

The two microRNAs modulate when muscle precursors commit and mature. Timing is everything in building muscle, since cells must stop dividing before they fuse and specialize. A pair of tiny RNAs acting as schedulers fits that need neatly. The findings add to the picture of microRNAs as master timers of tissue development. Muscle repair in adults replays these programs, so the regulators matter beyond development.
plos-pone-0007707:
Alessandra Girasol and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It concerns leptin, a hormone best known for controlling hunger and body weight. Leptin also shapes the immune system, in part through the thymus. In that organ, it alters cytokine signals and cell survival.

Some of leptin's effects in the thymus run through a pathway that does not use its usual switch. The authors show that an enzyme called Fyn carries those signals in rodents. Tracing this route helps explain how body weight and immunity influence each other, a link seen in both obesity and malnutrition.
plos-pone-0007807:
Jennifer Apple and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It explains an odd pattern among plants on Mount St. Helens. Lupins recolonized the volcano's slopes after its eruption. Where lupins grow dense, insect damage is low; where they are sparse, damage is high.

That inverse pattern puzzled ecologists. The authors point to phosphorus balance as the key. As the plant community changes over time, the ratio of nitrogen to phosphorus shifts. Insects need phosphorus more than leaves provide. Changing plant chemistry thus reshapes how hard herbivores can feed, and where lupins thrive.
plos-pone-0007907:
Aubree Gordon and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It tests how well a rapid flu test works in children in Nicaragua. Influenza is a major public health threat worldwide. In poor countries, doctors often rely on quick bedside tests.

The accuracy of those tests in developing-country clinics was not well described. The team evaluated the QuickVue Influenza A+B test in a primary care setting. They measured how often it caught true flu and how often it cried wolf. Honest accuracy numbers help clinics decide when a negative result can be trusted.
plos-pone-0008007:
Karen Drahos and colleagues tracked a clotting brake in blood platelets for PLOS ONE in 2009. The brake protein, Disabled-2, slows platelet clumping. At a wound, platelets must clump fast, so the brake has to move aside at the right moment.

Fatty molecules called sulfatides do the moving. When platelets switch on, sulfatides shift the brake protein to the surface and out of the way. That swap lets a clot form in a rush yet stay bounded. The work explains a fine piece of timing in how bleeding stops. It is one more sign that fats in membranes do active work, not just packing.
plos-pone-0008107:
Manuel Buscarlet and colleagues found the trigger that arms a brake on new brain cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. The brake protein, Groucho/TLE1, silences genes and can bar young cells from becoming cortical neurons. Its family guides growth in animals from flies to people.

The brake only works after a helper-driven step tags it with phosphate. Without that tag, neurons form freely despite the brake's presence. Knowing the arming step shows how the growing brain times the birth of its cells, holding some back until their turn comes. The tag itself may be a handle for future drugs.
plos-pone-0008207:
Dimitri J. Bayle, Marie-Anne Henaff, and Pierre Krolak-Salmon studied fear and vision in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. In real life, threats often appear at the edge of sight first. The brain must shift attention there fast to allow a quick response. The authors asked whether unseen fear signals in peripheral vision alert the limbic system.

They used MEG, a method that records magnetic fields from the brain. Faces showing fear were presented so subjects did not consciously perceive them. Brain responses showed the alarm system reacting anyway. The result helps explain how danger can move us before we notice it.
plos-pone-0008307:
Tom A. de Graaf and colleagues combined two brain methods in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. fMRI shows which brain areas are active during a task. Transcranial magnetic stimulation, or TMS, temporarily interferes with an area's work. Both methods address how brain organization causes behavior. They were traditionally quite distinct approaches.

The team paired fMRI effective connectivity with TMS chronometry. Chronometry reveals when an area matters during visuospatial judgment. Together the methods give complementary accounts of causality in that network. The approach shows how to test brain pathways, not just map them.
plos-pone-0008407:
Daniel R. Zerbino and colleagues improved a genome assembler in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Short-read sequencing technologies are useful for building genomes from scratch. Complex repeat patterns, though, block large assemblies, especially in eukaryotes. Repeated stretches confuse programs about how pieces join. The Velvet assembler is a widely used tool for short reads.

The authors present two heuristic algorithms, Pebble and Rock Band. They resolve repeats and improve scaffolding of assembled pieces. Better assemblies make every downstream analysis more reliable. The work helps labs sequence new genomes with short reads.
plos-pone-0008507:
Susann Becker and co-authors test a gut protein in transgenic mice in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The protein CD97 sits in normal colon lining cells. It is overproduced in colorectal cancer, where levels run too high. To learn its function, the team bred mice that overproduce CD97 in gut lining cells. Those mice let them watch CD97 effects apart from cancer. They then induce colitis, an inflammation of the colon.

Mice with extra CD97 develop milder colitis than normal mice. The protein strengthens adherens junctions, seals that hold lining cells together. Stronger seals may protect the gut barrier in inflammation. The result reframes CD97 as a guardian, not just a cancer marker.
plos-pone-0008607:
Yigal Senderovich and co-authors test fish as cholera carriers in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Vibrio cholerae is the agent that causes cholera. It is native to various aquatic environments, but its ecology remains an enigma. Copepods and chironomids were suggested as natural reservoirs of the germ. Fish live in the same waters and eat such organisms. The team ask if fish also serve as reservoirs and vectors.

They find evidence that fish carry and spread V. cholerae. Fish could move the germ between water bodies and to humans who handle or eat them. That route would change cholera surveillance and food safety advice. It adds a mobile reservoir to a puzzling ecology.
plos-pone-0008707:
Jacklin Mosha, Lesong Conteh, Fabrizio Tediosi, and colleagues priced a common mistake in malaria care. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study comes from dispensaries in north-eastern Tanzania. Many fevers there are treated as malaria without a firm test. Wrong treatment wastes drugs and helps real malaria parasites resist them. Better testing costs money up front, though.

The team measured how often children were overdiagnosed with malaria. They then weighed the cost of better diagnosis against savings from fewer wrong treatments. Their figures give health planners a concrete trade-off. Spending on tests may pay for itself while protecting drug supplies.
plos-pone-0008807:
Ian Mitchell, Timothy Brown, Lance Terada, and colleagues weakened a vessel glue protein in growing zebrafish. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. VE-cadherin holds the cells lining blood vessels together. It also guides new vessel sprouting. Its exact role in building the heart and vessels was becoming clear only slowly. Zebrafish embryos develop fast and stay transparent, easing observation.

Knocking the protein down produced visible vessel defects during development. The pattern of defects shows where the glue is most needed. Such knowledge underpins work on vessel leaks and malformations. It also guides drugs that aim to grow or prune vessels.
plos-pone-0008907:
Jameal Samhouri, Phillip Levin, and Cameron Ainsworth set out to name the trigger points for ecosystem-level management. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Managing whole ecosystems, not just single species, is a widely shared goal. Practice lagged because no one defined when action should start. Reference points that trigger a response are standard for single fisheries. Whole ecosystems needed their own versions.

The authors propose a systematic way to set ecosystem thresholds. Indicators crossing a threshold would call for management action. Clear triggers turn a vague concept into workable policy. Coastal and ocean managers gain a decision framework they can defend.
plos-pone-0009007:
Ufuk Nalbantoglu and co-authors compared the genomes of two rabbit-fever bacteria, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Francisella tularensis is a highly infectious germ behind tularemia. One branch, called A1, splits into separate populations across North America. The team sequenced a fresh A1 isolate taken from a Nebraska patient in 1998.

They set the new genome beside Schu S4, the standard lab strain. Large repeated DNA stretches flanked the places where the genomes were reshuffled. Those repeats likely let the genome swap blocks around as it evolves. Knowing how this germ rearranges itself helps track its family history and spread.
plos-pone-0009107:
José Oliveira-Martins and co-authors probed a routine cut made in the prion protein, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The normal prion protein sits on brain cells and gets snipped at its alpha site. Mice whose prions cannot be cut show signs of nerve damage. That suggested the cutting is important for the protein's normal job.

The team varied the amino acids around the cut site. Cleavage went ahead despite changes they expected to block it. The cutting machinery is more forgiving than its reputation. Robust cutting may protect the brain even when the protein mutates.
plos-pone-0009207:
Wes Toller and colleagues published this marine survey in PLOS ONE in 2010. It covers Saba Bank, a huge submerged platform in the northeastern Caribbean Sea near Saba Island. The bank spans about 2,200 square kilometers of carbonate seafloor. Reef-like shapes and coral growth along its edge mark it as an active reef system.

The team catalogued the reef fishes living across the bank's range of habitat types. They describe how the fish community changes from one habitat to the next. Such a baseline matters because remote banks are hard to study and easy to overlook. The survey gives managers a picture of what lives there before pressures grow.
plos-pone-0009307:
Steven Collins and Arthur Kuo published this walking study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Human walking wastes a surprising amount of energy at each step change. The ankle then pays energy back at push-off to keep us moving. When ankles are impaired, walking almost always becomes costlier.

The authors explored a device idea: capture energy that would be lost and recycle it into push-off. Restoring the ankle's lost energy should restore a more normal, cheaper gait. Their approach treats the leg like a machine whose losses can be partly recovered. It points toward prosthetics and braces that help rather than merely support.
plos-pone-0009407:
Catharina Lavebratt and co-authors published this depression genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The body clock often runs wrong in major depression and bipolar disorder. Clock genes are therefore prime suspects in these illnesses. One of them, CRY2, helps run the evening side of the daily oscillator.

The team tested whether CRY2 is associated with depression. They report that it is. An evening-clock gene linked to depression fits the sleep and energy patterns patients describe. The finding gives researchers a specific gene to probe for how clock faults become mood disorders.
plos-pone-0009507:
Daniele Klett and colleagues tested hormone like chemicals on a cell enzyme in PLOS ONE in 2010. The enzyme, called PDI, helps new proteins fold in the cell's inner workshop. It also binds hormones such as estrogen and thyroid hormone. Some man made compounds can mimic hormones and disrupt the body. The team asked whether such compounds also impair PDI.

Using a lab assay for one of PDI's tasks, they measured how the compounds changed its activity. Several of them did alter the enzyme's work. That finding flags a new route by which hormone mimics could harm cells. The harm would come not just from false signals, but from faulty protein folding.
plos-pone-0009607:
Claude Everaerts and co-authors revisited the scent chemistry of fruit flies in PLOS ONE in 2010. Flies talk to each other with chemicals worn on the skin, called cuticular hydrocarbons. Those chemicals help drive courtship and mating choices. Earlier work treated a fly's chemical profile as fixed. The team asked whether mating itself changes the profile.

After mating, a fly's skin chemicals did change in measurable ways. So the profile works like a status signal, not a fixed badge. Other flies can read that history from the scent. The finding reshapes how we think about insect social signals, since experience writes on them.
plos-pone-0009707:
Embryonic stem cells can become many kinds of tissue. Shuxian Jiang and colleagues explored an unusual path for them in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. They used mouse embryonic stem cells that were first guided toward becoming blood-forming stem cells.

Those cells then helped rebuild mammary epithelial tissue, the lining that forms milk ducts in the breast. Morphogenesis means the shaping of a tissue as it grows into form. The result suggests stem cells can cross expected boundaries between tissue types. Findings like these inform work on tissue repair and breast biology.
plos-pone-0009907:
Vitamin D compounds can slow leukemia cells, but many also raise blood calcium dangerously. Andrzej Slominski and colleagues tested safer products made from vitamin D building blocks. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Calcemic activity means raising calcium levels in the blood.

The products came from vitamin D3 or from 7-dehydrocholesterol, processed by the enzyme cytochrome P450scc. They showed anti-leukemia effects in the tests. Crucially, they had low or absent calcemic activity, so they did not spike calcium. Safer vitamin D relatives could widen treatment options. Low calcium risk is the key gain here.
plos-pone-0010007:
Leena Kovanen, Sirkku Saarikoski, Arpo Aromaa, and co-workers examined clock genes and human fertility in PLOS ONE in 2010. Body clocks time sleep, metabolism, cell division, and seasonal change. Faults in those clocks have been tied in earlier work to troubled sleep, low mood, and metabolic problems.

The team looked at variants in two clock genes, ARNTL, also called BMAL1, and NPAS2. They tested whether those variants track with fertility and with seasonal patterns in people. Their title reports that both genes contribute to those traits, tying daily body timing to reproduction in a direct genetic way.
plos-pone-0010207:
The authors were Natsuhiko Kumasaka, Yusuke Nakamura, and Naoyuki Kamatani. Their 2010 PLOS ONE paper presented a new chart for genetic data, called the textile plot. Genetic studies now use very dense sets of SNP markers, single letter DNA variants. Linked markers, in linkage disequilibrium, can tangle statistical analysis and hide true patterns in the data.

The textile plot displays genotypes for many markers in a woven, visual form. A clearer display helps researchers spot linked blocks and odd samples at a glance. Better views of dense data can prevent errors in large gene studies.
plos-pone-0010307:
The authors were Steven Reynolds, Cissy Kityo, Claire Hallahan, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE trial tested HIV treatment breaks in Uganda. Taking antiretroviral drugs in short cycles, with planned pauses, could cut toxicity and drug costs. Cheaper, gentler regimens could extend treatment programs to more people in low-income settings, if breaks prove safe enough in controlled testing.

The seventy-two week trial enrolled 146 HIV-positive people already on therapy. It compared short cycle intermittent treatment with continuous treatment, testing non-inferiority. Results from such trials guide policy where drug budgets are tight and demand keeps growing.
plos-pone-0010407:
Muriel Nguyen and co-workers charted how babies' immune defenses grow up during the first year, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Newborns catch infections easily and respond weakly to many vaccines. Their immune sensors are often blamed for that weakness. Two sensors, TLR4 and TLR9, detect germ patterns and rouse defenses. The team measured how responses through these sensors change with age.

They used cord blood as the newborn starting point, then followed later samples. Responses gradually reached adult-like strength over the year. Knowing that timetable helps time vaccines for when babies can answer them. It also explains part of the early vulnerability to infection. Development, here, is an immune system slowly turning up its own volume.
plos-pone-0010507:
Ricardo Valladares and colleagues fed a gut bacterium to diabetes-prone rats and slowed the disease for PLOS ONE in 2010. Type 1 diabetes arises when immunity attacks insulin-making cells. The gut lining and its microbes shape that immunity daily. A leaky gut barrier and skewed immune activity may help trigger the disease. The team gave rats a Lactobacillus strain, N6.2, and watched diabetes develop.

Rats receiving the bacterium developed diabetes less or later. A single microbe strain easing an autoimmune disease is a notable result. It supports the idea that gut microbes can be therapy, not just passengers. More work must find how the effect works. Still, this study gives the probiotic approach a concrete success.
plos-pone-0010607:
Pai Ching Yu and colleagues described surgery outside the heart in Brazil, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Rich countries account for most operations worldwide. Far less is recorded about surgical care in poorer nations, where records are thin.

The team gathered data on non-cardiac operations, patients, and costs across Brazil. They found wide gaps in access and a heavy load of urgent cases. Many operations treated problems that earlier care might have prevented. The authors argue that better surgical planning could save lives and money. Their numbers give health planners a starting point for reform.
plos-pone-0010707:
Hongshan Liu and colleagues tested stem cell therapy for a blinding cornea disease in mice, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some children are born with cloudy corneas because a protein called lumican is missing. Donor cornea transplants can help, but donors and surgeons are scarce in many countries.

The team placed mesenchymal stem cells from umbilical cord tissue onto the eyes of lumican-free mice. The clouded corneas grew clearer and more normally structured. The donor cells also quieted inflammation in the eye. A cell treatment that avoids scarce donor tissue could widen care for corneal blindness worldwide.
plos-pone-0010807:
Ricardo Ataíde and colleagues improved a test of immunity to malaria in pregnancy, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Malaria in pregnancy harms mothers and babies, causing anemia and low birth weight. The parasite hides in the placenta, and antibodies that help immune cells eat it are a key defense. HIV weakens that defense, but measuring the weakening was crude.

Their improved assay measures how well antibodies drive white cells to swallow the parasite. With it, HIV's erosion of that protection could be quantified. Sharper measurement matters for vaccine trials in pregnant women, since the endpoint is exactly this eating response. It also guides care where both infections overlap.
plos-pone-0010907:
Noa Sela, Britta Mersch, Agnes Hotz-Wagenblatt and co-authors published this genome evolution study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Transposable elements are DNA stretches that copy themselves around the genome. When one lands inside a gene, it can sometimes be recruited as a new exon, a coding segment, an event called exonization that adds variety to proteins.

Comparing human and mouse genes, the authors found exonized elements cluster toward the start of the coding region in both species. They also found cases where exonization exists in one population but not another, suggesting these events can differ between groups and fuel divergence. Sela and colleagues chart the rules that govern how jumping DNA gets domesticated into genes, a quiet engine of mammalian evolution.
plos-pone-0011007:
Hany Arab, Gulzar Wani, Alo Ray and co-authors published this DNA repair study in PLOS ONE in 2010. TFIIH is a two-part machine: a core that helps open DNA for repair and gene reading, and a kinase module called CAK. Certain mutations in its XPG subunit cause severe repair diseases, and the authors asked how those mutations change the machine's assembly at damage sites.
