In healthy cells both parts rushed to DNA damage, but in cells from severe XP-G and related patients, the kinase module never arrived, while another part recruited normally. Blocking CAK's activity did not stop the repair machinery assembling or lesions being removed; instead CAK handled later steps such as tagging the gene-reading enzyme. Arab and colleagues link disease severity to whether the machine falls apart at the right moment.
plos-pone-0011107:
Leonardi, Rehg, Rock and colleagues published metabolism research in PLOS ONE in 2010. Between meals, the body must switch from burning food to burning stored fuel. The team studied an enzyme needed to make a key helper molecule for that switch.

They found the enzyme is required for the body to move smoothly from the fed state to the fasted state. Without it, the normal fuel shift breaks down. That finding names a gatekeeper in energy control. It matters for research on fasting, diabetes and other states where fuel use goes wrong.
plos-pone-0011307:
Bernardo, Wachtmann, Cosgrove and colleagues combined two treatments in obese mice for PLOS ONE in 2010. One drug mimics part of exercise by activating a metabolic regulator. The other blocks myostatin, a brake on muscle growth. Both were given after birth to mice that were obese and insulin resistant.

The two treatments exerted distinct yet complementary effects on the mice's metabolic profile. One leaned toward burning fuel, the other toward building muscle, improving the overall picture together. Pairing unlike mechanisms is a common path in diabetes therapy. The study shows these exercise linked routes can add to each other.
plos-pone-0011407:
Gustavo Miranda Rocha and colleagues watched in 2010 how a parasite's swimming aid changes shape while it beats. Trypanosoma cruzi causes Chagas disease and moves with a whip-like tail stiffened by an inner rod. That rod was thought to be a fixed brace, but the team suspected it flexes as the tail swings through water and blood.

Using microscopy on beating tails, they found the rod changes its structure during each stroke. A flexible brace explains how the parasite tunes its swimming for thick and thin surroundings. Movement is not a side detail for this parasite; it must swim to spread through the host and reach new tissue. A structure that only exists in these parasites, and that swimming depends on, is a tempting target for future drugs against Chagas disease.
plos-pone-0011507:
Thomas Bürli and co-authors followed single nicotine receptors in living mouse neurons in 2010. The alpha7 nicotinic receptor sits on hippocampal neurons, cells central to memory, and shapes learning and attention. Where a receptor wanders on the cell surface decides which signals it can join, so the team tracked individual receptors with single-particle methods.

They found the receptors are held in regulated confinement near synaptic sites, both at excitatory and at inhibitory junctions. The cell parks its receptors with care rather than letting them drift freely. That placement matters for drugs aimed at memory and schizophrenia, many of which target this receptor. A drug's effect will depend on the receptors it can actually reach, in the pens where they are kept, so the map of confinement is practical pharmacology.
plos-pone-0011607:
Ying Wang and colleagues examined a plant-related compound called DCB-3503 in PLOS ONE in 2010. The compound slowed growth of human pancreatic and liver cancer tumours grown in mice. Rather than killing the cancer cells outright, it pushed them to mature into a less harmful state, an unusual and promising effect.

Wang's team traced the effect to a block in protein building inside the cells. They show the compound halts that process through a mechanism not seen with known drugs. A fresh way to stall protein production gives cancer researchers both a lead compound and a probe for studying how cells make proteins.
plos-pone-0011707:
Xingxing Kong and co-authors identified a new partner in the cell's energy control system, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Sirtuin 3 is one of seven mammalian sirtuins and the only one linked to human life span. Another regulator, PGC-1 alpha, is well known for driving cells to build fresh mitochondria, their energy factories.

The team showed sirtuin 3 is a direct target switched on by PGC-1 alpha. Once active, it curbs harmful reactive oxygen species while supporting the building of new mitochondria. That double duty makes sirtuin 3 a key switch for healthy cellular power.
plos-pone-0011807:
Aissam Ikmi and Matthew Gibson characterised a glowing protein from a sea anemone, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Nematostella vectensis has become a key model animal for comparing genomes and studying development. Anthozoan cnidarians are famous for producing many diverse fluorescent proteins, yet this species' own set was incompletely known.

The authors identified a red fluorescent protein, NvFP-7R, that is regulated during development, and characterised it in the living animal. A development-timed red beacon gives laboratories a new marker for watching young animals take shape, in a species central to evolutionary comparisons.
plos-pone-0011907:
Andrew Ahn and colleagues measured in 2010 the electrical properties of the lines that acupuncture maps draw on the body. Earlier work suggested these meridian lines carry lower electrical impedance than nearby skin, and that they line up with planes of connective tissue under the skin. The scientific basis of meridians remains unsettled.

The team tested whether bands of collagen, the main connective tissue protein, sitting under the skin explain the electrical readings along meridians. Tying a traditional map to a measurable tissue feature would give acupuncture research something concrete to test. If collagen bands account for the signal, the mystery shifts from energy channels to ordinary anatomy with unusual placement.
plos-pone-0012007:
Kristina Schmidt and co-workers studied in 2010 how yeast chromosomes break and rejoin in unstable arrangements. Genome instability underlies chromosome breakage syndromes and most cancers, yet its mechanics are still poorly understood. Baker's yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, has given science many of the known genome-protection genes, and checkpoint-defective yeast strains expose what happens without them.

The team followed the formation of complex, unstable translocations, in which chromosome pieces swap places in tangled ways. Unstable rearrangements keep changing in later generations, unlike clean swaps. Watching them form in yeast reveals early steps in the chromosome chaos seen in cancer cells, at a scale experiments can actually follow.
plos-pone-0012107:
Philippe Gannon, Jessica Godin-Ethier, Matthew Hassler, and co-authors studied prostate cancer cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. Prostate cancer is the most often found cancer in North American men, and standard care often blocks male hormones to slow it. That treatment also draws immune cells into the prostate, but the ways hormones steer the tumor's immune setting were poorly understood.

The team tracked three genes whose activity shifts under hormone control: two that make an enzyme handling a basic building block of cells, and one that calls in immune cells. Changes in these genes may help a tumor hide from the immune system. Knowing which switches hormones flip gives immunotherapy research new points to target.
plos-pone-0012207:
Pamela Pulimeno, Christoph Bauer, Jeffrey Stutz, and co-authors charted where a cell-junction protein appears in the body, in PLOS ONE in 2010. PLEKHA7 had just been found linking the glue complex between cells to the cell's inner scaffolding. Little was known about which tissues use it or where inside the cell it sits compared with better-known junction proteins.

Their mapping shows its tissue pattern and cell location differ clearly from those familiar markers. A distinct pattern suggests a distinct job at the junctions where cells hold together. Such groundwork matters because junction faults feed into cancer spread and gut diseases, and each new junction protein is a possible clue.
plos-pone-0012307:
Abra Brisbin, Myrna Weissman, Abby Fyer, and co-authors built a statistical method for gene hunting in families, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Family studies of inherited disease often record traits that are categories, like severity grades, rather than measurements, and their pedigrees come in every shape, with data missing here and there. Standard linkage methods handle such messiness poorly, which wastes expensive family data.

Their Bayesian method, built for ordinal and categorical traits, analyzes complex family trees while filling gaps by principled guessing. Psychiatric genetics, the authors' home field, runs on exactly such families and graded traits. Better tools mean the same hard-won pedigrees can answer more questions before they are exhausted.
plos-pone-0012407:
Richard Giannone, Hayes McDonald, Gregory Hurst and colleagues mapped the protein partners that cluster around chromosome end guards, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Telomeres cap chromosome tips, and three binding factors — TRF1, TRF2, and POT1 — anchor the protective complex. Their partner proteins control telomere length and stability, which matter for aging and cancer.

The team pulled down each factor and listed the proteins that came with it, sketching the neighborhood around the telomere guards. New partners in the list are fresh leads for how telomeres are maintained and repaired. That knowledge feeds both cancer research, where telomere control fails, and the study of premature aging diseases.
plos-pone-0012507:
Sandra Negro, Abigail Caudron, Michel Dubois and colleagues linked rank, hormones, and parasites in a harem-living mammal, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Life history theory says energy spent on status and mating cannot be spent on immunity. Testosterone, which fuels male competition, is often blamed for weaker parasite defense in high-ranking males.

The team measured social status, testosterone, and parasite loads in the polygynous species and tested how the three move together. Their results test the simple trade-off story in a wild social setting. Findings like these sharpen predictions about disease spread in animal groups, where dominant males can become parasite hubs.
plos-pone-0012607:
Castro, Romao, Carvalho and co-authors probed how parasites of the trypanosomatid family handle chemical stress inside their mitochondria. These parasites, which include the agents of leishmaniasis and sleeping sickness, use a thiol system unlike our own. A protein called tryparedoxin was thought to carry reducing power through that system.

Their 2010 work found that the mitochondria can keep their redox balance even without tryparedoxin activity. That surprise means another route must do the job, or the system is more flexible than thought. Knowing the backup routes matters for drugs that aim at parasite chemistry.
plos-pone-0012707:
Goncalves, Pistilli, Balduzzi and co-authors asked whether a growth signal called Akt is needed for a muscle-building drug to work. Akt drives normal muscle growth as animals develop. Blocking a muscle brake called ActRIIB makes muscles bigger and stronger, a route eyed for wasting diseases.

Their 2010 mouse study found that lacking Akt leaves muscles smaller and weaker, yet the ActRIIB blocker still worked. That split means the drug route does not depend on Akt, good news for patients whose Akt signalling is low. Separate paths to growth give doctors more options.
plos-pone-0012807:
Kuffner, Petri, Windhager and co-authors merged two modelling styles to rebuild gene networks from data. The DREAM4 contest set network rebuilding teams a hard, blind test with computer-made data. Their 2010 method uses Petri nets, a diagram style for stepwise processes, softened by fuzzy logic that allows in-between values.

The mix aims to recover network wiring and also set its numbers, not just its shape. Rebuilding gene networks from data is a core task in systems biology. Their entry adds a flexible option for noisy real data.  Their entry was scored blind against the hidden networks.
plos-pone-0335107:
Sadiksha Pokhrel and colleagues studied why some babies are born too small at Kathmandu's main maternity hospital. Low birth weight means under two and a half kilos. It is tied to illness in infancy and slow growth later. The team compared fifty-seven mothers of small babies with over a hundred mothers of normal-weight babies. The groups were matched by age. Interviews and hospital records supplied the facts.

The risk list maps a mother's hardships before birth. Little schooling and low income raised the odds. So did anemia, low weight before pregnancy, and chronic illness. Sickness during pregnancy, diet, early delivery, and many past births added risk too. Most of these causes sit far from the delivery room. Prevention belongs in food, rest, and antenatal care.
plos-pone-0339107:
Bernard Gyamfi Anane, Victoria Bam, Gertrude Boafo, Emmanuel Osei-Peprah, and Jacob Tetteh published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It asks how satisfied healthcare providers are with the electronic records systems they use each day. The setting is the Ashanti region of Ghana, studied through a multicenter cross-sectional survey.

Electronic records only improve care if the staff who use them daily find them workable. A survey across several centers can separate problems tied to one site from problems built into the system itself. Hospital leaders rolling out digital records in Ghana and similar countries can use these determinants to fix what frustrates clinicians most.
plos-pone-0339707:
Jianqin Huang and a large team asked whether wild swings in blood sugar, not just high average sugar, spell danger for older patients with sepsis in intensive care. They reviewed records for more than twelve thousand elderly patients admitted for the first time, grouped them by how much their glucose varied, and tracked confusion and death over the following months.

Patients with the widest swings developed delirium more often and died at clearly higher rates within both three and six months. The risk rose in a curved pattern as swings grew, and it stayed after other factors were taken into account. The authors propose that glucose variability, easy to compute from routine readings, could flag the intensive care patients most in need of close watching.
plos-pone-0341107:
Fiona Doherty, Travis Scheadler, and Nadia Matin set out in 2026 a protocol for reviewing how collisions between animals and vehicles affect human health beyond broken bones. Millions of animals are struck worldwide, and people who hit them or come across carcasses may suffer in body, mind, or community life. No review has yet gathered that wider evidence in one place.

Searches across six databases will feed a scoping review guided by a joint human, animal, and environment health view. Three reviewers will screen records and chart themes about harm. The protocol itself reports no findings; its product will be a first map for policy and transport planning.
plos-pone-0343007:
Liankun Zhang led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study of blasting coal with microwaves to open its pores. Coal seams hold methane gas, and freeing it depends on tiny connected pores. Samples of three coal grades were microwaved for repeated cycles, then probed with gas and mercury methods that map pore sizes and roughness.

Microwaves grew the total pore volume, widened some tiny pores into larger ones, and linked fractures better, though effects differed by pore size. Zhang's results support microwave treatment as a way to prime coal seams for gas extraction.
plos-pone-0344207:
Sam Daftari, Mojgan Salavati, and Manoochehr Mortazavi Chamchali published this 2026 study of cleaning copper and zinc out of water with treated Iranian clay. They modified bentonite clay two ways, with nitric acid and heat, or with hydrochloric acid plus chitosan, a natural polymer from shells. Batch tests in the lab varied acidity, dose, time, and starting metal levels.

Both versions pulled metals from water well near neutral acidity, with uptake patterns suggesting chemical binding at the surface. The authors present the clays as cheap, green sorbents that could serve in wastewater treatment plants and factories.
plos-pone-0344407:
Jeanne Seressia, Vitor Hugo Bessa Ferreira, and co-authors compared two bred lines of Japanese quail, one strongly drawn to companions and one far less social, across three tests of social cognition. Sociability varies within species and may shape how animals use social information. Their 2026 study tested gaze following, comfort from a companion's presence, and learning from others' choices about food.

Quail of both lines followed a companion's gaze, the first demonstration of this skill in the species, and sociability made no difference there. Highly social quail, though, were rattled more by isolation and calmed strongly by company, while low-social quail learned the food task faster by exploiting social cues. The authors conclude social motivation tunes social skills by situation rather than raising or lowering them overall.
plos-pone-0345107:
Laura-Lynne Brandt and colleagues asked people in a rural South African community how they would feel about a gentler way of finding out why someone died. The method, called minimally invasive tissue sampling, takes small tissue samples instead of a full autopsy. The team interviewed twenty bereaved residents and held six discussion groups with community members, healers, and health workers.

Most people found the method acceptable, largely because families strongly want to know the cause of death. The study covered community deaths at all ages, wider ground than earlier work on children in hospitals. Knowing what families accept, and what worries them, helps health programs offer the procedure in ways a community can trust.
plos-pone-0346007:
Lily Chu and co-workers interview people who declined to join a Long COVID study to learn what stops or helps enrollment. Long COVID research needs volunteers badly, yet recruitment often stalls. Their 2026 study speaks with thirteen such people and codes their reasons into fifteen factors, then compares them with earlier work on research participation.

Personal and social motives, fair incentives, and trust in known institutions drew people in. Invasive procedures, the charged politics around COVID, and lack of time pushed them away. Trust mattered even more than usual in this divided climate. Studies that trim burdens on daily life and build credibility early, the authors say, will fill their rosters faster.
plos-pone-0346607:
Lisa Baluta and colleagues describe a planned study of sleep apnea screening for people with head and neck cancer. Tumors and their treatment reshape the airway, so apnea is common in this group, yet its fatigue is often blamed on the cancer care itself and the diagnosis is missed. The study tests a phone app, Apneal, that uses the phone's own sensors overnight to flag breathing pauses.

Fifty patients at one center will record two nights at home, once at diagnosis and again six months after treatment, with questionnaires alongside. App estimates will be checked against symptoms and, where needed, standard sleep testing. As a protocol, it reports no findings. If the app proves workable, clinics could screen a vulnerable group cheaply at home instead of sending everyone to a sleep lab.
plos-pone-0347107:
Mst Sonia Parvin and her team took meat and waste water from live bird fairs in Bangladesh. They hunted gut germs that shrug off strong drugs. Such fairs crowd birds, folk, and waste in one place. The team grew the germs, tried drugs on them, and read their genes.

Drug-proof germs were rife. Seven in ten meat germs beat a broad class of drugs. Proof against the last-line class was wide too. Near all proof germs beat drug class on drug class. One grim gene sat in a third of last-line proof germs from meat. The team wants tight drug rules and clean fairs.
plos-pone-0347207:
Petter Törnberg challenges two popular explanations for online echo chambers: that platforms sort people with personal algorithms, and that users simply prefer like-minded company. In his 2026 paper he builds a simple computer model of online communities where neither force is present, then watches what happens when a few members leave groups where they feel outnumbered.

Even when users left only after facing near total disagreement, small departures triggered chains of further exits. Mixed communities gradually sorted themselves into uniform ones. Surprisingly, adding personal algorithms sometimes slowed this sorting by keeping members content enough to stay. A look at one long-running Reddit community matched the model's pattern, with departing users speaking the group's language least.
plos-pone-0347307:
Emily Maria Croasdale, Timothy A C Lamont, and co-authors listened to a coral restoration site in the Seychelles to hear whether a rebuilt reef sounds like a healthy one. Reef soundscapes reflect the animals living there, and underwater recordings offer a gentle way to monitor recovery. Their 2026 study recorded the restored site and neighboring healthy and degraded reefs, then analyzed the recordings two ways: by hand, counting fish sounds, and by machine learning over the whole soundscape.

The two methods disagreed about recovery. Fish calls at the restored site resembled the healthy reef, suggesting real progress, while the broad soundscape still clustered with the degraded reef. The authors conclude restoration does change reef sound, that different creatures likely recover at different speeds, and that monitoring needs several measures at once.
plos-pone-0347607:
Stephanie Colwell and colleagues map breast cancer deaths across Kansas. Their statistics paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. Breast cancer is a top cause of death for US women. Rates vary sharply from place to place. The team modeled deaths across all one hundred five Kansas counties. They tracked change over time as well.

One model kept counties as single units. A second grouped counties into clusters. Both weighed income, care access, and habits as drivers. The team judged fit with three standard scores. Maps of this kind show where deaths run high. They also hint where screening or care may fall short. Health officials can aim effort at the worst spots.
plos-pone-0347907:
Athisake Ruangpracha and colleagues investigated a sugar-sensing protein, ChREBP, in lung adenocarcinoma, the commonest form of lung cancer. The protein normally manages glucose use, but its cancer role was murky. They measured its two versions across three cancer cell lines, then blocked it with a crippled mutant version in the highest-expressing line and watched growth, movement, and gene activity.

Blocking the protein slowed colony growth and migration. Nearly six hundred genes switched off, many driving cell division and the shape-shifting process cancers use to spread. Several of these genes predicted patient survival in real tumour data. The authors position the protein and its network as potential drug targets.
plos-pone-0348007:
Teklu Yitbarek and co-workers test plant extracts as a gentler way to kill cattle ticks in northeastern Ethiopia. Chemical tick killers are failing as ticks grow resistant to them. Their 2026 study soaks adult ticks in alcohol extracts from six local plants, then narrows in on the three that work best and tries them at several strengths.

Castor bean extract killed the most ticks and nearly shut down egg laying. Neem extract came close behind on both counts. A third plant, jatropha, worked far less well. Killing power rose with dose for the top two plants. Plant-based sprays from castor or neem could give herders an option that slows the march of resistance.
plos-pone-0348207:
Zhenhao Guan and his team spent two years on a tomato trial in poor soil. They fed plants a nano form of a known plant food at three dose rates. Some plots also got a spray of a plant hormone. The rest got the old food at the full rate. Rows grew under drip lines and plastic mulch.

The mid dose plus the spray matched the best yields of the full rate. It cut food use by up to a third. Fruit fit for sale rose, and waste fruit fell. The mix also made the most cash per field. The team calls it a sound way to grow more with less.
plos-pone-0348507:
Alesia A Zuccala, Anna Leoncini, and Andrea Bonaccorsi argued in 2026 that the United Nations development goals steer world research like a global directive. They tested the idea by tracking journals tied to three goals: education, work, and climate.

Tens of thousands of journals indexed over three decades were classed by age, field spread, and publishing model. Journal activity around the goals rose steadily, with entry surges near big global agreements. Young and mid aged journals drove the growth, and open access titles featured heavily. Climate research sat in top journals more than the other two goals, showing uneven prestige across the agenda.
plos-pone-0348707:
Henrik Loe and colleagues measured the fitness of one hundred and seventy-nine Norwegian adults living with substance use disorders, a group known to die younger and suffer more lifestyle disease. Each person pushed through a maximal treadmill test recording oxygen uptake. Each also completed a leg strength test. The results were set against large healthy reference populations of the same ages from Norway and the United States.

Across every age band, the patient group trailed badly: oxygen capacity ran roughly fifteen percent lower. A related pulse measure sat about ten percent lower. Leg strength was around thirty percent lower than healthy peers. The authors offer the figures as reference values clinicians can use when setting rehabilitation targets. They argue the deep fitness deficit likely feeds the group's heavier disease burden and shorter lives.
plos-pone-0348807:
Jin Huang and co-workers build a computer vision system that spots flaws on factory products. Finding small surface defects matters for quality and safety, but flaws vary in size and hide in busy textures. Their 2026 paper improves a real-time detection model by adding guidance from word-like meaning cues and a way to blend detail across picture scales.

Tested on three public sets of defect photos, covering steel, patterned cloth, and circuit boards, the new model beat strong rival systems. It found more flaws and drew tighter boxes around them, even in tangled textures. Visual maps showed the model looking at the right spots on each item. The work points toward faster, steadier checks on busy production lines.
plos-pone-0348907:
Md Shadin, Muhammad Torequl Islam, and co-authors pooled clinical trials to judge whether probiotics, synbiotics, and the plant compound berberine genuinely help people with type 2 diabetes control blood sugar. Each has been promoted as a gentle add-on, but results from single trials disagree. Their 2026 review combined more than thirty trials with over two thousand participants and also modeled how berberine might block a starch-digesting enzyme.

Across trials, the interventions lowered fasting blood sugar and a three-month average sugar measure by small but statistically real amounts, with wide variation between studies. Probiotics alone showed similar modest gains against placebo. In the computer model, berberine bound the enzyme more weakly than a standard drug. The authors support these options as add-ons only, and call for bigger, longer, more uniform trials.
plos-pone-0349107:
Diego Fernando Escobar Escobar and colleagues argued in 2026 for a middle path in plant conservation: planting rare species just outside their current range. Some Amazon plants cannot be saved by seed banks, and garden collections often hold too little genetic variety.

Their case study set up living plantings of an exceptional Amazon rainforest species under near natural conditions. The plantings aim to keep broad genetic variety, found self sustaining populations, and enrich the understorey of land being restored. The authors present the approach as a partner to protecting wild habitat, not a substitute for it.
plos-pone-0349207:
Ahmed Ali Hamad and colleagues created a perennial rye that farmers could sow once and harvest for years. The line eases the soil damage of annual planting. They then doubled its chromosomes to make a sturdier version. The new line crosses ordinary rye with a wild perennial relative whose foreign DNA is normally hard to track through breeding. Special fluorescent probes that light up known chromosome landmarks let the team follow the wild segments cell by cell.

Doubling the genome made plants shorter with heavier grains and more fertile shoots, though seed output per plant varied widely between individuals. The probes revealed telling marker differences on several chromosomes and frequent rearrangements, matching rye's outcrossing nature. The authors deliver both the new lines and the markers breeders need to keep the wild inheritance under watch.
plos-pone-0349407:
Andreas Themistocleous and three colleagues publish a protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026 for an Oxford study that will listen directly to pain fibres in people with chronic nerve pain. Neuropathic pain resists treatment partly because doctors cannot see which patients' pain fibres are overexcitable. A technique called microneurography can record single pain fibres in a living person, and this study pairs it with skin biopsies, sensory testing, and genetic analysis.

Adults with and without nerve damage and pain will be compared, then grouped by their fibre behaviour, sensory profile, and gene variants. The goal is a map from mechanism to patient: who has overactive fibres, and might therefore respond to drugs that calm exactly those fibres.
plos-pone-0349507:
Kseniia Skorentseva and colleagues validated a set of housekeeping genes for gene-activity studies in sponges, among the oldest animal groups. The standard measurement method only works if some genes stay steady and can serve as a ruler, and in sponges nobody had agreed on which. The team tested seven classic candidates in a calcareous sponge during normal life and during tissue regrowth.

Three genes, known by the codes RPL13A, ACT1, and GAPDH, proved the most stable by four different ranking methods. The team then checked whether the same panel works in three other sponge species from different groups and habitats. A shared, validated ruler saves every sponge laboratory from repeating the search and makes results across studies comparable.
plos-pone-0349607:
Adel Alshamrani presented a machine learning method in 2026 for catching advanced persistent threats, the slow, stealthy intrusions that slip past normal alarms. Such attacks behave much like malicious insiders when moving through a network and stealing data.

The method learns from a well known insider threat data set to simulate attacker behaviour. It joins log reading by language model agents, sequence modelling of behaviour, and clustering that admits uncertainty to cut false alarms. Reported detection accuracy was high with fewer false positives than rivals. The cross training idea is the novelty: insider data standing in for rare attack records.
plos-pone-0350007:
Guoliang Tang and colleagues ran a randomized trial comparing two airway devices used to collapse one lung during keyhole chest surgery for lung cancer. The devices are bronchial blockers, and a known problem is that they slip out of position mid-operation. Eighty patients at a Chinese hospital received either the standard single-cuff blocker or a new double-cuff design.

The team counted how often each device slipped, how long placement took, and harms such as low oxygen, poor lung collapse, and airway injury checked by camera afterward. Surgeon satisfaction was also scored. Device choice in one-lung ventilation is a practical safety question, and a fair randomized comparison tells anesthesiologists whether an extra cuff is worth adopting.
plos-pone-0350107:
New fashion items have no sales history, so Sanguk Park and colleagues built a forecaster that borrows the past of similar items. Their 2026 PLOS One model predicts a product's first twelve weeks of sales from its photos, text, and look-alike items' records.

First, a distance measure that tolerates stretched timing finds true look-alikes and shapes a comparison space. Then a transformer network reads the item's features, with sales values converted through a wave-based mapping that preserves their size. Because everything comes from in-house data, no outside feeds are needed. The authors report sharper forecasts than earlier models on their tests.
plos-pone-0350207:
Ruqaiah Ismael Bedaiwi, Marah Naif Alatawi, and Bernard Silvala published a 2026 laboratory survey in PLOS ONE on drug-resistant E. coli in hospitals in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. Some strains produce enzymes, called extended-spectrum beta-lactamases, that defeat many antibiotics. The team collected clinical isolates from inpatients over six months and used genetic testing to find which resistance genes the bacteria carried.

About a quarter of isolates were enzyme producers. Among them, one gene family dominated, appearing in about two-thirds, while other common resistance genes showed up in roughly half. Many isolates carried two resistance genes at once, and most positive samples came from urine, with the rest from blood and wounds. Despite the enzymes, the bacteria stayed sensitive to carbapenems and certain inhibitor combinations, though one older drug failed almost universally here. Local gene patterns like these, they say, should guide antibiotic choices in the region's hospitals.
plos-pone-0350307:
Haicheng Shen, Xun Xu, and Zhiqiang Miao present this 2026 PLOS One control-engineering paper on steering unmanned surface vessels along a set path in rough marine conditions. Traditional guidance methods lose accuracy when waves, currents, and the vessel's own quirks interfere. Their design stacks two layers: a reinforcement learning module that learns the environment and issues heading commands, and a predictive controller that turns those commands into thrust and rudder settings.

In simulations the hybrid system tracked its path far more tightly than a standard guidance-and-PID setup, cutting sideways drift by more than a third and heading error by about a fifth. Training tricks including gradient pruning and a custom reward kept learning stable. The authors offer the scheme as a step toward dependable autonomous boats.
plos-pone-0350507:
Olufeyisayo O Odebunmi and co-authors surveyed primary care staff across the United States in 2026 about their own role in HPV vaccine uptake. How clinicians speak to parents strongly shapes whether children get the cancer preventing vaccine.

Most respondents felt their communication greatly swayed parents' choices. Those who felt most influential were more likely to recommend the vaccine directly and confidently, and to report certain training and clinic habits. The survey ran in 2022 among staff serving children aged nine to twelve. Strengthening clinician confidence in the conversation may be as useful as new parent materials.
plos-pone-0350807:
Elias Chane and co-authors surveyed health workers in northwest Ethiopia in 2026 about a cluster of risks called metabolic syndrome. The condition links extra waist fat, high blood sugar, and poor blood fats, and it raises the chance of heart disease and diabetes. Long shifts may add to the risk.

Staff at three primary hospitals gave fasting blood samples and body measures, and answered questions about their lives. The team then checked who met the standard test for the syndrome and which habits or traits went with it. Results like these can guide workplace health checks for the very people who staff rural hospitals.
plos-pone-0351107:
After a stroke blocks blood flow, returning blood can itself injure the brain, partly because a waste chemical called glutamate piles up. Qiuling Li and colleagues studied rats with a temporarily blocked brain artery, focusing on the star-shaped support cells that normally mop up glutamate, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

A signaling pathway inside those cells switched on in the border zone around the injury and was tied to both cell growth and production of the main glutamate mop. The team traced a feedback loop within the pathway that earlier dish studies had only hinted at. Understanding the loop may point to treatments that help support cells clear glutamate faster after stroke.
plos-pone-0351207:
Yaming Zhang and Xiaoyu Song model the fight against rumours on short-video platforms as a three-player game, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The players are the people who spread falsehoods, the people who correct them, and the platform itself, which can police content or look away. Their mathematical model joins this game to a classic epidemic-style model of how information spreads through a crowd.

Simulations showed that when platforms intervene more reliably, and gain more from doing so, the system settles where platforms supervise strictly and correctors speak up. A real bus-related rumour case fitted the model's logic. The authors argue platform incentives, not just user behaviour, decide whether truth catches up with lies.
plos-pone-0351307:
Xiaohan Li and two colleagues test a blood sugar ratio as a warning sign for diabetic patients. Their 2026 study follows people admitted to hospital for the first time with type 2 diabetes. The ratio compares stress-driven blood sugar against a patient's usual level. That contrast captures acute disturbance better than a single reading. Over eleven hundred patients were tracked for years.

The link between the ratio and later death was curved, not straight. Below a threshold value, risk stayed low. Above it, risk climbed steeply. Patients past the threshold faced more than double the death risk at three and five years. Heart attack, heart failure, and stroke history changed the strength of the signal. As a prediction tool, the ratio performed well. A cheap calculation from routine blood tests could flag which newly admitted patients need closest watching.
plos-pone-0351407:
Nina Biačková and seven colleagues test brain stimulation for post-COVID symptoms in this 2026 trial. Survivors often report fatigue, brain fog, poor concentration, and low mood. The team applied mild direct current stimulation to the forehead. Thirty-five patients enrolled, split between real and sham treatment. Twenty sessions ran across four weeks. Brainwave recordings before, during, and after measured two things: brief recurring brain patterns called microstates, and coordination between the two stimulated sites.

The honest result, announced in the study's own framing, is no change. Microstates did not shift with real stimulation. Functional connectivity between the forehead sites did not shift either. Exploratory endpoints can miss effects, and the sample was small. Still, a well-run sham-controlled null result is valuable. It warns clinics marketing stimulation for post-COVID brain symptoms that this protocol, at least, left no fingerprint on the brain measures chosen.
plos-pone-0351507:
A parrot virus known for beak and feather disease kept turning up in Spanish vultures, which made little sense. Iñigo Palacios-Martínez, Francisco Morinha, and Guillermo Blanco screened three vulture species breeding in Spain, in this 2026 PLOS One study, and concluded the birds are not infected at all.

Traces appeared rarely and unevenly in Egyptian and cinereous vultures and never in griffon vultures. The genetic variants were wildly diverse, with no pattern by place, year, or nest, the opposite of a spreading virus. The sequences look like ancient viral DNA built into the vultures' own genomes. Apart from one inbred nestling, the birds showed no illness.
plos-pone-0352207:
Johanna Morales, Allan Vásquez, and Irma Patricia Orellana Catalán describe this 2026 PLOS One materials study making a water-absorbing gel for farm soils from shrimp shell waste. The team blended chitosan, extracted from the shells, with a cellulose derivative in an alkaline bath and linked the chains with a crosslinking agent. The goal was a biodegradable sponge that holds water and fertilizer in soil and releases them slowly.

Instrument checks confirmed the gel's structure. It broke down steadily in testing, losing most of its weight within two weeks, and it earned the super-absorbent label for both plain water and a urea fertilizer solution. Absorption also responded to acidity, a useful trait for controlled release. The authors present the recipe as a workable route to soil conditioners that do not persist as plastic waste.
plos-pone-0352507:
Liza Dadone and seven colleagues examine the feet of zoo giraffes after death. Their 2026 retrospective study gathered seventy-three lower limbs from twenty-one giraffes. The animals lived at twelve North American zoos, with necropsies spanning 2004 to 2023. Frozen limbs were scanned with CT imaging. Targeted tissue samples confirmed what the scans suggested. Each lesion was graded for severity and assigned to the inner or outer toe.

Damage proved common and varied. Infected pedal bone, joint spurs, cyst-like hollows, and mineralised tendons all appeared. The navicular bone, deep in the foot, was a frequent trouble spot. Its neighbouring structures often deteriorated with it, especially in the front legs. That pairing points to a chronic disease complex giraffe keepers should watch. Lameness in a two-tonne animal is hard to treat late. A postmortem atlas of what goes wrong guides earlier detection, flooring choices, and trimming care in living giraffes.
plos-pone-0352907:
Safalta Khadka led a team of six authors on this 2026 study of painkiller prescribing in older Americans newly diagnosed with breast, lung, or colorectal cancer. Many already lived with chronic non-cancer pain. Linked cancer registry and Medicare records from 2006 to 2019 let them compare opioid patterns over a year of follow-up against patients without prior pain.

Patients with earlier chronic pain had markedly higher odds of long-term opioid use in every cancer type, highest in breast cancer. Khadka argues the overlap demands extra care in prescribing, given addiction risks layered onto cancer treatment.
plos-pone-0353107:
Devadharshini B and colleagues, in a 2026 trial, test a balance-focused training program for sprinters with pain around the kneecap. This pain is common in active people and is tied to poor balance and weaker performance. The new program trains body position sense through shifting, dynamic drills, rather than steady strengthening alone.

Sixty recreational sprinters with pain in one knee were split at random between the dynamic program and a standard strengthening program. Both trained three times a week for twelve weeks, with checks at the start, middle, and end. Both groups improved, but the dynamic group gained more: less pain, better scores on a reaching balance test, and longer single-leg hops. The authors conclude that training body position sense adds something strengthening alone misses, at least for sprinters. They suggest coaches weave such drills into rehab before sending athletes back to full speed.
plos-pone-0353207:
Matas-Granados, Trillo, and Vilà followed plant and pollinator links in city parks over a full year in a 2026 study. The parks sit in a Mediterranean city where many planted species come from other parts of the world. Earlier work often looked at brief snapshots or places with only a few foreign plants.

Foreign plants flowered on a different schedule than local plants, which can keep food available for shared pollinators for longer. Even so, both groups held the web of visits together across the year to a similar degree. Turnover in which insects visited which plants did not depend on the foreign share. The study urges year-round, whole-web views when judging invasion effects.
plos-pone-0353407:
Claire Carswell and colleagues present in 2026 a feasibility plan for treating depression in people who receive regular dialysis for kidney failure. Depression is common in this group, yet extra clinic visits are hard to add to an already heavy schedule. A brief therapy that rebuilds daily activity will be offered during dialysis itself, in a small grouped trial across two sites.

Checks will cover whether patients can be found and kept in the study, whether measures get completed, and how the therapy feels to patients, staff, and carers. Costs of gathering health use data will also be tested before any large trial.
plos-pone-0353607:
Adam King and an international team report the first direct evidence of cacao use in the Mississippian world. The Mississippian culture was the mound-building civilization east of the Mississippi River. Its people consumed cacao, the source of chocolate. Their 2026 archaeogenomic study extracted ancient DNA from two pottery fragments found at Etowah in Georgia. The fragments came from feasting debris of the eleventh to twelfth centuries. The DNA matched the cacao tree.

Cacao grows only in the tropics. So its presence in Georgia proves long-distance trade or exchange. That reach extended deep into North America centuries before Europeans arrived. It parallels earlier finds at Chaco Canyon in the Southwest. The feasting context matters too. Cacao was served at gatherings tied to building Etowah's first platform mound. It likely carried ceremonial weight from the city's beginnings.
plos-pone-0354207:
Haizhou Yang and co-authors compare in 2026 two treatments for stage three cervical cancer that has spread locally. Records came from one hospital in China and covered several years. One group had combined radiation and drug treatment alone, while the other had extra drug treatment afterward.

Extra treatment did not clearly improve survival or time without the disease returning, and severe side effects did not rise. Large involved lymph nodes and a high marker level after inner radiation pointed to worse outcomes. The authors treat those two signs as useful warnings and call for larger forward looking trials to find who might truly benefit from added therapy.
plos-pone-0354307: Subspace clustering — deep metric learning with graph regularization across views. This paper built that multi-view network. The methodological advance squeezes structure from complex, multi-faceted data — with applications from image analysis to bioinformatics.
plos-pone-0354507:
Niklas Dressler led a team of eight authors on this 2026 mouse study of a gut receptor that may shield newborn intestines. Premature babies face necrotizing enterocolitis, a severe gut inflammation tied to bacterial toxins. The team compared normal mice with mice engineered to overproduce the receptor CD97 in gut lining cells, then challenged the tissue with bacterial toxin.

Extra CD97 dampened the inflammatory signals, apparently by steadying a partner protein that calms the toxin response. The protection appeared only in young animals and in the small intestine. Dressler names a possible drug target for fragile newborns.
plos-pone-0354607:
Zhang and colleagues, in a 2026 computer-based study, ask whether PET microplastics, the tiny plastic bits shed by bottles and fabrics, could help drive fatty liver disease. Fatty liver tied to metabolic problems now affects a large share of adults worldwide. Plastic particles are known to reach the liver, but their exact targets there were unclear.

The team merged gene activity data from several liver studies with lists of proteins that PET is predicted to touch. Nineteen genes sat in the overlap, clustered around fat handling and energy pathways. Three stood out as hubs in the protein network. Immune profiles in diseased livers also shifted, and two of the hub genes tracked closely with immune cell changes. Computer docking suggested PET binds all three proteins snugly and stably. The authors stress the work is computational: it names suspects for lab testing, not proof that microplastics cause liver disease.
plos-pone-0354707:
Karlijn Demers and five colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on exercise testing in illness. Their patients live with inflammatory bowel disease. The authors ask whether oxygen uptake at peak exercise, a key fitness measure, can be predicted without pushing patients to their maximum.

Two gentler approaches are involved: a below-maximum exercise test that tracks heart and lung responses, plus the steep ramp test, which is presented as a practical field test. If peak values can be estimated from easier tests, clinics could judge fitness with less strain on patients. That matters for planning exercise and care in a group often limited by fatigue and gut symptoms.
plos-pone-0354807:
Rania Itani led a team of eight authors on this 2026 survey study of premenstrual syndrome among female students at Beirut Arab University in Lebanon today. A self-completed questionnaire covered symptoms, lifestyle, stress, social media habits, and how students manage the condition, using validated screening scales throughout.

The syndrome proved common, and a considerable share met criteria for its severe form, premenstrual dysphoric disorder. Higher perceived stress scores tracked with worse symptoms. Itani recommends university awareness, screening, and counseling services that tackle changeable habits and stress rather than symptoms alone.
plos-pone-0355207:
Josh M Colston led a team of eight authors on this 2026 mapping study of household livestock in poorer countries. Families keeping poultry, pigs, or cattle and goats gain food and income but also live close to animal germs. Using survey records tied to maps, the team modeled how common each kind of ownership is across regions.

Their maps, released in a format geographic software can read, lined up well with outside evidence. Predicted hotspots show where animal contact is densest. Colston offers the estimates to health planners who need to target zoonotic disease prevention where exposure runs highest.
plos-pone-0355607:
Shun Tamaki and co-authors probed gut immune moves after coronavirus infection in lab mice bred to carry the human door the virus uses. COVID-19 brings gut woes in many sick folks, yet gut immunity post-infection was dimly mapped. Their 2026 study read genes and stained gut tissue from the small bowel of sick mice.

Infection lit up a set of signals tied to eosinophils, white cells more linked to allergy and worms. The cells piled into the gut wall, and their grain proteins rose. Crystals long tied to these cells showed up too. Tamaki and colleagues say the gut mounts its own odd, eosinophil-led reply that merits checks in human cases.
plos-pone-0356107:
Rinat Nissim and colleagues set out a plan to review research on family accommodation in young people who have survived cancer. Accommodation means relatives changing daily behaviour to lower a survivor's distress. Their 2026 protocol covers survivors diagnosed from birth through young adulthood, along with their families.

No review results are reported yet, because the paper describes work still to be done. The team plans to search major medical and psychology databases and map how accommodation is defined and measured. They also plan to check its links with survivors' health and with caregivers' own wellbeing. The protocol was registered in advance, and the finished review should guide family-centred survivorship care.
plos-pone-0356507:
Luis Ángel Calvo Pascual and four co-authors tackle a pure combinatorics problem posed by earlier researchers about colored triangulations. A Sperner labeling paints the corners of a sliced-up triangle-like shape under strict rules. Rainbow-colored small pieces are guaranteed to appear. The open question asks how few such pieces can possibly occur. Working with the regular triangulation that packs in the most pieces overall, the authors prove a floor on the count of non-rainbow pieces.

Their lower bound answers the motivating problem in this maximal setting, showing that non-uniform pieces cannot be squeezed below a stated quantity. The paper is brief and proof-driven, with no data or experiments. Its audience is specialists in combinatorics and discrete geometry who use such labelings in fair division and fixed point arguments.
plos-pone-0356607:
Stefan Kulnik and seven colleagues ask what distinguishes active from inactive people whose hearts are already at risk, in this 2026 analysis from Salzburg, Austria. Their data come from a large population cohort of adults in their forties to early seventies. The team focused on nearly twelve hundred participants with raised cardiovascular risk or established disease. They tested twenty-nine possible influences on leisure activity.

Across statistical and machine learning models, a consistent cluster stood out. Retired people, those who had been active in earlier decades, and those eating a Mediterranean-style diet moved more. People carrying more illnesses, or living with depression, moved less. The authors say these patterns can help doctors target activity promotion: building on past habits and diet, and treating depression, may matter as much as urging exercise itself in cardiovascular care.
plos-pone-0356807:
Xavier Cheseto and Chrysantus Mbi Tanga analyzed oils pressed from seven edible insect species. They were hunting for the omega-3 fats usually sourced from fish. Their 2026 laboratory study used two kinds of mass spectrometry. It catalogued fatty acids, vitamin E, and plant-like antioxidant compounds in insect oils. Commercial sesame oil served as the comparison.

Every insect oil contained all three major omega-3s, which sesame oil largely lacks. Desert locust at its fifth growth stage led the field on all three. Most insect oils beat sesame on vitamin E. Locust and cricket oils were also rich in noted antioxidants like quercetin. Since these insects are already eaten widely and farm cheaply, the authors argue they deserve serious study as sustainable omega-3 sources.
plos-pone-0356907:
Manh Tuan Nguyen and colleagues built MeCoLog, a learning system that spots abnormal entries in computer system logs. It works even on a brand-new system with almost no labeled examples. Their 2026 paper tackles a practical headache. Every system writes logs differently. Detectors trained on one usually fail on another. New deployments have little history to learn from.

MeCoLog encodes each log entry by its type, value, and key parts. Unfamiliar wording still registers that way. It learns what normal behavior looks like across systems, while keeping anomalies strictly apart. Tested on five public log collections, it beat leading rival methods in the scarce-data cross-system setting. For operations teams, such transfer means a new service could gain decent monitoring from day one.
plos-pone-0357007:
Takuya Yoshida, Hiroyuki Yoshizawa, and Ryosuke Asano followed more than seventeen hundred Japanese parents across three survey waves to see what turns parental goodwill into actual teamwork at elementary schools. Their 2026 longitudinal study measured how parents viewed cooperation among families, teachers, and neighbors, how they rated school leadership, and how much they actually joined in.

When a parent's sense of team orientation or confidence in leadership rose above their own usual level, their cooperative behavior rose at the next wave. Extra helping, by contrast, did not lift later attitudes. People who started high on any measure stayed high on all. For schools courting volunteers, the lesson is to build shared purpose and visible leadership first; participation follows.
plos-pone-0357107:
Asima Razzaque led a team of four authors designing stronger tools for image encryption, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Encryption scrambles data using substitution boxes, called S-boxes, whose math decides how well the cipher resists attack. Weak boxes leave patterns that attackers can exploit.

Razzaque's two-stage algebraic framework builds S-boxes meant to be cryptographically strong for secure image encryption. A tested recipe helps other designers produce boxes that hold up under assault. Image data need special care because pictures carry bulky, patterned content. As images flow through health, media, and security systems, strong and checkable encryption parts are a basic need, and frameworks that can be shared and verified serve that need well.
plos-pone-0357207:
Michaela Škorvanová and colleagues published a 2026 pilot study in PLOS ONE on a blood marker of nerve damage in people with type 2 diabetes. Diabetic peripheral neuropathy, nerve damage in feet and hands, is common and hard to measure early. Neurofilament light chain, a protein leaking from injured nerve fibers, can be counted in blood with an ultrasensitive test. They compared diabetic patients with and without neuropathy diagnosed by a neurologist.

Marker levels were higher in the neuropathy group at first look. But once age and kidney function, both of which push the marker up alone, were accounted for, the neuropathy link weakened and lost statistical firmness. Age and kidney filtering together explained most of the variation between patients. This promising marker, they caution, cannot be read at face value in diabetes clinics: an older patient or one with poor kidneys may show high values without worse nerve damage.
plos-pone-0357407:
Yuuka Yasuura and coauthors published a 2026 cross-sectional study in PLOS ONE on knee pain in young soccer players. Pain around the kneecap tendon is common in growing athletes, but whether the tendon already looks abnormal on ultrasound was unclear. The team examined middle school players, rating pain and tenderness, testing function, and scanning both knees, ending with data on just over two hundred knees.

Painful knees were weaker in extension and more often showed two ultrasound signs: darker tendon patches and blood-flow signals. In adjusted modeling, only the dark patches mattered, carrying roughly ten times the odds of tendon pain, while other structural and functional measures fell away. Ultrasound, they suggest, could help spot the tendon state tied to pain in adolescents, though a one-time snapshot cannot prove cause; following players over time is next.
plos-pone-0358007: Kim and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on eye drops for dry eye disease. The drops contain a low dose of cyclosporine, a drug that calms immune activity on the eye's surface. The team compared how well the low-dose drops work in daily clinic use. Dry eye is common and nagging, and patients need options they can use for months without harm.
plos-pone-0359107: Sudhartio and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on charging a farm robot without cables. Their wireless power system uses a double-sided LCC compensation setup, a circuit design that keeps power transfer steady. They built the system and put it to work on the robot. A robot that charges itself on the field edge could work longer days with less human help.
plos-pone-0359207: Viáfara-Vega and one co-author published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on the gene pool of peppers in Southwestern Colombia. Using a fast DNA marker method called DArTseq, they assessed diversity and population structure across Capsicum types. Colombia sits near the peppers' homeland, so its gene pool is rich. Mapping that diversity helps breeders guard rare traits while improving crops.
plos-pone-0359407:
Adrienne Parkinson, Jihong Liu, Xingpei Zhao, and Kimberly Alston wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on maternal care in the United States. It studies why some low-income women miss postpartum care visits after giving birth. The authors frame the question with the Andersen Behavioral Model, a standard way of sorting what drives health service use.

Postpartum visits check healing, mood, and blood pressure at a risky time, yet attendance lags among women with low incomes. Finding the correlates of non-attendance shows which barriers, from transport to beliefs, matter most. Maternal health programs can then spend effort where this evidence says it counts.
pmc-13226507:
Le and colleagues edit a papaya gene to build resistance against papaya ringspot virus. The virus causes the crop's worst disease, cutting harvests across the tropics. In other plants, the gene eIF4E and its partner copy are known doors that such viruses use to infect cells, and blocking them can bring resistance.

Papaya's own versions had never been tested in a systematic way for this role. Using CRISPR and Cas9 editing, the team altered the gene and checked whether plants stood up better to the virus. Success would offer growers a built-in defence, bred into the plant rather than sprayed on it, for a fruit valued as food and medicine.
pmc-13237007: Hesamzadeh and colleagues publish an author correction to their paper on computer-designed antioxidant peptides. The correction fixes one methods sentence about the DPPH test, a standard lab check of antioxidant strength. The corrected sentence states that the peptide sample was mixed with the DPPH solution in ethanol, stirred in the dark for half an hour at room temperature. Small method details like solvent and timing decide whether other labs can repeat the test exactly, which is why journals correct them on the record.
pmc-13238007: Jiang and colleagues publish a correction to their review of selective autophagy in cancer. After publication, the authors found a large mismatch between the review's in-text citation numbers and its reference list, affecting more than half of all references. The correction realigns every in-text number with the reference it should point to. The authors also flag errors in several figures that had been reprinted from earlier sources, and put those right as well. Reference accuracy lets readers trace claims to sources, so journals fix such faults openly.
pmc-13240207:
Fast and colleagues show that a newly found chemical switch tunes an enzyme modern humans inherited partly from Neanderthals. The enzyme, NAT1, processes certain drugs and cancer-linked chemicals and helps handle folate. Most people today carry one form of it, but some carry the older Neanderthal version, gained through ancient interbreeding, with two small amino acid differences.

Those differences alone, the team found, do not change the enzyme's activity. The real control is a phosphorylation site, a spot where a phosphate tag can be attached, newly identified in modern humans. Such fine control may matter because NAT levels are tied to cancer risk and birth defects, and this work shows where evolution actually adjusted the dial.
pmc-13241507:
Mahran and co-workers at Menoufia University tested whether human placental extract can shield rat kidneys from methotrexate damage. The chemotherapy drug is known to injure the kidney through oxidative stress. Male albino rats were split into four groups for the experiment. Treatments covered plain saline, the extract alone, the drug alone, and both agents together.

Methotrexate alone cut body weight and drained antioxidant defenses, including glutathione and protective enzymes. It also raised a lipid damage marker, thickened the blood, and visibly harmed fine kidney structure. Rats given the extract alongside the drug fared better on weight, chemistry, tissue structure, and electrical tissue measures. The team credits the extract's antioxidant support for the protection.
pmc-13241607:
Ogunbode and co-authors at Bowen University surveyed how households store water in Iwo Township, in Nigeria's Osun State. Seasonal supply swings make home storage essential in the tropical town. The survey reached seven hundred fifty-six households across four sections during 2023. Female household heads were prioritized, since they usually manage the water.

Steel and plastic drums led storage choices, followed by buckets and overhead tanks. Wells and boreholes supplied nearly nine in ten households. Factor analysis distilled eight drivers of storage choices, led by household age makeup and toilet count. The authors argue that family traits and assets shape storage more than supply alone, and they recommend affordable, safe storage support.
pmc-13242307:
Liao and colleagues at Cornell mapped where the global land rush overlaps animal reservoirs of human disease. Large-scale land deals were overlaid on zoonotic host distributions worldwide. Administrative units were scored by hazard-exposure overlap. Investor and host country links completed the wider telecoupled picture.

Southeast Asia, Latin America, Eastern Europe, and Africa host most large deals. Spillover risk concentrates hardest in Southeast Asia and Latin America especially. High-risk units show more forest cover, bigger deals, and fewer roads and people. Domestic and intra-regional deals drive over half the total risk.
pmc-13242407:
Goetz Benndorf, a neurosurgeon, wrote this comment for Acta Neurochirurgica in 2026 in reply to a study claiming a previously unreported brain vein. Gurse and colleagues had described a “cuneus vein” found during surgery and urged preserving it during operations at the back of the brain. Benndorf questions whether the evidence shows that such a vein exists at all.

He notes the claim rests on one surgeon's retrospective review of 303 operations, with the variant reported in just 12 patients. His sharpest point is that the vein never appeared on preoperative MRI scans, even in those 12 positive cases. He also finds the published images and scan methods too thin to support the claim. The comment is a caution against naming new anatomy on surgical impression alone.
pmc-13242507:
Alexandra Israelsson and co-authors tested whether people can read blended emotions when face, body, and voice all speak at once. Their paper appeared in Scientific Reports in 2026. Actors portrayed pairs drawn from anger, disgust, fear, happiness, and sadness, mixing them in different proportions. In two preregistered experiments, viewers rated which emotions they saw and how strongly each one came through.

Viewers reliably picked out both intended emotions from the blends and ignored the ones that were absent. They could also tell which emotion in a pair was dominant and which was the minor note. Accuracy shifted a little with specific pairings, but the overall pattern held in both experiments, even when raters could choose any number of scales. The authors say this fine-grained reading helps explain how people manage a social world where feelings rarely arrive one at a time.
pmc-13242607:
Yalda Amiri Hezave, Rezvan Najafi, and Razieh Amini reviewed spiegelmers, mirror-image binding molecules, as a new platform against breast cancer. Their review appeared in Breast Cancer: Basic and Clinical Research in 2026. Ordinary aptamers, short synthetic strands that grip chosen targets, degrade quickly in the body. Spiegelmers are built from left-handed nucleotides, which enzymes barely recognize, so they survive far longer in blood while keeping tight, specific binding.

In breast cancer, the review sees spiegelmers serving both diagnosis and treatment. Tagged with fluorescent or radioactive labels, they could light up tumors on MRI or PET scans. They can also ferry drugs into tumors, support light-based therapies, and block harmful microRNAs such as miR-155, which drives aggressive triple-negative disease. Synthesis is difficult and the range of proven targets is still narrow. Even so, the authors judge spiegelmers a strong candidate platform for combined diagnosis-and-therapy tools.
pmc-13243307:
Turyalai Hakimi and Sultan Ahmad Halimi report an exceptionally young case of myxoid liposarcoma, a fat-tissue cancer. Their case report appeared in Oxford Medical Case Reports in 2026. The tumor usually strikes teenagers and young adults and is almost unheard of under age five. Their patient was a boy of three and a half admitted in Afghanistan with a large abdominal mass.

Surgeons removed the retroperitoneal tumor completely, with clear margins, and tissue analysis confirmed the well-differentiated myxoid type. He then received six cycles of cyclophosphamide chemotherapy at twenty-day intervals. Follow-up scans showed no return of the disease. The authors stress that such cases need a pediatric surgeon and oncologist working together, plus long-term surveillance. They also use the case to argue that policymakers should build stronger childhood cancer services, in Afghanistan and beyond.
pmc-13244507:
Masakazu Hamada and colleagues asked whether the look of a person's tongue predicts the microbes living in their mouth. Their study appeared in the Journal of Oral Microbiology in 2026. Ninety-three volunteers were grouped by tongue features from traditional exams: yellow coating, redness, fissures, swelling, geographic patterns, and tooth marks. Saliva and surface samples then went through diversity and composition analysis.

One feature stood out. People with fissured tongues carried less diverse oral communities, with more Firmicutes and sulfur-processing bacteria. Much of that signal faded once age was taken into account, since fissures and microbial shifts both grow with age. In age-restricted comparisons, two bacterial genera stayed lower in fissured-tongue saliva, an age-independent signature. The authors suggest tongue appearance could become a cheap, noninvasive marker of oral imbalance. Dentists already look at tongues; this study asks what else the look is telling them.
pmc-13247307:
Kurtz, McKinley, Mullet, and co-authors catalogued small signaling peptides in sorghum, in this 2026 Plant Direct study. Plants coordinate growth with tiny protein messengers, but in sorghum, an important grain and bioenergy crop, these peptides were barely characterized. Starting from known peptide families in five other plants, the team identified two hundred nineteen sorghum genes encoding such signals and sorted them into nineteen families.

Twelve of the families had never been described in sorghum. Gene activity patterns varied sharply by organ: some families spoke mainly in roots, others in stem skin and pith or in the seed head. During stem growth, twenty-eight peptide genes switched on strongly in zones where cells divide, including relatives of a known stem-cell signal. The catalogue gives breeders targets for shaping sorghum stems, which carry most of the harvested biomass.
pmc-13248107:
Keitel-Gröner and co-authors fed farmed salmon extra vitamin D through a Norwegian winter, in this 2026 Aquaculture Nutrition study. Modern salmon feeds use less fishmeal and fish oil, so the fish. Eventually the people eating them, get less vitamin D, and winter darkness cuts the fish's own supply further.
