Four years after Humanism, F. C. S. Schiller issued Studies in Humanism in 1907 as a second series of essays. The Oxford pragmatist returned to his central claim with fresh cases. Human thought, he held, is an active tool shaped by human aims. The new essays test that claim on new ground.

Schiller applies his view to logic, knowledge, and the disputes of his day. He answers critics who charged that pragmatism makes truth a matter of whim. His replies stress testing, results, and the slow work of inquiry. The volume shows a system in mid fight, still growing. It pairs directly with the 1903 essays.
schnitzler-the-dead-are-silent-1907:
Love, death, and self-deception in anxious, glittering Vienna fill The Dead Are Silent, Schnitzler's story collection in English from 1907. The title tale follows a man's guilt after a fatal carriage accident kills his lover, while her husband knows nothing. Secrecy poisons every scene that follows the accident's first shock.

Other stories in the set cut into Viennese society with the same fine blade. Schnitzler anatomized his city like no one else, and these pieces show the scalpel at its sharpest. Doctors, officers, and actresses all discover what their arrangements with truth really cost. The collection suits readers meeting Schnitzler for the first time. Its best pages rank with the finest short fiction of the period.
sidgwick-methods-ethics-1907:
Henry Sidgwick published The Methods of Ethics in 1874; the text here is the 1907 edition. Sidgwick studies three methods by which people judge right and wrong. Egoism pursues one's own good, intuition follows common moral rules, and utilitarianism seeks the greatest general happiness. He tests each with unmatched care and fairness.

Sidgwick finds deep merit in both common-sense morality and utilitarian reform. His honest puzzle is that reason seems to support both self-interest and universal good without full harmony. The book is often called the greatest work of English moral philosophy. Philosophers still study its final chapters. It set the agenda for modern ethics.
spr-proceedings-vol19-1905-1907:
Parts fifty through fifty two and an appendix form volume nineteen, for 1905 to 1907. The Society for Psychical Research marks twenty five years of work in these pages. Telepathy trials take modern forms, with targets chosen by lot. Reports on trance mediumship remain the longest and most contested items.

Sitters test Piper and her peers with false names and sealed facts. Apparition reports, gathered by the old census standards, keep arriving. The appendix tidies society business and stray evidence. Volume nineteen shows a research society in settled middle age. Its files joined the primary archive of the long evidential debate. The mix of rigor and wonder persists.
stirner-ego-and-its-own-byington-1907:
Steven T Byington published his translation of Max Stirner's The Ego and His Own in 1907. Stirner, a German schoolteacher named Johann Kaspar Schmidt, issued the work in 1844. It vanished, then returned as the founding text of individualist anarchism and egoism.

Stirner declared war on every abstraction set above the self: state, church, humanity, and morality itself. Only the Unique, the single ego owning itself, escaped his scorn. He urged each person to take their own cause as the only cause. Byington's English, the first full version, shaped American individualist anarchism for decades. The book still startles readers with the reach of its refusal.
suzuki-outlines-mahayana-buddhism-1907:
Suzuki's Outlines of Mahayana Buddhism, published in 1907, was his first major work in English. Mahayana, the Great Vehicle, is the branch of Buddhism that spread through China, Korea, and Japan. Suzuki wrote the book while living in America and working on Eastern texts.

He sets out the bodhisattva ideal, the saint who delays final bliss to help all beings, and the doctrines of emptiness and Buddha-nature. His chapters draw on Sanskrit and Chinese sources he was among the first to open to Western readers. The Outlines prepared the audience that his later Zen books would win.
synge-aran-islands-1907:
John Millington Synge spent parts of four summers on the Aran Islands, off Ireland's west coast, at the urging of William Butler Yeats. Yeats told him to go where life had not yet been expressed. Synge's prose account of those visits appeared in 1907.

Synge records island life in plain, beautiful prose: fishing in frail curraghs, funerals with wild keening, fairy tales by the fire, and evictions resisted by whole villages. He learned Irish and listened more than he talked. The islanders' speech, half English and half Irish in rhythm, later shaped his plays. The book is a classic of Irish travel writing and a key to Synge's art.
synge-playboy-western-world-1907:
J. M. Synge's The Playboy of the Western World opened in Dublin in 1907 and caused riots in the theater. Audiences took offense at its picture of Irish country life and at a mention of women's underclothing. Synge had built the story from tales he heard on the Aran Islands and in County Mayo.

Christy Mahon stumbles into a Mayo shebeen claiming he has killed his father. The villagers, bored with dull routine, treat him as a hero, and Christy grows bold and poetic in their praise. Then his very alive father arrives. The play's rich, musical language and its dark joke about fame have made it a cornerstone of modern Irish drama.
the-confessions-of-jean-jacques-rousseau: The seventh volume of the long Confessions records the great quarrels. Rousseau breaks bitterly with Diderot, Grimm, and all the encyclopedists. His burning sense of betrayal blazes ever more fiercely. Friendship's sad wreck, vividly and painfully told.
the-spell-of-egypt-pg3407: Robert Hichens's Spell of Egypt: the Nile's romance. The popular novelist's Eastern tale. Exotic and vivid. A desert romance, hichens's Nile romance, exotic and vivid, a desert tale, Robert Hichens, Egypt, Nile, desert, romance, Hichens.
the-wandering-jew-volume-07: Eugène Sue's Wandering Jew, volume seven: toward the climax. The plot races on. Melodrama's high tide. The serial's late middle, sue races toward the climax, melodrama's high tide, the late middle, Sue's serial, grand.
thomson-corpuscular-theory-matter-1907:
Three years after Electricity and Matter, J. J. Thomson gave his corpuscular theory its full form in 1907. The Corpuscular Theory of Matter pushes the electron account as far as he could take it. Thomson asks how many corpuscles an atom holds. He also argues that mass itself may have an electrical origin.

New evidence from positive rays joins the older cathode ray work in these pages. Thomson weighs rival readings and defends his own atomic picture. The book stands as a sequel that tests the theory's limits. Soon other models would pass it by. Still, it records a great physicist thinking at full stretch. Its care rewards close study.
titus-andronicus-pg1507: Revenge feeds on revenge in this edition of Shakespeare's bloodiest tragedy: the Goth queen Tamora and the Roman general Titus trade ever worse horrors, ending in a feast no reader forgets. Savage, stagey, and thrilling, it was the young Shakespeare's first smash hit.
tob-0007:
Farmers and priests of Sumer, in what is now Iraq, pressed wedge-shaped marks into wet clay about five thousand years ago. Their tablets are the oldest writing on earth. Temple accounts, hymns, law lists, school exercises, and early forms of the Gilgamesh tales all survive in baked mud.

No single edition unites the thousands of tablets, and the evidence notes none is attached to this entry. Scholars still piece the record together shard by shard from museum stores. What the tablets prove is large: writing began with accounts and stories together, and literature is as old as the ledger.
tob-0107:
Basil Valentine, a monk said to have lived in the fifteenth century, hid the stages of the Great Work inside twelve pictures and texts called keys. Each key is an allegory: a king, a queen, a wolf, a dragon. Together they map the path toward the philosopher's stone.

Readers must decode the images, since plain speech would betray the secret. The emblems are among the most beautiful in all alchemical books, copied and reprinted for centuries. This entry draws on a verified pre-1930 edition. Chemists of the time read real laboratory steps in the riddles; artists simply loved the pictures.
tob-10407:
Thomas Aquinas organized the Summa Theologica as questions with objections, answers, and replies, and this volume holds Part II-II, the second half of his moral theology. Aquinas treats the virtues and vices one by one in systematic order. Faith, hope, and charity come first, as the theological virtues.

Prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance follow, each shadowed by opposing sins and each broken into precise cases. A reader can look up anger, usury, war, or lying and find a reasoned verdict. The result remains the most systematic ethics in Christian thought, and a reference theologians and philosophers still argue with today.
tob-10807:
Otto Henne am Rhyn chronicled the secret doctrines of the ages in Mysteria, moving from ancient mystery cults through Gnostics, Templars, and Rosicrucians to Freemasons. His guiding curiosity asks what was really hidden behind their veils of secrecy and symbol. The flavor is encyclopedic and nineteenth-century.

Rather than treating each movement separately, Henne am Rhyn presents esoteric history as one continuous underground stream, surfacing in different costumes across centuries. Rites, grades of initiation, and legendary founders fill the pages. Modern scholars would dispute the single-stream picture, but as a period survey it preserves how an earlier age organized its fascination with hidden knowledge.
tob-11107:
Eiríkr Magnússon and William Morris translated the Volsunga Saga, the Norse prose saga of the Volsung clan. Sigmund and Signy open the line's grim history, and Sigurd the dragon-slayer stands at its center. The cursed gold of the dragon Fafnir poisons generation after generation, and Brynhild's tragic love completes the pattern.

Morris, a poet devoted to the North, worked to keep the saga's stark music in English. The telling is swift and pagan to the bone: oaths, vengeance, and fate bind every character. Wagner drew raw material for his Ring cycle from these same legends, and readers can compare the colder original with the opera.
tob-13507:
John Wesley's collected Works open with volume one, Sermons on Several Occasions, the preaching that fueled the Methodist revival. Wesley, an Anglican priest who took his message outdoors, preached on salvation by faith, the new birth, and Christian perfection. His audiences ranged from coal miners to, on occasion, the well placed and powerful.

The sermons are plain, urgent, and practical, built to be understood by unlettered hearers and to press for a decision. Wesley revised and republished them as standards of Methodist doctrine. Readers hear the voice that changed England's religious landscape, and they can watch a revival leader define his movement in its own pulpit language.
tob-14507:
F. Max Müller's classic translation presents the Buddha's 423 verses in the Dhammapada, drawn from his Sacred Books of the East series. Müller's version introduced Victorian readers to Buddhist scripture. The mind as master, hatred never conquered by hatred, and the path of diligence stand among its most quoted teachings.

Chapters proceed by topic, pairing fools and wise men, anger and kindness, craving and release. Müller renders the Pali verses in plain, dignified English that stays endlessly quotable. Readers who want the Dhammapada in the form nineteenth-century Britain first received it, with a great scholar-translator's care behind every line, will find this edition historically central.
tob-4007:
Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa published his Three Books of Occult Philosophy in 1533, and Western occultism took its lasting shape from them. The entry uses a checked 1919 public-domain printing. Agrippa, a restless scholar and soldier, set out to organize all magic into one system.

Book one treats the natural world of elements, stones, and herbs. Book two climbs to the heavens, numbers, and stars. Book three reaches ceremonial magic, divine names, and spirits. Charms stand beside high philosophy without apology. Later magicians from Barrett to the Golden Dawn worked from Agrippa's plan. His three books remain the Renaissance summa of the occult arts.
tob-4107:
Purity law fills the Vendidad, the Zoroastrian book at the head of Darmesteter's Zend Avesta in the Sacred Books of the East. Darmesteter translated part one of the Avesta from the ancient tongue with Max Muller editing the series. Ancient Persia's rules for keeping demons and corruption at bay fill the chapters.

Corpses, sickness, and unclean acts require set cleansings, some lasting days. Priests, dogs, and sacred fires all play their parts in the system. The Vendidad is law, ritual manual, and myth at once, with tales of Yima's golden age woven through. Verified from the 1919 edition, it opens the Avesta for English readers.
topsell-historie-four-footed-beastes-160:
Edward Topsell, an English clergyman, published The Historie of Four-footed Beastes in 1607. It was the first great English book of animals, built from older writers like Conrad Gessner. Topsell wrote for readers who wanted the whole animal kingdom set out in their own language.

Lions, apes, horses, and stranger beasts fill its pages, each with a woodcut picture. Topsell reports habits, uses in medicine, and tall tales, all told straight. He rarely doubts what his sources say, so fact and fable stand side by side. The book shows natural history before it learned to doubt. Shakespeare's England read its beasts here.
traite-de-la-poudre-de-projection-divise: Traité de la poudre de projection, 1707. The projection powder. This book preserves that treatise. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
un-sc-res-107:
Tension along the armistice line between Egypt and Israel drew the Council's attention on 30 March 1955. The chief of staff of the United Nations Truce Supervision Organization had reported on conditions there. His report also covered the causes of the strain between the two sides. The Council acted under the General Armistice Agreement that Egypt and Israel had signed.

The resolution asks the chief of staff to keep consulting both governments. He had already offered concrete proposals to calm the border. The Council calls on Egypt and Israel to cooperate with him. It notes his view that cross-border infiltration could shrink to a minor nuisance. That gain would follow if both sides accepted his plan.
un-sc-res-1307: Under number 1307, the catalog lists a Security Council resolution dated to 1999 in the official UN record. The Council is the UN body charged with world peace and security, and it speaks formally through texts like this one. For students of the UN, the record offers the Council's language itself rather than a summary written later. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-1407:
Weapons kept flowing into Somalia despite a decade-old embargo. On 3 May 2002 the Security Council moved to give that embargo teeth. The chairman of its Somalia sanctions committee planned a visit to the region. The Council noted the continued flow of arms with serious concern. That flow, it said, hurt peace and reconciliation in Somalia. A presidential statement in March had set up this step.

The Secretary-General had one month to set up a two-person expert team. The team would work for thirty days. Its job was an action plan for a full panel of experts. The plan would list the skills and resources needed to track embargo breaches. The Council promised to weigh the findings by the end of July.
un-sc-res-1507:
Ethiopia and Eritrea's border mission was renewed by the Security Council on 12 September 2003. The peace process had reached the key phase of marking the border on the ground. The Council voiced concern at delays in demarcation and at the cost of the mission while demand for peacekeepers grew elsewhere. Hunger crises in both countries also threatened the process.

The Council extended the United Nations Mission in Ethiopia and Eritrea, UNMEE, at its authorized troop and observer levels to 15 March 2004. It called for demarcation to begin on the Boundary Commission's schedule. Both parties had to name field liaison officers and give the commission full cooperation. The Council repeated its demand that UNMEE move freely, with all restrictions lifted at once. It also pressed the two governments to open political dialogue, saying lasting peace needed more than a marked line on a map.
un-sc-res-1607:
The Council dealt with Liberia in Resolution 1607, adopted on 21 June 2005. No illegal timber exports had shown up in the expert reports. Yet few of the needed forestry reforms were in place. Unlicensed diamond mining and shady exports were on the rise. The interim government still lacked control over the diamond and timber areas.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the diamond ban for six more months. The arms, travel, and timber measures stay in force until 21 December 2005. The asset freeze on the old regime's circle also stands. The government must build a clear certificate system for rough diamonds and fix its forestry body. The Panel of Experts serves until 21 December 2005.
un-sc-res-1707:
ISAF's authorization was renewed amid a Taliban resurgence on 12 September 2006. Violent and terrorist attacks by the Taliban, Al-Qaida, illegal armed groups, and the narcotics trade had grown. The Afghanistan Compact, launched at London, set the frame for work between Kabul and its partners. Security, governance, and development were judged to rise or fall together.

The Council extended the International Security Assistance Force's authorization for twelve months beyond 13 October 2006. The states serving in the force could take all necessary measures to carry out its mandate. The need to strengthen the force further was recognized, and states were called to give staff, funds, and equipment. The force had to keep working in close consultation with the Afghan government and the Secretary-General's representative. Its leadership owed the Council quarterly reports. The text covered the year in which the force took charge of security across the whole country.
un-sc-res-1807:
Council members took up the Democratic Republic of the Congo and adopted Resolution 1807 on the Democratic Republic of the Congo on 31 March 2008. The Goma conference and the Nairobi statement had raised hopes for peace in the east. Weapons still flowed to armed groups, and stolen minerals still paid for them. The old embargo treated the government and rebels much the same.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council rebuilds the sanctions to run until 31 December 2008. The arms embargo now binds only non-government groups and people. The government may receive arms again, but every shipment must be reported to the committee in advance. Travel bans and asset freezes stay in force for listed violators. Aircraft checks and customs controls also continue.
un-sc-res-1907:
Eritrea received the Council's formal attention in Resolution 1907, adopted on 23 December 2009. United Nations monitors said Eritrea had given money, arms, and training to Somali armed groups. Eritrea also still held ground seized from Djibouti in June 2008. It refused all talks and mediation on that border clash.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council imposes an arms embargo on Eritrea in both directions. States must inspect suspect cargo bound to or from Eritrea and Somalia. Travel bans and asset freezes can now hit Eritrean leaders and firms that break the embargo or back armed groups. Eritrea must pull its troops back, open talks with Djibouti, and share news of missing Djiboutian soldiers.
un-sc-res-207: Numbered 207 in the Council's sequence, this resolution is catalogued as a 1965 entry in the United Nations official record. Formal decisions of this sort guide UN staff, peacekeeping forces, and governments in the years that follow. What is preserved is the exact formal wording, transcribed on English Wikisource from the official record of the Council. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-307: For the year 1971, the catalog lists Resolution 307 among the Security Council's formal decisions. The Council's fifteen members vote on draft texts, and adopted ones enter the record as numbered resolutions. The library holds the complete text in the form transcribed for English Wikisource from the official UN record. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-407: Entry number 407 in the Council's official sequence is a resolution the catalog dates to 1976. Council texts of this kind carry weight under the UN Charter, since the Council holds the main duty for peace and security. The entry gives the decision in full, as transcribed on English Wikisource from the records of the United Nations. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-607: As number 607 in the Council's series, the resolution is catalogued in this library under 1987. The Council's fifteen members vote on draft texts, and adopted ones enter the record as numbered resolutions. The library holds the complete text in the form transcribed for English Wikisource from the official UN record. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Tension along the Egypt-Israel armistice line drew the Council in during 1955. On 30 March, it adopted Resolution 107 without dissent. Cross-border raids and infiltration had strained the 1949 armistice deal. The UN truce chief of staff had reported on the line's state. He had also floated concrete steps to calm it.

The text asks him to keep consulting both governments. The goal is practical steps that guard safety in the area. It calls on Egypt and Israel to work with him on his plans. His view is recorded in the text. Infiltration could drop to a rare nuisance if the two sides agreed. The fragile calm defended here broke down in the Suez war a year later.

On the Prevlaka peninsula, a narrow strip claimed by both Croatia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, United Nations observers kept watch over a demilitarized zone. Their mission, UNMOP, is the subject of this text from 13 July 2000. The ground itself was calm, even though no one had settled who owned the land.

The Council left the observers in place and noted that crossing points in the zone let people and goods move both ways without trouble. Still, it flagged breaches of the demilitarization rules and limits placed on the observers' movement. Both sides were urged back to talks, to settle the dispute under their 1996 agreement on normal relations.

Weapons kept flowing into Somalia a decade after its embargo began. Warlords and dealers ignored the 1992 arms ban. Resolution 1407, adopted unanimously on 3 May 2002, took a first step toward real enforcement. It followed a presidential statement that March. The sanctions committee's chairman was about to tour the region.

The Secretary-General had one month to form a small expert team. Two members would serve for thirty days. Their job was drafting a detailed action plan. It would map the skills needed to document embargo violations by land, air, and sea. States had sixty days to report their enforcement steps. A full expert panel was expected to follow.

Resolution 1507, adopted unanimously on 12 September 2003, presses Ethiopia and Eritrea to finish making peace. The two countries had signed the Algiers Agreements in 2000, and a boundary commission had ruled on their disputed border in April 2002, a decision both accepted as final and binding. Marking the border on the ground, though, was falling behind schedule.

The Council kept the UN mission in Ethiopia and Eritrea, UNMEE, deployed in support of the process, extending its mandate into March 2004. It stressed that demarcation had to move quickly while calm held in the areas the ruling touched. Running a large mission while demarcation stalled cost money at a time of growing demands on peacekeeping, a frustration the text states openly.

Liberia's diamond ban alone is renewed in Resolution 1607, adopted on 21 June 2005. The Panel of Experts found no illegal timber exports, but few forestry reforms had been made. Unlicensed diamond mining and illegal exports were rising. One company had quietly been granted exclusive mining rights. The transitional government still lacked authority over the diamond and timber areas.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the diamond measures of Resolution 1521 (2003) for six months. The arms, travel, and timber measures continue to 21 December 2005 under the earlier renewal. It urges Liberia to take control of the diamond areas. It urges it to build a transparent Certificate of Origin regime toward joining the Kimberley Process. It also urges it to reform the Forestry Development Authority on the Forest Concession Review's lines. The Panel of Experts is re-established until 21 December 2005, reporting by 7 December 2005.

Resolution 1707, passed on 12 September 2006, keeps the world force in Afghanistan for one more year. The force, ISAF, had grown from a Kabul guard to a land-wide shield. Afghans hold the chief charge for law and order in their land. Gains in safety, state craft, and growth stand or fall as one, the Council said. The same held for the fight on drugs. The London pact of that year bound Afghan and world work in one frame.

The force won twelve more months, to October 2007. The stock lines frame the grant. The Council backs the land's unity and its free choice of rule. It backs the drive to root out terror. It praises the close work of Kabul and the force. The grant came as Taliban raids grew sharp once more.

Congo's sanctions are renewed, with the embargo refocused on armed groups, in Resolution 1807, adopted on 31 March 2008. The Group of Experts had traced the illicit weapons flow, and the Nairobi communiqué and the January 2008 Goma conference had moved the eastern peace process forward.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the arms, transport, financial, and travel measures until 31 December 2008. The arms embargo now binds supplies to non-governmental entities and individuals in Congo and no longer applies to supplies for the Congolese government. Other shipments for Congo must be notified to the sanctions Committee in advance, with end-user and delivery details. Aviation and customs controls on the Ituri and Kivu borders continue. The travel ban and asset freeze apply to Committee designees. They include embargo violators, foreign armed-group leaders blocking repatriation, militia leaders blocking disarmament, and those recruiting children.

Eritrea is placed under sanctions in Resolution 1907, adopted on 23 December 2009. The Monitoring Group found Eritrea gave political, financial, and logistical support to armed groups destabilizing Somalia. Eritrea had not withdrawn its forces after the June 2008 clashes with Djibouti at Ras Doumeira as Resolution 1862 (2009) demanded. The African Union's Sirte assembly called for sanctions.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council imposes an arms embargo on Eritrea in both directions, with cargo inspection and seizure. It adds a travel ban, asset freeze, and arms-supply ban on Committee-designated individuals and entities, including Eritrea's political and military leadership and parastatal entities. It demands Eritrea withdraw to the status quo ante, acknowledge and negotiate the border dispute with Djibouti, and give information on Djiboutian combatants missing since June 2008. It demands that Eritrea stop arming or supporting groups such as al-Shabaab that undermine Somalia's Transitional Federal Government.

Tension rose again in Cyprus in the summer of 1965, and the Council answered on 10 August 1965. Resolution 207 was adopted unanimously after new reports warned the island had become less calm. The text reaffirms Resolution 186 of 1964, the decision that created the United Nations peacekeeping force in Cyprus. It then calls on all parties to avoid any action that is likely to make the situation worse. That is the whole content: the text backs the earlier decision in full and tells everyone to hold back.

The war between India and Pakistan was ending in December 1971 when the Council adopted Resolution 307 on 21 December. A cease-fire had taken hold in the west from 17 December. India had declared it first, and Pakistan had then agreed. The Council had heard statements from both governments.

The Council demanded that a durable cease-fire be strictly kept in every area of conflict. The stop to all hostilities had to hold until armed forces withdrew to their own territory. In Jammu and Kashmir, the lines of the cease-fire line had to be respected. The Geneva Conventions were to be applied in full. That covered the wounded, prisoners of war, and civilians. The Council also called for international help to relieve suffering and to return refugees to their homes in safety and dignity.

Lesotho still bore the cost of its stand against the Transkei in the spring of 1977. South Africa kept up its pressure on the small country. A mission sent under Resolution 402 had now assessed the aid Lesotho needed. Resolution 407, adopted on 25 May 1977, carries that support forward.

The Council praised Lesotho's refusal to recognize the so-called independent Transkei once more. The Secretary-General was thanked for arranging the mission. The Council fully endorsed the mission's findings. It also endorsed his appeal to all states for immediate financial, technical, and material help. A special account had been opened to receive contributions for Lesotho, and that step was welcomed. United Nations agencies were told to keep assisting the country, and the Secretary-General had to keep the Council informed.

At the start of 1988, the first Palestinian uprising was under way in the lands held by Israel since 1967. Israel had announced that it would go on deporting Palestinian civilians from those lands. The Council had passed Resolution 605 on the matter the month before. Resolution 607 followed in early January 1988.

The Council said again that the Fourth Geneva Convention covers the lands held since 1967. That pact protects civilians in time of war, and Jerusalem is part of it. Israel was called on to stop the deportations at once. It was firmly told to obey the pact in full. The Council kept the matter under review, so it stayed open for further action.
vivekananda-complete-works-vol1-1907:
Swami Vivekananda carried Hindu thought to America and Europe in the 1890s, most famously at the Chicago Parliament of Religions. The first volume of his Complete Works, published in 1907 after his death, gathers his core teaching books. Karma Yoga and Raja Yoga stand at its head.

Karma Yoga teaches work without selfish grasping as a path to freedom, while Raja Yoga trains the mind through breath and focus. Lectures from his Western tours fill out the volume with talks on Vedanta for new hearers. These pages brought Vedanta, the philosophy of the Upanishads, to the West in a living voice.
wallace-is-mars-habitable-1907:
Alfred Russel Wallace, who found the law of natural selection with Darwin, turned his keen mind to Mars in this book of 1907. He wrote it to test Lowell's famed canal claims. Wallace was in his eighties, and his hand had lost none of its force.

With maths and physics he shows Mars to be too cold, too dry, and too thin of air for life. The canals, he holds, are a trick of the eye at the edge of sight. The book gave the canal scheme its death writ from a voice none could brush off.
wharton-fruit-of-the-tree-1907:
Edith Wharton published The Fruit of the Tree in 1907, two years after The House of Mirth made her famous. Wharton turned from drawing rooms to a New England mill town. The novel joins her interest in reform with a hard moral question about mercy and death.

Justine Brent, a trained nurse, cares for Bessy Westmore, the mill owner's wife, after a riding accident leaves her paralyzed and suffering. Bessy's husband, John Amherst, dreams of reforming his mills but is trapped by money and marriage. When Justine ends Bessy's pain with an overdose, love and guilt poison everything after. Wharton weighs industrial reform against private morality with unusual severity. Few of her novels end so darkly.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol07:
The seventh volume of the Journal of Discourses appeared at Liverpool in 1860, on the eve of America's Civil War. Its sermons, reported in shorthand, come from Brigham Young and the leading elders of the church. They preach to settlers in Utah while converts abroad read the same words in print.

A reader finds core teachings restated, sharpened, and aimed at the troubles of the hour. The Journal served as both pulpit and archive, fixing spoken doctrine before it could drift. Volume VII holds its place in that archive, part of the fullest sermon record any American faith produced.
young-lectures-natural-philosophy-vol1-1:
Thomas Young delivered his Course of Lectures on Natural Philosophy at the Royal Institution in London, and the first volume appeared in print in 1807. Young was a physician and scholar of rare range, at home in physics, languages, and the study of the eye. The lectures aimed to survey the whole of physical science for a general audience.

Volume one moves through motion, machines, fluids, sound, and light, with plates and a rich list of sources. Here Young set out his wave view of light and the tests with split beams that made his name. Few single works cover so much ground so clearly, and science historians treat it as a landmark.
young-lectures-natural-philosophy-vol2-1:
Thomas Young was an English polymath known for work on light, sound, and language. Volume 2 of his Course of Lectures on Natural Philosophy appeared in 1807. The lectures sum up what he taught on the physical world at the time.

Light holds a central place here, with Young's case for its wave-like nature. Sound, heat, and moving bodies get the same close, clear treatment. Young ran the famed double-slit test that backed his claims on light. Readers meet a mind that seemed to know each science at once, teaching the whole field in one sweeping course.
zohar-de-pauly-french-vol-2-1907:
Jean de Pauly's French Zohar reached its second tome in 1907. The Zohar itself, the Book of Splendor, is the chief text of the Kabbalah. It is cast as the talks of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and his companions on the road in Galilee. Its Aramaic pages read the Torah as the secret body of God.

Through its long commentary on the weekly portions, the work unfolds the ten sefirot and the balance of mercy and judgment. It traces the fate of souls through exile and return. De Pauly's six-tome French version, finished in 1911, is the only complete rendering in the public domain. English readers who want the whole Zohar still depend on it. This tome carries the commentary forward.
